Declarack is a configurable administration framework with Docker and Swarm as its most complete integrations. It does not claim full Portainer parity, notification delivery, distributed scheduling or SSO/RBAC. See current coverage for the exact boundaries.

items.title: Working on Declarack
items.text: Declarack is a configurable administration framework. Docker Swarm is its first full management application; standalone Docker, SSH hosts and HTTP APIs are also supported. SwarmDeck and swarmpit are historical names. Use Declarack for new product-facing text.

items.title: Start with the source of truth
items.text:
• Check the current branch, working tree and applicable instructions before edits. Preserve unrelated changes and follow the user's current Git/publishing instructions.
  • Read ARCHITECTURE.md for boundaries and docs/CODE_ORGANIZATION.md for module ownership and checks.
  • For configuration work, use CONFIG_SKILL.md. The implemented schema and execution code take precedence over aspirational architecture notes.
  • Distinguish shipped workflows from capabilities merely possible through custom operations. Record material limitations in the relevant maintained documentation.

items.title: Architecture and implementation
items.text:
• Keep the core generic. Resource-specific connections, execution, validation and coordination belong in adapters discovered under backend/adapters/.
  • Describe navigation, columns, mappings, forms, details, actions and layouts in feature/operation YAML. Use JSONata for result mapping. Add React behavior only when it is a reusable renderer capability; avoid Docker/Swarm-specific JSX.
  • A feature belongs to a target. Environments group targets and reference pages; pages can query multiple targets. Settings and authentication are installation-wide.
  • Keep backend modules cohesive and pass explicit collaborators. Organize frontend code by feature and reuse shared UI, table and workflow components. Avoid duplicate implementations, forwarding-only modules and splits driven solely by file length.
  • Do not add compatibility layers without a concrete requirement. When changing a contract, update its callers, examples, documentation and relevant tests together.
  • Keep runtime dependencies intentional. Development/build tools stay out of the runtime image. When reporting image size, distinguish compressed from local size.

items.title: Execution and deployment invariants
items.text:
• Swarm mode connects to a manager. Node-local work uses short-lived Swarm jobs from the controller's image. Swarm workflows never SSH into individual workers. Manager SSH tunnels and SSH Git sources are separate from worker execution.
  • Make manager-engine, selected-node and cluster-wide scope explicit. A working worker terminal does not make every Docker resource/action cluster-wide.
  • Metrics are on demand unless the user explicitly configures scheduled behavior.
  • Preserve preview/digest/version checks for reviewed writes and deployments. Configuration saves and activation are separate; restoring history loads a draft. The database owns active configuration; files are import/write-back sources. Preserve explicit FORCE_LOAD/WRITE_BACK behavior and recovery journal ordering.
  • Prefer dedicated resource/detail/edit pages. Use confirmation dialogs for destructive actions and preserve navigation grouping and visual hierarchy.
  • Keep Git and registry authentication separate. Prefer mounted credential-file references; preserve target isolation, ephemeral CLI auth and documented source persistence. Saved metadata and runtime history still require persistent storage.
  • Use disposable, clearly identified fixtures for live mutation tests. Preserve existing workloads and clean up only resources created by that test.

items.title: Verification and documentation
items.text:
Storage changes must pass the shared SQLite/PostgreSQL contracts using a disposable database; see storage verification.

Run checks appropriate to the change; install development dependencies only when needed. The complete application checks, from the repository root, are:

.venv/bin/ruff check backend tools
npm --prefix frontend run lint
npm --prefix frontend run format:check
.venv/bin/python -m unittest discover -s backend/tests
npm --prefix frontend test
npm --prefix frontend run test:views
npm --prefix frontend run build

See code organization for dependency setup and the runnable tutorial check. For docs, install docs/requirements.txt in a suitable environment and run python tools/docs.py build; it validates local links and anchors. Changes to snippets must validate with their documented prerequisites and remain shared between the app and generated docs.

Verify changed UI flows in a browser. Integration execution changes also need the relevant live workflow when a suitable lab is available: unit tests cannot prove worker helper startup, registry pulls, tunnel reachability or terminal transport. Report what was actually tested and any unverified scope. Documentation-only changes need relevant link/example validation, not an unrelated Docker rebuild.

Keep session ports, passwords, temporary paths, test totals and work logs out of this file. Put durable behavior and setup instructions in maintained docs.

items.title: Declarack adapter architecture
items.text:
For the implemented configuration schema and operational behavior, see the system configuration guide. The main YAML configures the system, including its dashboard presentation. This architecture document also contains adoption goals; the guide distinguishes those from current behavior.

Declarack is a configurable administration framework with Docker Swarm as its first full application. The same Python backend and React frontend can connect to a standalone Docker engine, an SSH host, or a generic upstream HTTP API. Adapters ship in the same production image. The dashboard can discover additional adapter packages from an operator-mounted directory when it starts.

items.title: Repository layout
items.text:
• backend/ contains the Python application, built-in adapters and their YAML definitions, the worker entry point, and backend tests.
  • frontend/ contains the React renderer, shared workflow controls, styles, and Vite package files.
  • The repository root contains deployment files, dependencies for the Python backend, and example configuration.

items.title: What goes where
items.text:
Layer Owns Core Authentication, configuration loading, target resolution, operation validation and dispatch, and consistent results and errors Adapters Connections and reusable execution behavior such as Docker socket requests, SSH commands, HTTP requests, and short-lived Swarm jobs Operation definitions Named calls, typed arguments, request or command configuration, result format, and supported execution scopes Feature definitions Navigation, routes, tables, forms, metrics cards, actions, and JSONata display mappings Deployment configuration Config storage selection, target addresses, enabled features, adapter directory, and references to mounted credentials

An adapter implements a reusable mechanism. Adding a new list or inspect operation that uses an existing mechanism usually means adding configuration. Adding a new connection type or a workflow that needs coordination means adding adapter code.

items.title: Adapter discovery
items.text:
Each adapter occupies one directory with a manifest and a Python entry point. The image includes the built-in packages under /app/backend/adapters. Operators can mount an optional read-only directory at /etc/declarack/adapters for additional packages.

adapters/
  docker/
    adapter.yaml
    adapter.py
  swarm/
    adapter.yaml
    adapter.py
  ssh/
    adapter.yaml
    adapter.py
  http/
    adapter.yaml
    adapter.py

Example manifest for the Swarm adapter:

id: swarm
api_version: 1
entrypoint: adapter.py:register
depends_on: [docker]

At startup, the core reads the manifests, checks their IDs and interface versions, then loads adapters in dependency order. Each entry point registers the connection types and execution methods it supplies, along with schemas for their configuration. The core validates the target, operation, and feature definitions against that registry before serving the application. Duplicate IDs, missing dependencies, unsupported versions, and unknown references are startup errors that name the affected package or config entry.

An adapter can also bundle operation and feature definitions. Its manifest lists those files by path relative to the package directory. Discovery makes the definitions available, and the installation config chooses which features to enable on each target. A package that registers only a connection or executor can be used by definitions supplied elsewhere in the deployment.

To add an adapter, put its directory under one of the discovery roots, make its dependencies available in the image if it has any, reference its registered connection or execution method in config, and restart the dashboard. The core and generic UI renderer require no changes. Feature definitions can use the shared UI components. A bespoke React page still needs a frontend build.

Adapter Python runs inside the dashboard process with its credentials and connection permissions. Treat an adapter directory like application code and restrict who can modify it. The Settings UI edits supported target settings. Top-level operation, feature, authentication, and legacy-workspace changes happen through deployment; see the configuration guide for the exact restriction. Adapter installation also happens through deployment.

The initial implementation includes Docker socket, Swarm node jobs, SSH, and HTTP adapters. Stack, config, and secret views use the same renderer as other features. Use legacy_workspace to associate an existing database and bookmarks with one configured Swarm target. See README.md for deployment switches.

items.title: Connections and operations
items.text:
A target defines where a request goes. An operation defines what happens there. The names a feature invokes exist only when the loaded operation definitions register them.

targets:
  production:
    connection: docker_socket
    socket: /var/run/docker.sock
    swarm: true
    agent_image: registry.example.com/declarack:0.3
    features:
    - services
    - volumes
    - host_metrics
  lab:
    connection: docker_socket
    socket: /run/docker-lab.sock
    features:
    - volumes
    - networks
  backup:
    connection: ssh
    host: backup.example.com
    features:
    - host_metrics
    credential: ssh_backup
  inventory:
    connection: http
    base_url: https://inventory.example.com
    features:
    - asset_inventory
    credential: token_inventory
auth:
  provider: local
  bootstrap_credential: declarack_login
  session_hours: 8
credentials:
  ssh_backup:
    type: ssh
    username: dashboard
    private_key:
      file: /run/secrets/backup_ssh_key
    known_hosts:
      file: /etc/declarack/known_hosts
  token_inventory:
    type: token
    token:
      file: /run/secrets/inventory_token
  declarack_login:
    type: basic
    username: admin
    password:
      file: /run/secrets/declarack_admin_password

An operation can have more than one binding. Here, volumes.list uses a node-local collector on Swarm and an engine request on standalone Docker.

# operations/volumes.yaml
operations:
  volumes.list:
    bindings:
      docker_swarm:
        executor: swarm.exec
        inputs:
          node_id: {type: string}
        all_nodes: true
        command: [python, -m, backend.adapters.docker.node_agent, volumes]
        mount_profile: docker_socket
        output: agent_json
      docker_standalone:
        executor: docker.volumes
        operation: volumes

A Docker socket target with swarm: true selects the docker_swarm binding and must reach a manager. Other Docker socket targets select docker_standalone. An operation call identifies the target, the operation, and its declared inputs. The core selects the matching binding before dispatch.

An upstream integration can use the same model with an HTTP target and a request binding. The trusted config supplies the origin, credentials, method, and route. Calls supply typed values for declared fields. Request runners encode path segments and query values. Command runners pass declared arguments to the configured executable. SSH verifies host keys and quotes remote command arguments. The dashboard does not forward credentials across HTTP redirects to a different origin.

Multiple bindings for an operation should expose a documented shared result shape. The volume collectors return name, driver, and local container attachments on both targets. Swarm adds node identity. All-node results wrap the individual responses so the view can report partial failures.

items.title: Swarm behavior
items.text:
Swarm uses the manager's Docker socket for all cluster access. An inspect operation is a direct request. An exec operation scoped to a Swarm node uses the same connection to start a short-lived job pinned to that node. The job runs from the dashboard image, emits structured output to stdout, and exits. The manager reads the task logs and removes the job. Worker operations have no SSH fallback or network callback.

An explicit All nodes request takes a snapshot of the selected nodes and fans out with bounded concurrency. The runner returns one result or error per node, including unavailable nodes. The feature can flatten successful results into a table or calculate a summary while showing how many nodes reported. Volume writes stay scoped to one node. If a write times out and its outcome is uncertain, refresh the affected node's state before retrying.

Keep coordination in reusable code. Swarm owns job placement and cleanup, version-aware service and node updates, and stack deployment through the manager. Simple inventory requests belong in operation config. Stack workflows can call code for Git checkout, preview validation, and deployment.

items.title: Views, state, and settings
items.text:
Feature definitions tie operations to routes and shared UI components. For example, Volumes declares an inventory table, a node selector on Swarm, and create and remove actions. JSONata can transform rows or compute totals. Resource IDs, action inputs, and authorization remain independently validated by the backend. Details and creation forms retain their own URLs.

Metrics are on demand for every target. Opening a view launches no collector. An explicit request can sample counters briefly and return one snapshot. Keep snapshots in memory with their timestamps. Swarm and SSH can expose the same host metrics page by returning the same fields.

The database owns the saved and active system configuration revisions. Files, folders, Git and Swarm configs supply import/publication sources. Sources seed an empty database; subsequent startup loads its active revision unless DECLARACK_CONFIG_FORCE_LOAD=1. Local DECLARACK_CONFIG_WRITE_BACK=1 publishes documents with recovery journaling before activation. See configuration storage. Source providers retain these publication mechanisms:

Storage Apply behavior Mounted file Atomically replace a validated file and retain the previous revision Git Open a pull request and apply the merged revision through deployment Swarm config Create a versioned config and update the dashboard service to mount it at the same path

Validate the expected revision before saving. Prefer mounted secrets for credential values; inline profile values also persist in configuration history and exports. A Swarm config can reference an already mounted secret for first-administrator bootstrap. Swarm config storage manages the system configuration, not all application state. GUI-managed sources, legacy encrypted PATs/keys, checks and history use the shared SQLAlchemy persistence service: SQLite by default or PostgreSQL. Adapters use namespaced documents; Compose inline files are reconstructed locally. Persist the selected database. See storage for explicit upgrade/import and execution boundaries. A fully stateless source-management mode remains an architectural goal.

items.title: Adoption
items.text:
1. Introduce the adapter registry and extract Networks as the first configured feature. Prove the same network view works on a Swarm manager and a standalone Docker engine.
  2. Extract Volumes and Host Metrics. Verify direct engine calls, node-pinned jobs, explicit fan-out, and SSH collection with a shared metrics response. Confirm that opening a metrics page launches no work.
  3. Migrate the remaining Swarm features and prove a generic upstream HTTP integration by adding its adapter and config without changing core code. Preserve the existing single-manager setup and bookmarks during the migration.
  4. Add the Settings storage adapters and test config conflicts, reload, rollback, and mounted-secret authentication. Run live smoke tests with a Swarm manager and worker, a standalone engine, and a Linux SSH host. Measure the production image against the 50 MB compressed target.

items.title: Current implementation boundaries
items.text:
The application composition in backend/server.py installs settings, operation and check endpoints, static assets and the backend/auth/http.py cookie/CSRF boundary. backend/auth/store.py owns database administrators, bootstrap, password hashes, sessions and login limits. backend/serving.py owns the Cheroot listener, native TLS and explicit immediate-proxy trust. Docker/Swarm services are grouped under backend/adapters/docker/ and backend/adapters/swarm/. The runtime module composes those services, and legacy_routes.py adapts old URLs to them. Node helper commands live in backend/adapters/docker/node_agent.py. Adapters do not call back into the HTTP server to perform resource operations.

Resource selectors map lookup responses through JSONata. Terminal fields come from operation input schemas, while backend/terminal_sessions.py manages bounded PTY sessions with adapter-supplied commands and ownership scopes. Docker exec, Swarm worker relays and SSH host sessions implement that same contract. File views consume a file-tree response with provider-advertised limits; adapters choose the root and execution location. String identifier constraints and navigation icons are explicit configuration rather than resource-name branches in core.

See generic capabilities for schemas and the pre-release configuration changes.

See code organization and development checks for module responsibilities and the contributor verification commands.

items.title: Installation identity and transport
items.text:
Local database administrators are independent of target credential profiles and YAML configuration revisions. auth.provider is local; an optional bootstrap_credential basic profile seeds only the first account when no users exist. Otherwise bootstrap uses DECLARACK_ADMIN_USERNAME and a password file or environment value. Existing accounts ignore subsequent bootstrap secret changes. session_hours defaults to 8 (1–168). All administrators have full installation, credential and workload access; environment grouping is not a permission boundary. There are no granular roles, teams or SSO, and HTTP Basic Auth is unsupported.

Passwords use scrypt hashes; opaque session tokens are stored as hashes in the database. The HTTP layer requires cookies and action/CSRF headers for authenticated writes. Cookies are HttpOnly/SameSite=Lax and Secure when HTTPS is observed. Account writes revalidate the actual session hash under the database account lock after password hashing, so revoked sessions cannot finish queued account writes. Account mutations record secret-free events in generic documents under framework.auth.audit (newest 1,000 retained; activity API returns newest 100). Actors identify the administrator or bootstrap/host operator. Operation-plan metadata.actor records request identity, preserved through ContextVar propagation in batch fan-out. Bounded account events and plan metadata are not a complete generic resource audit log; direct calls do not all produce recorded plans. Demo bypasses login and does not expose account management.

Native TLS accepts mounted PEM files or persisted self-signed identity under <DECLARACK_DATA>/tls; it is separate from database transfer. There is one listener, startup-only certificate loading, and no ACME, automatic renewal or redirect listener. Explicit trusted proxy IPs/CIDRs permit one forwarded proto/client hop, never forwarded host/prefix. See administrators, recovery and TLS.

items.title: Configure Declarack
items.text: Produce a configuration that matches the user's installed Declarack version and actual targets, with clear prerequisites and a verified save/apply workflow. This file is a portable agent instruction document: ask an assistant to read it before setting up configuration. It does not require a particular AI product. If a skill loader requires a directory entrypoint, copy this file into that skill's SKILL.md; keep its frontmatter and instructions together.

items.title: Configuration authority
items.text: The database holds saved and active configuration revisions. Files seed an empty installation; later external edits require explicit import or startup DECLARACK_CONFIG_FORCE_LOAD=1. GUI save and activation are separate. Optional DECLARACK_CONFIG_WRITE_BACK=1 publishes local files before activation; otherwise GUI edits do not change import files. Both flags default to off. Use the current storage contract for source imports, publication, recovery and backup requirements.

items.title: Credentials
items.text: Use top-level credentials profiles for connection credentials and optional first-administrator bootstrap, including file references. Login accounts live in the database separately from YAML. Targets/tunnels select credential; registries map hostnames to basic profile IDs; Git uses an allowed ID list. Do not emit removed target fields identity_file, known_hosts_file, user, bearer_token_file, or target-local credential objects. See the schema.

items.title: Locate the relevant references
items.text:
When a checkout is available, use its maintained files and adapter definitions. Otherwise use the linked repository references, matching the installed release rather than assuming main matches an older installation. If the files cannot be accessed, request the relevant configuration/schema instead of inventing fields.

Task Reference in this repository Schema, operation bindings, features, auth and storage docs/CONFIGURATION.md Folder merge, GUI editing, review, history and reload docs/CONFIG_FOLDERS.md Ready-made fragments and prerequisites configurations/snippets and its catalog.json Multi-target page layouts and JSONata context docs/CUSTOM_PAGES.md Environments, target grouping and scheduled checks docs/ENVIRONMENTS_AND_CHECKS.md Generic forms, dynamic selectors and workflows docs/FRAMEWORK_WORKFLOWS.md Git stack sources and registry credentials docs/REGISTRIES_AND_GIT_SOURCES.md Local administrators, session/CSRF clients and native/proxy TLS docs/USERS_AND_TLS.md Database setup and storage migration docs/STORAGE.md Runnable HTTP API tutorial examples/tutorial-api Built-in capabilities and executor contracts backend/adapters

Read only the references needed for the requested configuration. The app also provides Settings → Example snippets with search, categories, prerequisite links and Copy YAML. The documentation site publishes the same catalog.

items.title: Establish the inputs
items.text:
Inspect an existing config before proposing a replacement. Determine the intended connections, target IDs, enabled capabilities, environment/page placement and storage source. For an HTTP integration, obtain representative JSON responses and verified methods/paths for reads and actions. Identify container-visible socket, source, credential and SSH known-hosts paths; a host path is not automatically available inside Declarack.

Reuse supplied values and existing IDs. Ask for missing facts that affect correctness; for illustrative output, mark assumptions and placeholders plainly. Do not fetch credentials from unrelated accounts or treat example endpoints as real deployment destinations. Stay within the user's requested setup scope.

items.title: Choose the configuration layer
items.text:
• Deployment/bootstrap: container mounts, Docker socket, environment variables, Docker secrets, selected config path and data-volume persistence.
  • System YAML: targets, operations, features, environments, pages, checks, batches, integration_templates and optional installation auth. At least one target is required.
  • Application source: a managed application's Compose YAML and its saved stack/project source. This is different from Declarack's own system config.
  • Runtime state: saved application-source metadata, checks, operation history and configuration revisions. Persist the selected database for those features (SQLite by default, or PostgreSQL).

Prefer a configuration folder for editable installations. DECLARACK_CONFIG selects one file or a recursively merged folder. Every fragment needs its root section wrapper; filenames do not imply sections. Visible .yaml/.yml files merge in case-sensitive relative-path order. Mappings merge recursively; lists, scalars and different types replace earlier values. Lists do not append. Duplicate keys within a YAML document are rejected. There is no include syntax, deletion marker or automatic environment interpolation in system YAML.

Use numbered filenames and dependencies from the snippet catalog as a starting point. When overriding an existing list, supply the complete desired list. Do not concatenate examples that repeat root keys into one document; keep separate files or explicitly merge their mappings. Do not point the application at the entire example catalog: it contains alternative configurations and incomplete fragments.

items.title: Assemble targets and presentation
items.text:
1. Choose the supported connection: docker_socket for Docker/Swarm, ssh for host operations, or http for an upstream API. Explicit Docker targets use swarm: true or false to choose mode. Inspect built-in YAML for feature IDs available on that provider. Docker standalone has no native Swarm configs/secrets.
  2. Reuse built-in features before defining custom ones. A custom feature names an inventory operation, JSONata rows/columns and optional details/forms/actions; the target enables it in its features list. Custom IDs must not collide with built-ins. New execution mechanisms require adapter work, not invented YAML.
  3. An operation selects a registered executor in a provider binding, with declared inputs and execution definitions. Feature/action bindings pass inputs to named operations. Use the installed schema for allowed request fields and validation.
  4. Environments group target IDs; they do not own the targets' feature definitions. Explicit grouping can leave check-only targets outside environment navigation. Settings and auth remain top-level. Navigation visibility is not authorization.
  5. A custom page defines named sources referring to enabled read operations on specific targets. Page expressions receive data.<source-name> results; feature expressions receive that feature's result/rows. Inspect actual response envelopes before mapping. Action-only operations cannot become page read sources.
  6. Place pages through environments.<id>.pages; set environments.root.pages explicitly to control home placement. top_level is no longer supported. On-demand/manual sources remain explicit collection actions; opening a dashboard should not silently launch node metrics.

items.title: Minimal HTTP integration example
items.text:
This is a complete system-config example assuming GET /items returns {"items":[{"id":"one","name":"Example","status":"running"}]}. Replace the reserved .invalid address with the real API. No connection is tested by this example, and it adds no writes or scheduled work.

targets:
  example_api:
    label: Example API
    connection: http
    base_url: https://api.example.invalid
    features: [example.items]
operations:
  example.items.list:
    bindings:
      http:
        executor: http.request
        path: /items
features:
  example.items:
    title: Items
    group: Applications
    operation: example.items.list
    rows: items
    columns:
      - {label: Name, value: name}
      - label: Status
        value: status
        badges: {running: active, stopped: muted}
environments:
  example:
    label: Example environment
    targets: [example_api]
pages:
  example-summary:
    title: Example summary
    sources:
      inventory:
        target: example_api
        operation: example.items.list
    cards:
      - label: Items
        value: $count(data.inventory.items)

Read the linked workflow and page guides before extending this with forms, mutations, related resources, bulk actions or dynamic lookup operations. Add confirmed actions with appropriate labels/icons only for verified API behavior.

items.title: Credentials, scheduling and Swarm scope
items.text:
Prefer credential references to mounted files or Docker secrets. Installation auth uses auth: {provider: local, bootstrap_credential: PROFILE, session_hours: 8}; the basic profile reference is optional and seeds only the first administrator when users are empty. Otherwise use DECLARACK_ADMIN_USERNAME (default admin) and either DECLARACK_PASSWORD_FILE or DECLARACK_PASSWORD. Existing users ignore bootstrap secret changes; use Administrators or host recovery to reset passwords. Do not emit removed auth.provider: basic or auth.credential; clients must use login cookies and CSRF/action headers. All administrators have full installation access. Inline bootstrap values remain in configuration history and exports. Native TLS is configured through deployment environment variables, not YAML; persist generated /data/tls files even with PostgreSQL and configure explicit proxy trust for HTTPS termination. There is no ACME or automatic renewal. Supported Docker targets have separate registry_credentials and git_credentials mappings. Git access and image-registry access are distinct. Registry profiles match image hostnames; Git profiles match host and transport. Select a configured Git profile in the Swarm stack editor. Read the source guide for persistence and current Git/Compose limitations rather than assuming parity between source modes.

For SSH, mount the identity and known-hosts files. Swarm uses a manager socket or manager tunnel and short-lived jobs for worker-local work; it never SSHs into workers. Downloaded repository files do not provision bind-mount paths on workers.

Add checks only when scheduled behavior is requested. A check refers to a target and optionally an eligible read/check-safe operation, with healthy JSONata, interval and failure/recovery thresholds. A connector check omits the operation. Loading/reloading checks starts their schedules; results need persistent storage. Checks are not automatic GitOps deployment or a complete notification-routing system. Batches expose explicit multi-target operations; use the batch schema for inputs, results and confirmations rather than inventing a per-target loop in JSX.

items.title: Validate and apply
items.text:
Validate the complete merged config, not just each fragment's YAML syntax. In a checkout with dependencies installed, a non-applying validation can use:

.venv/bin/python - /path/to/config-or-folder <<'PY'
import sys
from pathlib import Path
from backend.server import load_dashboard
config = load_dashboard(Path(sys.argv[1]))
print(f"Valid configuration: {len(config.targets)} targets")
PY

Use an environment with the required mounted files for configurations that refer to credentials or SSH identities. Report missing paths rather than bypassing validation. Schema validation does not prove connection reachability or JSONata mapping correctness against real responses; verify those separately with read operations and sample data. For catalog edits, run python -m unittest backend.tests.test_configuration_snippets in the project Python environment. Do not start a full application test suite for ordinary operator YAML edits unless its scope makes that useful.

In an editable folder installation, a writable config mount and DECLARACK_CONFIG_EDIT=1 enable GUI edits and new files. Use Review & save file or Review new file to validate and inspect source/effective merged diffs, then Save file. Reload configuration separately applies the saved source. Test all connections checks reachability without saving or applying. Auth and legacy-workspace changes can require restart. Local history restores one file to a draft, not an atomic whole-folder rollback. Single-file, Git-backed and Swarm-config-backed stores have different edit/publication limits; use the installed provider's documented flow.

Return the exact filenames/YAML or minimal patch, required mounts/credential references, validated assumptions and steps to apply. State what was actually validated, which connections were tested, and whether changes were only drafted, saved or applied. Preserve existing unrelated definitions and runtime workloads.

items.title: Declarack
items.text:
Connections select reusable credential profiles, managed through Settings → Credentials. Paste/upload a value or reference a mounted file; both use the same named configuration model.

Configuration is database-managed: files seed the first startup, GUI edits are reviewed and saved, and Activate configuration makes a saved revision active. Optional DECLARACK_CONFIG_FORCE_LOAD=1 imports files at each startup; DECLARACK_CONFIG_WRITE_BACK=1 writes them before GUI activation. Both default to off. See storage and configuration ownership.

Administration interfaces, defined in configuration.

Declarack turns connections, operations, and YAML definitions into a working admin interface: searchable tables, dedicated detail pages, forms, confirmed actions, terminals, and environment summaries. Start with Docker and Swarm management, then bring your own HTTP APIs or SSH hosts into the same workspace.

Manage a homelab, operate a small Swarm, or assemble an internal administration portal without writing a new frontend for every integration.

  • One view across environments. See configured systems together, or define custom pages that query multiple targets and combine their results with JSONata, including charts, filterable tables and opt-in refresh.
  • Useful Docker management from day one. Manage Compose projects and Swarm stacks; inspect resources, read logs, open container terminals, and clean up storage. Edit or duplicate standalone containers with reviewed plans and retained backups.
  • Configuration-driven extensions. Define API operations, map results with JSONata, and reuse views and workflows across environments.
  • A small, modular core. Python backend, React UI, folder-discovered adapters, and on-demand node work. Swarm workers are reached through jobs, not SSH.

items.title: Documentation
items.text: Read the quickstart, follow the runnable API interface tutorial, or browse the configuration reference. To preview the complete searchable documentation website locally, see documentation development.

items.title: Start with a configuration
items.text:
Already running with a writable configuration folder? Open Targets → Add integration to generate and review a Docker, Swarm, SSH, Grafana, Prometheus or HTTP API configuration. Save it as a new YAML fragment, then reload.

Your use case Included starting point Standalone Docker / Compose apps Docker management Swarm services, stacks, and nodes Swarm management A custom page across Docker, Swarm, and monitoring Operations dashboard Local Docker plus a remote Swarm Multiple environments Linux host metrics SSH host Existing target health and alerts Prometheus Existing dashboard inventory Grafana Your own application API Complete custom application example

Docker/Swarm presets include management actions. Prometheus/Grafana presets are read-only integrations with existing services. See the configuration catalog for connection requirements, API/version notes, and instructions for combining them. The Docker image includes these presets at /app/configurations.

items.title: Try the complete multi-environment lab
items.text:
Run the real Docker-in-Docker lab: two Swarms with one manager and one worker each, running services, Grafana, Prometheus, and your host Docker engine, connected through direct access or SSH tunnels.

python3 examples/multi-environment/lab.py up --http-mode ssh

The lab GUI uses port 9080 and keeps the normal port-8080 installation separate. See the lab guide for generated credentials, host SSH commands, transport choices, and the complete five-target Declarack configuration.

items.title: Run locally
items.text:
From a checkout with Docker available:

export DECLARACK_PASSWORD='replace-with-a-strong-password'
docker compose up -d --build

Open Declarack and sign in as admin on the login page. The password seeds the first database administrator only; later environment changes do not rotate that account. Manage accounts under Settings → Administrators. The default setup detects a local Swarm manager or standalone Docker engine. To choose an explicit configuration, follow the catalog setup. No Docker/Swarm experience is required to configure an HTTP API integration, but you do need a reachable API and knowledge of its response shape.

The Compose service publishes to loopback and persists saved sources/credentials in its declarack-data volume. For remote access, use an SSH tunnel or a trusted HTTPS reverse proxy, or configure native TLS. See administrators, password recovery and TLS for bootstrap files, session/CSRF clients, certificate persistence and proxy trust. All administrators have full installation access. Docker socket access gives Declarack administrative control of the connected engine. Keep its data volume private and back it up.

Set DECLARACK_STACKS_DIR to a host directory for local stack sources; Compose mounts it read-only at /stacks. Use DOCKER_SOCKET for an alternate socket when running Python directly, and mount/select that socket explicitly in container deployments.

items.title: Make it your administration interface
items.text:
The system configuration controls environments, enabled capabilities, operation definitions, views, workflows, and authentication. It is broader than a dashboard layout. Existing adapters cover Docker, Swarm jobs, SSH, and HTTP; new execution mechanisms can be added as trusted adapter packages.

This is a configurable administration framework with Docker/Swarm as its most complete application. Config-defined charts and persisted scheduled checks are available. Visual chart builders, SSO/RBAC and outbound check notifications are not implemented; see health checks.

Upgrading from the previous product name? Read the rename guide before changing your Compose service or data-volume mapping.

items.title: Deploy stacks
items.text:
1. Open Stacks, create a stack or edit the source of an existing stack, and choose one source.
  2. Compose editor stores the YAML in Declarack.
  3. Mounted folder loads docker-compose.yml or docker-compose.yaml from a directory relative to the mounted source root. Enter . to use the root.
  4. Git repository (HTTPS / SSH) supports branches, tags and commit IDs across Git providers, with target-scoped credential references. See registry credentials and Git sources.
  5. GitHub tag loads the Compose path from an owner/repository and tag. For private repositories, enter a username and a PAT with read access to repository contents. Declarack stores the source metadata and encrypted PAT in its configured database. The Source page shows the saved repository, tag, Compose path, token status, and last deployed commit. A blank PAT retains the saved credential for the same repository and username. Clear the username to remove the saved credential.
  6. Save the source and preview it. For GitHub, the preview displays the exact commit. Use Validate to run docker stack config.
  7. Choose Deploy and confirm. Declarack checks the preview against the current Compose file and Git commit, then runs docker stack deploy. Check the stack’s service and task views while Swarm converges.

For an existing stack, choose Update in place to keep services absent from the reviewed file, Update and remove orphaned services to prune those services, or Replace stack to validate the Compose file, remove the deployed resources, and redeploy. Replace causes downtime and keeps volumes by default. Turn on Clear selected volumes during replacement to scan nodes and explicitly select volumes to delete. Only existing, stack-labeled local volumes referenced by the deployed services and declared under their default stack-scoped name in the reviewed source are eligible. External, shared-driver, and volumes attached to unrelated containers are excluded. Use the same updated image for Declarack and its node jobs. If the new deployment fails after removal, inspect the cluster and redeploy when the cause is resolved.

To tear down a deployed stack, open its Source page, choose Remove deployed stack, and confirm. Docker removes services and stack-owned networks, configs, and secrets. The saved source and volumes are retained. Preview and deploy the source to recreate the stack.

Deployments are manual. Updating a tag or a folder does not trigger a deployment. GitHub sources are bounded to 16 MiB compressed and 64 MiB extracted and support regular files and directories. Use stack files from trusted sources. Target-scoped registry credential files now support private image pulls, Compose up, Swarm stack deployment with worker authentication, and reviewed service edits. Bind mount paths in service definitions must exist on the target Swarm nodes.

items.title: Manage configs and secrets
items.text:
Use Configs or Secrets to create a resource from pasted text or a file of up to 500 KiB. The GUI displays references from running service definitions. To rotate a config or secret, create a new version, update your Compose source to use it, redeploy, and remove the old version after it has no service references. Reference Swarm resources as external: true in Compose and keep secret values out of Compose files. Docker Swarm returns metadata and usage for secrets after creation.

The dashboard also supports scaling services, node scheduling changes, and recent logs. A standalone engine or worker can display local container data and logs.

items.title: Demo and development
items.text:
For a backend-free playground, run npm run demo --prefix frontend after installing frontend dependencies. This serves the existing GUI with a browser-only simulated API. See static browser playground for free static hosting, supported workflows and limitations.

Run the demo directly from the production image:

docker build -t declarack .
docker run --rm -e DECLARACK_MODE=demo -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 declarack

The demo uses sample inventory and temporary data. For local development with Node 22.12+ and Python 3.12+, run:

npm --prefix frontend ci
npm --prefix frontend run build
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt
DECLARACK_MODE=demo .venv/bin/python -m backend.server

A local Docker CLI enables Compose validation in the demo. Networks with a private CA can pass a host CA bundle to Docker BuildKit with --secret id=build_ca,src=/path/to/ca-bundle.crt. This only affects dependency installation during the build.

items.title: Node jobs, volumes, and host metrics
items.text:
Build and publish this same image to a registry that the Swarm nodes can pull from. Set DECLARACK_AGENT_IMAGE to that image reference on the manager, preferably by digest. Use the same version for the dashboard and node jobs.

  • In Volumes, choose a node or all nodes and select Refresh volumes. Each result shows the node, volume driver, and local container attachments. Create a named local volume on a selected node or remove an unused volume. Docker enforces its own in-use checks. Removing a volume deletes its data.
  • To enable host metrics, set DECLARACK_HOST_METRICS=1 on the dashboard. Open Host metrics, select a node, and choose Collect to see CPU, memory, host disk, swap, network throughput, kernel, and uptime. Each snapshot shows its collection time. Disk capacity is measured on the filesystem containing /etc by default. Set DECLARACK_HOST_DISK_PATH to an absolute directory on a different node filesystem, such as the Docker data directory, to measure it instead.
  • Volume jobs mount the selected node’s Docker socket. If all worker sockets use an alternate path, set DECLARACK_WORKER_SOCKET to that host path. Metrics jobs use read-only Linux host mounts.
  • Jobs require a ready, active Linux node and a Docker Engine with support for replicated jobs. The manager pins each job by node ID, reads its JSON result via Docker task logs, and removes the job. A timed-out write can have an unknown outcome, so refresh the volume list before retrying. No inbound callback or persistent worker process is required.

items.title: Networks and detail pages
items.text:
Networks lists Swarm overlays and networks known to the connected Docker engine. Open a network to see its scope, driver, IPAM subnets, Swarm service references, and endpoints reported by that engine. Worker-local network inventory and network creation or removal are outside this view.

Resource details and creation forms have their own URLs. Use the back link or your browser history to return to the inventory.

items.title: Configured targets and adapters
items.text:
DECLARACK_CONFIG can point to one file or a folder. Folder YAML fragments merge into one system configuration; Settings can show each file and reload validated changes without rebuilding the application. Start with the folder example and merge/reload guide.

The main YAML is Declarack's system configuration: it controls connections, capabilities, execution definitions, UI presentation, and authentication. Read the complete configuration guide for schemas, examples, storage modes, edit restrictions, and runtime settings. A complete custom API example is included.

The original single-manager setup works without a config file. To use configured targets, start with dashboard.example.yaml, mount it as /etc/declarack/dashboard.yaml, and set DECLARACK_CONFIG=/etc/declarack/dashboard.yaml. Mount the sockets and credential files referenced by that config. Use auth: {provider: local, bootstrap_credential: login, session_hours: 8} with a named basic login profile referencing a mounted password file, or use DECLARACK_PASSWORD_FILE / DECLARACK_PASSWORD for first-account bootstrap. Existing provider: basic / credential configuration must migrate to local / bootstrap_credential; HTTP Basic Auth clients must use login cookies and CSRF/action headers. Accounts are stored separately from YAML.

The example enables standalone Docker. Add a Swarm manager, an SSH host, or an upstream HTTP API as another target. Swarm never uses SSH to reach workers. SSH host metrics require python3 on the remote Linux host and an OpenSSH-format identity readable by the dashboard. Enable stacks, configs, and secrets in each applicable Swarm target. The same YAML renderer serves configured targets and single-manager installs. Use legacy_workspace: <swarm-target-id> to associate pre-existing saved stacks and bookmark routes with that target. Other targets keep source records in separate logical database scopes. SQLite is the default; PostgreSQL is optional. See storage and migration.

The app discovers built-in adapters in /app/backend/adapters and additional packages in /etc/declarack/adapters or DECLARACK_ADAPTER_DIR. Mount additional adapters read-only and restart to load them. An adapter can register a connection, operation executor, and optional YAML files with operations and features. See the architecture writeup for the boundaries and the existing backend/adapters/ packages for the actual config schema.

items.title: Settings storage
items.text:
Settings can validate supported target changes and test a target connection. Changes to top-level operations, features, authentication, or legacy-workspace settings currently require deployment and restart; see the configuration guide. Choose how supported edits apply:

  • File is the default. Set DECLARACK_CONFIG_EDIT=1 and mount the enclosing directory writable for atomic saves. The preceding revision is retained next to it with a .previous suffix.
  • Swarm uses DECLARACK_CONFIG_STORE=swarm and DECLARACK_CONFIG_SERVICE to select the dashboard service. The mount target defaults to DECLARACK_CONFIG and can be overridden with DECLARACK_CONFIG_MOUNT. The service update uses the manager socket, optionally overridden by DECLARACK_CONFIG_SOCKET. Docker service rollback can restore the prior config attachment while its config still exists.
  • GitHub uses DECLARACK_CONFIG_STORE=git with DECLARACK_CONFIG_GIT_REPO in owner/repo format. Set DECLARACK_CONFIG_GIT_BRANCH and DECLARACK_CONFIG_GIT_PATH as needed. DECLARACK_CONFIG_GIT_TOKEN_FILE is a mounted credential. Creating pull requests requires repository Contents and Pull Requests write access. The running dashboard still boots from the mounted file, so arrange for merged revisions to update that mount and restart or redeploy it.

Authentication provider/session configuration, adapter packages, and operation and feature definitions are deployment settings. They cannot be changed from the dashboard's Settings editor.

Run the adapter and storage tests with python -m unittest discover -s backend/tests after installing the Python dependencies.

items.title: Remote Docker over a managed SSH tunnel
items.text:
For a remote manager, replace the target's socket setting with ssh_tunnel. The dashboard container starts OpenSSH as a subprocess when the connection is needed, keeps it alive, and reconnects after a failure. No host-side tunnel service or Docker TCP listener is required.

targets:
  production:
    connection: docker_socket
    swarm: true
    ssh_tunnel:
      host: swarm-manager.example.com
      remote_socket: /var/run/docker.sock
      credential: tunnel_production
    features:
    - overview
    - services
    - nodes
    - tasks
    - stacks
    - configs
    - secrets
    - networks
    - volumes
    - host_metrics
    agent_image: registry.example.com/declarack:0.3
    host_metrics: true
credentials:
  tunnel_production:
    type: ssh
    username: dashboard
    private_key:
      file: /run/secrets/production_ssh_key
    known_hosts:
      file: /etc/declarack/known_hosts

Mount the OpenSSH-format private key and a verified known_hosts file in the container. Set the private key mount to mode 0400 and make it readable by the dashboard process. The manager's SSH server must allow stream-local forwarding and the SSH account must be able to access the manager's Docker socket. A nonstandard SSH port can be set with port. The socket is private to the dashboard container. Use a separate target for each manager. Swarm reaches workers via the manager's Docker API.

Stack operations and the bundled Docker CLI use the selected manager connection too. The Swarm-backed Settings store still uses its deployment-side manager socket, configured separately with DECLARACK_CONFIG_SOCKET.

items.title: Docker actions and interactive terminals
items.text:
See Docker GUI action coverage for the implemented action matrix, configuration examples, terminal behavior, and remaining CLI coverage.

Standalone Docker targets also expose Compose projects for discovery, saved inline/mounted sources, and reviewed lifecycle actions. Swarm task terminals use temporary node relay jobs when agent_image is configured. See the action coverage document for setup and constraints.

items.title: View existing Compose files from the host
items.text:
Optionally mount the host filesystem read-only and expose reported Compose files:

# Native Linux Docker host:
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.host-files.yaml up -d --build

# Docker Desktop on macOS (reported paths under /Users):
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.host-files.macos.yaml up -d --build

These optional overrides set DECLARACK_COMPOSE_HOST_ROOT=/mnt/host. Native Linux mounts / there; the macOS override mounts /Users at /mnt/host/Users because Docker Desktop's / is the Linux VM filesystem. Narrower read-only binds work too when they preserve the reported absolute path beneath /mnt/host.

Open a Compose project and select View host Compose files. Missing, unreadable, non-regular or oversized files are reported individually. The viewer reads files; it does not save a deployment source or alter the project. A host-root mount grants the dashboard read access to the selected host paths, so it is opt-in.

For multiple targets, set each target's host_root to the matching mounted host filesystem. A local mount cannot expose a remote Docker host's files; SSH-tunnel targets require an explicit per-target mapping. When running the Python development server directly on the same host as the Compose source files, use DECLARACK_COMPOSE_HOST_ROOT=/ without a container bind mount.

items.title: Multi-environment dashboard
items.text:
For custom pages with cross-target queries, shared JSONata context, cards, and tables, see the custom pages guide. The Environments page below remains the navigation view for individual targets.

The home page (#/environments) summarizes all configured targets. Each environment has its own snapshot, refresh button, feature links, and Open workspace action. Search by label, target ID, or provider. Existing target and resource bookmarks continue to work. Add environments under targets in the configured dashboard; this page does not discover or create remote connections automatically.

Standalone Docker summaries show Compose projects, total/running/not-running containers, and image counts when those features are enabled. Swarm overview summaries show services, ready nodes, stacks, and services below desired replicas. A failed summary is isolated to its environment; partial results remain usable. Loaded means summary requests succeeded, rather than a health guarantee. Targets without summary definitions still offer links into their workspaces, including SSH hosts whose metrics require manual collection.

Collection runs only on page entry or explicit refresh, with at most four requests in flight and a 15-second client timeout per request. Leaving the page cancels pending browser requests; it does not guarantee cancellation of work already started on a remote server. No host-metric or volume-inventory jobs are started by this dashboard.

Adapters and custom features opt in using the existing feature operation and JSONata expressions, for example:

features:
  asset_inventory:
    title: Assets
    operation: inventory.list
    rows: items
    columns: [{label: Name, value: name}]
    environment:
      cards:
        - {label: Assets, value: '$count(items)'}
        - label: Unhealthy
          value: '$count(items[healthy = false])'
          tone: '$count(items[healthy = false]) > 0 ? "destructive" : null'

Each card supports label, JSONata value, optional JSONata caption and tone, and an optional destination feature. Environment summaries must use operations without inputs and cannot be marked manual or on demand. Declare summaries only for inexpensive read operations. They inherit each target's enabled features and operation permissions; connection settings and credentials are not sent to the UI.

See Targets, environments, and persisted checks for grouping connections and scheduled monitoring.

See Portainer parity review and volume browsing / multi-target batches.

Resource editing is driven by adapter YAML and reusable workflow capabilities, including typed JSON forms, change previews and version-checked Swarm updates.

See source-based forms and tracked operation plans for reusable row editors, adapter plans, recovery behavior and container recreation limits.

Tables, bulk actions and charts explains reviewed resource selection, CSV/JSON exports and multi-source chart configuration.

See integration templates and dynamic form options for the Add integration workflow, adapter-owned presets, dependent dropdowns and validation.

Contributor setup, module boundaries and local verification commands are in the code organization guide.

Configuration folders can be edited from Settings with full-merge validation, source and effective-config diffs, and local revision history. Save a reviewed file, then reload to apply it. Historical content restores into a draft for review. See configuration editing and recovery.

For AI-assisted setup, load CONFIG_SKILL.md: a portable guide for creating, validating and applying Declarack configuration. Contributors and coding agents should start with AGENTS.md.

Persistence defaults to a local SQLite database. PostgreSQL is available through a database URL or mounted URL secret. Existing installations need an explicit storage import; both backends currently support one active controller.

items.title: Ready-to-use Declarack configurations
items.text:
Each YAML file is a complete system configuration. Choose one, edit connection settings, mount it in Declarack, and set DECLARACK_CONFIG to its container path. No adapter installation or frontend rebuild is needed for these definitions. The runtime image also includes them at /app/configurations. To select an unedited built-in preset, set e.g. DECLARACK_CONFIG=/app/configurations/docker.yaml without a config mount. Use an edited mounted copy for real remote addresses/credentials.

Configuration What it provides Setup folder-example/ Ordered config fragments and a local Engine dashboard Mounted host Docker socket; explicit reload docker.yaml Containers, Compose projects, images, networks, volumes, disk usage Mounted Docker socket swarm.yaml Services, nodes, tasks, stacks, configs/secrets, node-local volume/metrics jobs Manager socket; matching published job image operations-dashboard.yaml Custom cards/tables combining Docker, Swarm, and Prometheus sources Production socket mount and existing Prometheus API remote-swarm.yaml Local Docker and remote Swarm in one workspace SSH manager address, identity and known-hosts mounts ssh-host.yaml On-demand Linux host metrics SSH files and remote Python 3 prometheus.yaml Target health, active alerts, summary counts Existing Prometheus HTTP API grafana.yaml Dashboard inventory and returned-dashboard count Existing Grafana API; anonymous read access or service-account token Custom application example Application inventory, details, restart action, summaries An API implementing the documented example contract

Docker/Swarm configurations expose management actions. Prometheus and Grafana configurations are read-only views; they do not install these services, create Grafana dashboards, or define new Prometheus alert rules. SSH metrics remain manual. None of these templates adds background polling or persistent health history.

items.title: Run a selected configuration
items.text:
From the repository root, save this as compose.config.yaml:

services:
  declarack:
    environment:
      DECLARACK_CONFIG: /etc/declarack/dashboard.yaml
    volumes:
      - ./configurations/docker.yaml:/etc/declarack/dashboard.yaml:ro

Change the source filename to the selected template. Keep the base Compose password setting and socket/data mounts. Mount any referenced credentials separately. Then:

docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.config.yaml up -d --build

Set DECLARACK_PASSWORD before running. For Swarm jobs, publish the same Declarack version, configure registry access where necessary, and preferably pin agent_image to its digest. The sample latest reference is a starting point, not a guarantee that a private registry image is accessible to your workers.

To combine solutions, merge their targets, operations, and features mappings into one file. Do not repeat top-level keys. The monitoring definitions use namespaced IDs to avoid collisions. Multiple environments can reuse the same feature definitions. JSONata and request templates are explained in the configuration guide.

items.title: API and compatibility notes
items.text:
The Prometheus preset follows its HTTP API for /api/v1/targets and /api/v1/alerts. Alert results contain current active alerts; Prometheus owns their evaluation and history. The alerts endpoint has weaker stability guarantees than the overall v1 API.

The Grafana preset uses the legacy dashboard Search API. Grafana documents that legacy /api routes remain operative but are deprecated starting with Grafana 13. This preset intentionally uses the widely deployed response shape; review it against your version. Only dashboards visible to the credential are returned. The preset fetches page 1 (up to 1000 results), not every page. Declarack's frontend paging does not fetch further upstream pages.

Templates are validated against Declarack's schema and representative API fixtures. They are not a claim of live integration certification against every provider version.

For smaller building blocks, use the snippet catalog, also available in Declarack under Settings → Example snippets. Search examples, inspect prerequisites, and copy YAML into the reviewed configuration editor.

items.title: Configuration folder example
items.text:
This folder is one merged system configuration. Its paths have an intentional order: system settings, target definitions, a page, then an override.

  • 00-system.yaml
  • 10-targets/host.yaml
  • 20-pages/engine.yaml
  • 90-overrides.yaml

Mappings merge recursively; later lists and scalar values replace earlier ones. See the folder guide for mounting, editing, new files and reload behavior. The configuration workflow walks through an editable installation.

items.title: Configuration snippets
items.text:
Open Settings → Example snippets in Declarack for searchable examples with copy buttons. The documentation site publishes this same catalog under Guides → Configuration snippets.

Each YAML file is a configuration fragment. catalog.json defines its title, category, description, prerequisite snippet IDs and adaptation notes. Prerequisites are separate files, including their own prerequisites. Copy them first, then add the dependent fragment. Use existing definitions instead where appropriate. Filename prefixes place definitions before overrides; actual deployment files may need a later name. Mappings merge recursively and lists replace earlier lists. Replace example target IDs consistently when adapting a snippet to your system.

To contribute an example, add a YAML file and catalog entry. Include placeholders, required response shapes, mount requirements and whether the example performs mutations or starts scheduled work. The app bundles these maintained files at build time; they are not a runtime plugin or an auto-install mechanism. The docs stager generates its copyable library from the same source. Backend tests compose every example with its prerequisites and validate the resulting configuration; no external commands or connections are executed by those tests.

Run python -m unittest backend.tests.test_configuration_snippets and the frontend build after changing snippets. Review the copied fragment through Settings before saving and reloading it. Do not concatenate fragments with duplicate root keys into one YAML file; use separate files or merge their mappings explicitly.

items.title: Authorization design proposal
items.text: Status: proposal, not implemented. All current Declarack login accounts are installation administrators. The Users UI explicitly preserves that behavior. This document separates a recommended first version from later extensions.

items.title: Recommended model
items.text:
Use roles that grant named permissions within explicit scopes. Adapter operation IDs are the natural permissions for target work; installation APIs need reserved permission IDs too. A single backend authorizer should answer:

allowed(principal, permission_id, target_id=None, resource=None)

Authentication establishes the principal; authorization decides each request. Roles alone are insufficient without target scope: permission to stop a container on a test host must not grant that operation on a production host. Environments organize navigation and can overlap; they are not security boundaries by default. Start with explicit target IDs. Environment-derived target selectors can follow later, with clear warnings that changing membership changes access.

A role would grant swarm.services.list, swarm.services.inspect, swarm.services.scale and swarm.services.restart on target production-a, while granting no user administration, raw container inspection or shell access. Represent this as a list of grants, each with permission IDs and target IDs, rather than independent global lists that accidentally create a cross-product.

Use default deny and the union of explicit role grants in the first version. Avoid deny-rule precedence, resource-label policies and arbitrary policy scripting until there is a concrete need. New custom operations should not become authorized automatically because their names match a broad viewer wildcard. Built-in administrator access is an explicit privileged role.

items.title: Permissions beyond target operations
items.text:
Reserve installation-level IDs, for example system.users.read, system.users.manage, system.roles.manage, system.config.read, system.config.review, system.config.save, system.config.activate, and credential permissions for use, management and disclosure. These are proposed names, not shipped operation IDs. Self-service account actions should be distinct from managing other accounts.

  • Configuration and adapter-definition editing are effectively administrative: they can add commands, change target connections or alter an already granted operation's meaning. Keeping the same operation ID must not bypass a review of changed effects. Limit this editing to trusted installation administrators.
  • Credential use is different from credential disclosure. An operator can be allowed to use a target's registry authentication without retrieving its PAT. Grants must not allow arbitrary selection of another target's credential.
  • Raw inspection and configuration reads can disclose environment variables, credential values and mounts. Read-only does not automatically mean low risk.
  • An arbitrary SSH command or interactive shell is code execution within its target's privileges. Grant these explicitly; do not include them in an observer role simply because their transport uses a read endpoint.

items.title: Derive the UI from effective permissions
items.text:
The backend should return effective capabilities alongside filtered metadata. Use the same decision function for rendering hints and actual execution:

UI element Required access Target/navigation group At least one accessible feature on that target Resource list Its inventory operation Resource detail Its inspect operation and any explicit detail dependencies Action Its operation and applicable target/resource scope Create/edit workflow Required lookups, preview and execute operations Custom dashboard Each authorized source, independently Settings section Its installation permission Terminal Open permission plus matching session ownership and transport access

A feature is a presentation bundle, not the security unit. A user might view services but lack scale or delete, or view a summary but lack sensitive inspect. Role editing should explain required dependencies and offer maintained capability bundles instead of requiring administrators to discover every transport operation. Dependency resolution must not silently grant unrelated write operations.

Mixed-target dashboards should omit unauthorized sources without describing them as failed targets. Do not leak hidden target names, resource counts or data via aggregates, exports, searches, filters, errors or historical results. Define how partial dashboards render before exposing them to restricted users.

Operation outputs also form part of the permission contract. For example, swarm.tasks.list resolves service names and node hostnames internally. Granting that operation grants its documented result, not general permission to execute all service/node APIs. Similarly, a node-local read may internally create a short-lived Swarm job; authorization should cover the requested operation and its scope, not expose helper-job creation as a separate user power.

items.title: Enforce at every entry point
items.text:
Filtering buttons is usability, not enforcement. Named operation dispatch, direct Docker routes, settings/users/credentials APIs, bulk previews and execution, terminal/file transports, downloads, run history and scheduled execution all need the same authorization boundary. A direct URL or crafted request must not bypass it. Internal dependencies execute on behalf of the authorized operation, not as an unrestricted user-callable shortcut.

Bind terminal/file sessions to the principal, target and resource. Possessing a session token alone should not authorize another user to read or write it. Audit and run history also need ownership/visibility rules because results can be sensitive. Keep permitted execution scope even when work moves to a worker job.

Recheck permission at execution, not only during preview. Role revocation must invalidate stale capability metadata, reviewed writes and new background steps. Existing approvals/digest/version checks remain necessary and complementary. In-flight external effects cannot always be undone; document revocation behavior rather than promising rollback of a Docker operation already issued.

Scheduled checks and jobs need explicit, scoped service principals or delegated identities. They must not silently acquire all installation-admin privileges, or retain a user's old access forever after role changes. Define delegation and revocation before enabling non-admin schedule creation.

items.title: Storage and rollout
items.text:
Store role definitions and user assignments in the shared database, alongside accounts, using existing SQLite/PostgreSQL infrastructure. This avoids a second live file-based policy authority. A future export/bootstrap mechanism can be separate from normal GUI administration. Record role changes and assignments in the audit log without recording credential values.

Migrate existing administrators explicitly to the administrator role. Preserve host recovery and transactional protection against disabling or removing the last enabled administrator. Editing roles must not let an operator elevate their own access beyond delegated authority.

Recommended implementation order:

  1. Inventory every externally reachable operation/API, classify its effect and sensitivity, and define the shared authorizer and operation dependency model.
  2. Implement roles with per-target grants plus installation permissions; enforce them on all entry points, including session/run ownership. Keep background administration privileged until scoped delegation exists. Test direct requests as well as filtered UI metadata.
  3. Add role assignment and an effective-access preview to Users, with initial Administrator, Observer and Operator presets. Presets list explicit permissions.
  4. Add scoped background identities, resource/argument constraints and optional environment selectors where real workflows require them.

Resource constraints such as “scale only this service, up to five replicas” are useful later. They require adapter-aware resource resolution and fresh validation; operation names alone cannot express them. Keep the policy evaluator generic and let adapters supply the resource context it evaluates.

items.title: Static browser playground
items.text: The browser playground runs Declarack’s existing React renderer against a simulated API in a service worker. It needs static hosting only: no Python, Docker socket, remote hosts or hosted database. Every visitor gets their own browser-local configuration and inventories; tabs on the same origin share them.

items.title: Run locally
items.text:
npm ci --prefix frontend
npm run demo --prefix frontend

Open http://localhost:9083. This builds the demo and starts a static preview server. The existing Python DECLARACK_MODE=demo remains a separate option.

The banner labels the infrastructure as simulated and offers Reset demo. Changes survive reloads in the browser’s Cache Storage, including saved and active configuration revisions and up to 20 document snapshots. Reset restores the supplied configuration and inventories. Clearing site data also removes them. There is no shared server-side state or account system. Use example credentials only; entered values are browser-local data, not a secure credential vault.

items.title: Try the workflows
items.text:
1. Open Production → Swarm A → Services. Scale a service, then reload its overview. Swarm B has an independent inventory.
  2. Open standalone Docker to start/stop/pause containers, inspect health-check JSON, remove resources, pull a simulated image, or collect volume sizes.
  3. Open Fleet dashboard to query both Swarms and standalone Docker together. Monitoring includes simulated Grafana dashboards and Prometheus scrape targets; the SSH host supports sample metrics and simulated command output.
  4. Open Settings, select dashboard.yaml, change a page title or columns, then Review & save file → Save configuration → Activate configuration. Saving and activation remain separate, just as in the real application.
  5. Try the Credentials editor using synthetic values, or copy example snippets.
  6. Reset the playground when finished.

This is a curated simulation, not a Docker emulator. Unsupported actions return an explicit demo error. Terminals, real connection tests, stack deployments, arbitrary command/HTTP execution, scheduled check execution and source-provider import/publication require the real backend. Configuration validation checks the demo’s supported structure; it does not execute Python adapter validators. New custom pages/features can reuse simulated operations, but new operation definitions do not automatically gain an executable simulation. Configuration containing scheduled checks does not start a scheduler in the browser.

items.title: Publish on static hosting
items.text:
npm ci --prefix frontend
npm run build:demo --prefix frontend

The same demo can be built at a domain root or under a subpath. For a subpath, include its leading and trailing slashes:

npm run build:demo --prefix frontend -- --base=/declarack/demo/

Publish frontend/dist-demo/ at that exact directory on an HTTPS static host. Asset URLs, API requests, the worker registration/scope and Reset demo all use the build base. The emitted worker filename contains a content hash so CDN caching does not pin visitors to an older simulation after deployment. The worker handles only API paths inside its own directory; sibling documentation and the rest of the website are outside its scope. State is stored under a key derived from that scope, so different demo paths remain independent. HTTPS is required except on localhost. If a normal app replaces a demo at the same path, its bootstrap unregisters that path’s known worker and reloads before making API calls.

Our public locations are:

  • Browser demo
  • Documentation
  • Project links

The Documentation and demo workflow builds both outputs, validates links and demo contracts, then publishes generated files to public/declarack/ in daniellmorris/daniellmorris.github.io. Its existing Astro Pages workflow deploys them with the personal website. Application source remains in the private repo; only the curated docs and compiled demo are copied. The website’s other source files and pages are preserved. Pull requests build an artifact without publishing.

Publishing uses the DECLARACK_SITE_DEPLOY_KEY Actions secret: an SSH deploy key restricted to the website repository. Its GitHub permission allows repository writes; the publisher script limits its own changes to generated Declarack paths. Rotate it by replacing the website deploy key and the private repository secret. Do not add real credentials or private environment snapshots to demo fixtures or published documentation. The output is public by design.

For local verification of the complete site bundle:

npm run build:demo --prefix frontend -- --base=/declarack/demo/
DOCS_SITE_URL=https://daniellmorris.com/declarack/docs/ .venv-docs/bin/python tools/docs.py build
.venv/bin/python tools/site.py

The assembled .site-build/ contains demo/, docs/ and a link page. The regular Build workflow still offers a standalone declarack-browser-demo artifact for root hosting; no Python server, Functions or database binding is required.

items.title: Maintain the simulation
items.text:
• frontend/src/demo/config.yaml: editable default configuration; uses production schemas, features, operations and JSONata mappings.
  • frontend/src/demo/seed.json: generated, checked-in adapter contracts and synthetic Docker fixtures. No real environment snapshots or credentials.
  • state.mjs, api.mjs, operations.mjs: demo-only state, API contracts and explicit simulated operations.
  • worker.js: intercepts same-origin /api/ requests, serializes updates and persists state. Unknown API requests fail locally; there is no network fallback. Static asset requests continue to the static host.
  • bootstrap.js: registers the worker before the renderer mounts and adds the demo banner/reset control.

After changing built-in feature/operation YAML, fixtures or default demo config:

.venv/bin/python -m tools.demo_seed
npm run test:demo --prefix frontend
npm run build:demo --prefix frontend

The exporter validates the default configuration using the actual Python Dashboard and adapter discovery without opening network connections. CI runs python -m tools.demo_seed --check to detect stale generated contracts. The JSON is checked in so static hosts need only Node to build the playground.

A normal npm run build --prefix frontend excludes the demo modules, worker and YAML parser from its emitted JavaScript. The Docker image continues to serve that normal production build. Simulation code stays outside the framework and adapters.

items.title: Code organization and development checks
items.text: Declarack separates framework mechanisms from adapter semantics and groups UI code by the feature a contributor is changing. Prefer cohesive modules with explicit dependencies over file-size targets, forwarding wrappers, or a generic service locator.

items.title: Backend
items.text:
