Location Owns server.py, api_support.py Application composition, endpoints, startup and response/request handling auth/store.py, auth/http.py, auth/__main__.py Database administrators, password hashes, bootstrap, sessions/throttling, cookie/CSRF HTTP boundary and host password recovery identity.py Request actor context for recorded operation-plan metadata serving.py Single-listener Cheroot host, native TLS identity and explicit one-hop proxy trust adapter_registry.py Package discovery, dependencies and connection/executor registration configuration_types.py YAML parsing and shared configuration values input_schema.py Operation input declarations and execution-time validation dashboard_core.py Assemble enabled features, target capabilities, public metadata and operation dispatch view_schema.py, workflow_schema.py, form_options.py Renderer/workflow contracts and permitted lookup operations checks.py, operation_runs.py, batches.py, bulk_actions.py Distinct framework execution features terminal_sessions.py, file_tree.py Bounded PTY sessions and rooted read-only filesystem mechanisms adapters/docker/context.py Deployment settings and request-local Docker target context adapters/docker/client.py Socket transport and manager checks adapters/docker/resources.py Docker inventory/network inspection and Swarm config/secret operations adapters/docker/legacy_routes.py Translate legacy HTTP requests into calls to the same services used by configured operations adapters/docker/lifecycle.py Tunnel retention and expired node-job cleanup adapters/swarm/stacks.py Stack source persistence, credential encryption, source retrieval, deploy/replace and reviewed volume cleanup adapters/swarm/jobs.py Manager-scheduled node jobs, bounded collectors and job cleanup adapters/swarm/workflows.py Swarm overview and resource workflow dispatch adapters/docker/runtime.py Compose the built-in service instances and default installation settings

The runtime composition module wires explicit collaborators. For example, StackService(context, client, jobs) receives the services it uses. Service implementations do not import the HTTP host, Flask, or their composition module. A blueprint translates requests into explicit service arguments; services do not read a request object to discover what an operation means. This lets configured operations, old URLs and tests exercise one implementation.

Core errors are in errors.py. Import helpers from their owning modules rather than relying on dashboard_core.py to re-export every backend utility. Additional adapters still use the same manifest and registration interface.

items.title: Frontend
items.text:
frontend/src/
  app/                    # Shell, navigation, header and workspace view selection
  features/
    resources/            # Generic inventory, details, actions, related rows,
                          # terminal/file views and action state
    dashboards/           # Configured multi-target pages and charts
    environments/         # Environment groups and target summaries
    auth/                 # Session gate, login and installation administrators
    settings/             # Source editing and integration setup
    checks/               # Check state and history
    operations/           # Run history and multi-target batches
    workflows/            # Configured workflow editor
  components/ui/          # Shared presentation primitives and controls
  lib/                    # Pure mapping, sorting, routing and execution helpers

Within the resource feature, resource-page.jsx coordinates collection and view state. resource-table.jsx, resource-toolbar.jsx, resource-action-dialog.jsx, resource-summary.jsx, resource-workflow.jsx and resource-session.jsx render specific parts. use-resource-actions.js owns action review, execution and output state. The shell delegates view choice to workspace-content.jsx using explicit branches rather than a nested chain of JSX ternaries.

The main inventory, dashboard panels and related tables all use lib/table-rows.mjs for JSONata cell/filter/sort/tone/link/eligibility mapping, SortableHeader for sorting controls and TablePagination for page controls. view-values.mjs owns shared value formatting and path access. Keep the actual column definitions, operation bindings and resource-specific wording in YAML.

An extraction should have a recognizable responsibility. Do not split a function into several files just to reduce line counts or pass the whole application as a mutable dependency object. Prefer passing the collaborators or props a feature uses, and keep state close to its owner.

items.title: Local verification
items.text:
From the repository root, using your existing Python virtual environment:

.venv/bin/pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
npm --prefix frontend ci
.venv/bin/ruff check backend tools
npm --prefix frontend run lint
npm --prefix frontend run format:check
.venv/bin/python -m unittest discover -s backend/tests
npm --prefix frontend test
npm --prefix frontend run test:views
npm --prefix frontend run build
.venv/bin/python tools/check_tutorial.py

Use ruff check --fix backend tools to remove unused imports and sort import blocks. Use npm --prefix frontend run format for consistent frontend formatting. Ruff checks undefined names and import mistakes; ESLint checks undefined/unused names and JSX usage/keys. Prettier provides one frontend format. These are development tools; none are added to the final runtime image's Python environment.

The Build workflow runs the static checks, formatting check and tests before its image build. The Documentation workflow separately verifies the runnable tutorial and documentation links. Tests cover target context isolation, service dependency boundaries, cleanup failures, default Docker mode detection, shared table mapping, and server-rendered feature compositions. Browser globals that can hide missing props (such as bare navigation) are rejected by the frontend lint configuration.

After changing integration execution, also run the relevant live workflow: a unit test cannot prove that a Swarm node can start its helper image or that a terminal relay can reach a running worker task. The helper image must match the controller.

Configuration editing is grouped in backend/configuration/: editor.py validates reviews and revision-checked saves, history.py stores bounded local snapshots, and routes.py exposes their HTTP boundary without owning active configuration state. The frontend settings feature composes separate review and revision-history components.

backend/sources/git.py isolates Git fetch/ref resolution and bounded source extraction from the Swarm adapter. Docker deployment credential profiles live in backend/adapters/docker/credentials.py, shared by image pulls, Compose CLI commands, Swarm deploys and service edits. UI fields remain adapter YAML.

backend/storage/ owns SQLAlchemy Core connections, Alembic migrations, versioned documents, and explicit legacy-import/backend-transfer commands. Framework stores and adapter source repositories use it; adapters receive services["storage"]. runtime_settings.py owns the data-directory setting independently of Docker. See storage setup and boundaries for SQLite/PostgreSQL behavior.

Environment grouping and root navigation validation live in backend/environments.py; checks retain monitoring definitions and execution, and batches retain bounded fan-out.

backend/configuration/environments.py projects structured environment forms into source-file drafts for the shared configuration editor. The dedicated frontend settings page is features/settings/environment-editor.jsx.

configuration/managed.py owns immutable YAML document revisions and saved/active database pointers. configuration/writeback.py handles journal recovery and local file publication. Storage write transactions reserve the SQLite writer before reading state; PostgreSQL uses normal transactional locking.

items.title: Account and transport boundaries
items.text:
auth/store.py owns account validation, scrypt password hashing, first-user-only bootstrap, hashed opaque sessions, shared login throttling and bounded account audit documents in framework.auth.audit (1,000 retained; activity reads return 100). Account writes revalidate the actual session hash under the account lock after password hashing, preventing revoked sessions from finishing queued writes. auth/http.py installs the cookie/CSRF boundary and account endpoints; auth/__main__.py provides host-only password recovery. Migration 0002 adds the four authentication tables. Login accounts are distinct from configuration credential profiles. identity.py supplies metadata.actor to recorded operation plans, and batches.py propagates ContextVars into fan-out threads to preserve that actor. Bounded account activity plus plan metadata is not a complete generic resource audit log; direct calls do not all produce recorded plans.

serving.py loads TLS certificates at startup, persists self-signed files under <DECLARACK_DATA>/tls, and accepts forwarded proto/client information only from explicit immediate-proxy IPs/CIDRs. The frontend features/auth/session-gate.jsx unmounts protected children after logout, the session expiry timer or an API 401; the header owns the signed-in username and sign-out control. users-page.jsx owns the dedicated #/settings/~users list, ~new creation and user-ID detail routes, consequential-change confirmations and account-filtered activity. The shell owns the shared refresh button; users/activity data subscribe to its revision. See users and TLS for maintained operator behavior.

Action output presentation uses backend/view_schema.py for configuration validation, frontend/src/lib/action-output.mjs for identity/extraction and result state transitions, features/resources/use-resource-actions.js for execution, and components/ui/action-output.jsx for shared viewers. ResourceTable anchors each result beneath its stable row; adapters do not own output JSX.

items.title: Declarack configuration guide
items.text:
New to the model? Read How configuration fits together for diagrams, an example and the edit/review/save/reload workflow.

Declarack's main YAML is the system configuration. It describes the environments Declarack connects to, the capabilities it exposes, the operations it can execute, how their results appear, and the installation's authentication. A dashboard layout is one part of that configuration.

The existing filename dashboard.yaml, environment variable DECLARACK_CONFIG, Python class Dashboard, and Settings terminology remain supported. This guide uses “system configuration” to describe their scope; it does not rename those interfaces.

items.title: Contents
items.text:
• The configuration layers
  • Loading and validating configuration
  • Targets and connections
  • Operations, bindings, and inputs
  • Features and the UI renderer
  • Environment summaries
  • Custom cross-target pages
  • Actions and workflows
  • Related resources and child rows
  • A complete HTTP integration
  • Settings editing and storage
  • Authentication and credential files
  • Runtime environment variables
  • Application sources and persistent state
  • Adapter packages and extension boundaries
  • Troubleshooting and current limits

items.title: The configuration layers
items.text:
Layer Examples Where it lives Deployment/bootstrap Port mapping, socket/host mounts, config source, process environment, Docker secrets Docker Compose, Swarm service spec, environment variables System configuration Targets, environments, views, operations and auth references Active database revision; DECLARACK_CONFIG supplies import/export source documents Adapter definitions Connection/executor code, built-in operations and UI definitions backend/adapters/*, optional mounted adapter packages Application source An application's Compose YAML, GitHub repository/ref, stack deployment inputs Saved source records, mounted folders, GitHub Runtime state Administrators, sessions, login limits, saved stack metadata/PATs, Compose sources, browser table preferences, terminal sessions Database, data directory, browser storage, process memory

The system config does not replace an application's Compose file or the Docker daemon's daemon.json. It does not continuously reconcile container state. Its operations run when requested; enabling a feature is not a command to deploy an application. An HTTP environment is just as valid as a Docker environment.

Start with the included configuration catalog for Docker, Swarm, SSH, Prometheus, or Grafana. See health checks for current health integrations, persisted checks and notification limits. Upgraders should read the Declarack rename guide.

The main file has these recognized top-level sections:

targets: {}           # Required: at least one connection
operations: {}        # Optional: additional named operations
features: {}          # Optional: additional UI features
credentials: {}       # Named inline/file-backed credential profiles
pages: {}             # Optional: custom pages querying multiple targets
environments: {}      # Optional: groups of targets
checks: {}            # Optional: scheduled read/connection checks
batches: {}           # Optional: multi-target operation pages
integration_templates: {} # Optional: trusted setup templates
# auth: ...          # Optional: local account bootstrap and session settings
# legacy_workspace: production

Built-in operations and features are loaded from adapters before custom definitions. Custom names must be unique: system config adds definitions; it cannot override a built-in definition with the same ID. Enable only the desired features per target.

items.title: Database authority and file synchronization
items.text: The active system configuration lives in the database. YAML files seed an empty installation and remain explicit import/export sources. GUI saves create a saved database revision; Activate configuration updates the active revision. On restart, the active revision is loaded, not pending saved changes or edited files. DECLARACK_CONFIG_FORCE_LOAD=1 imports the configured source on every startup; DECLARACK_CONFIG_WRITE_BACK=1 writes local files before GUI activation. Both default to off. GUI editing defaults to enabled; disable it with DECLARACK_CONFIG_EDIT=0. See configuration authority and recovery for exact flag combinations, publication providers and write-back recovery.

items.title: Loading and validating configuration
items.text:
Without DECLARACK_CONFIG, Declarack generates a single local Docker target. It checks the Docker socket to choose Swarm or standalone features. If that check fails, the current fallback assumes Swarm; use an explicit file to remove ambiguity. The Settings editor is available only when an explicit config file was loaded.

With a file, Declarack loads exactly the targets in that file; it does not add the automatic local target. Mount the configuration and all referenced paths into the container, then set the environment variable. For the repository's compose.yaml, a small override can be:

# compose.config.yaml; paths assume this file is in the repository root.
services:
  declarack:
    environment:
      DECLARACK_CONFIG: /etc/declarack/dashboard.yaml
    volumes:
      - ./docs/examples/http-environments.yaml:/etc/declarack/dashboard.yaml:ro

# Set DECLARACK_PASSWORD in your shell or deployment environment first.
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.config.yaml up -d --build

The base Compose deployment supplies its existing socket and data mounts. Change the example API addresses before using those environments. Settings load at startup. Local files and folders can also be explicitly reloaded from top-level Settings after external edits. Reload validates before swapping the running model; invalid changes retain the previous model. Authentication and legacy-workspace changes still need restart. There is no automatic file/Git watcher. See the folder merge/reload guide for exact rules and limits.

For a local schema check from the repository, with backend dependencies installed:

python - <<'PY'
from backend.server import load_dashboard
config = load_dashboard("docs/examples/http-environments.yaml")
for target in config.public()["targets"]:
    print(target["id"], target["provider"])
PY

This loads trusted adapter Python and validates references and executor definitions. It does not execute inventory operations or prove upstream connectivity. Credential files referenced by the configuration must exist even for validation. JSONata expressions are evaluated in the frontend; startup validation checks required field shapes, not every expression's syntax or every UI option.

General rules:

  • YAML files are limited to 1 MiB. Swarm config saves have a stricter 500 KiB limit.
  • Duplicate YAML keys fail validation. Merge into existing top-level mappings.
  • IDs for targets, features, operations, and adapters start with a lowercase letter, followed by lowercase letters, digits, _, ., or -; maximum length is 80.
  • Labels and titles are human-readable and may contain spaces/capitalization.
  • Paths refer to the filesystem inside Declarack, unless a particular setting explicitly identifies a remote or worker-host path.
  • The YAML loader does not perform environment substitution, includes, or shell expansion. ${TOKEN} in this YAML is a literal string. Docker Compose's own ${...} substitution applies to deployment Compose files, a separate layer.

items.title: Configuration folders
items.text: A folder is one large recursive configuration merge, not a collection of separate apps. Files load in relative filename order, mappings merge, and later scalars/lists replace earlier values. Use CONFIG_FOLDERS.md for source browsing, manual reload, a working example, and the current local-storage-only boundary.

items.title: Root environment and navigation
items.text:
Use Settings → Home & environments for a form editor backed by the same YAML review/save/reload workflow. See the environment editing guide.

environments.root is the reserved Home environment and always exists. Configure its label, pages, batches, targets and ordered navigation just like other environment placement. Root defaults to no targets or batches and all custom pages. An explicit root pages list replaces the default. Built-in installation tools can be ordered, grouped, renamed or hidden through root navigation; Settings remains installation-wide. See page and fleet placement for the complete schema and example. The former page top_level flag is removed.

items.title: Targets and connections
items.text:
A target is a named environment. Its connection selects an adapter; that adapter reports a provider used to choose operation bindings.

Connection/settings Selected provider Purpose docker_socket, no swarm or swarm: false docker_standalone Standalone Docker engine docker_socket, swarm: true docker_swarm Swarm manager ssh ssh Commands/collectors on an SSH host http http An upstream API

Common target keys are label, connection, and features. features is an ordered list of enabled feature IDs, not inline feature definitions. Navigation preserves that order within feature groups. Feature lists must match available bindings; enabling Swarm configs/secrets on standalone Docker fails validation.

items.title: Built-in feature availability
items.text:
Feature IDs Compatible providers / scope overview, services, nodes, tasks, stacks, configs, secrets Swarm manager compose, images, disk_usage Standalone Docker containers Standalone engine or selected/all Swarm node inventories; manager-engine lifecycle actions, worker inspection and task terminals networks Standalone engine or selected/all Swarm node network instances; mutations use the manager volumes Standalone engine or node-local Swarm jobs; automatic inventory on page open; explicit size collection host_metrics Swarm node jobs or SSH host; manual collection

Resource-specific behavior and current action coverage are documented in DOCKER_ACTIONS.md. This list does not imply every Docker CLI flag is exposed by every feature.

items.title: Local Docker and Swarm
items.text:
targets:
  lab:
    label: Local Docker
    connection: docker_socket
    socket: /var/run/docker.sock
    features: [compose, containers, images, networks, volumes, disk_usage]
  production:
    label: Production Swarm
    connection: docker_socket
    socket: /run/production-docker.sock
    swarm: true
    agent_image: registry.example.com/declarack@sha256:REPLACE_WITH_IMAGE_DIGEST
    host_metrics: true
    worker_socket: /var/run/docker.sock
    metrics_disk_path: /var/lib/docker
    features: [overview, services, nodes, tasks, stacks, configs, secrets, networks, volumes, host_metrics]

These socket paths must already be mounted or otherwise supplied. Defining two targets pointing at one socket does not create two independent environments.

Docker target key Meaning socket Absolute Unix socket path inside Declarack; mutually exclusive with ssh_tunnel swarm Boolean, default false; Swarm operations require an active manager agent_image Same Declarack image available to worker nodes, preferably pinned by digest host_metrics Enable Swarm host-metric jobs; enabling the feature alone is insufficient worker_socket Docker socket on each worker host, default from runtime settings metrics_disk_path Absolute worker-host path whose filesystem capacity is measured stack_root Mounted source-folder root; falls back to DECLARACK_STACK_ROOT, then /stacks host_root Optional host filesystem mapping for viewing reported Compose source files

Swarm node-local work uses short-lived jobs pinned to nodes. The manager reads the results and removes jobs. It never SSHes into individual workers. Remote terminals also use temporary Swarm relay jobs, not worker SSH. See action coverage.

items.title: Remote Docker or Swarm through a manager tunnel
items.text:
targets:
  remote_swarm:
    label: Remote production
    connection: docker_socket
    swarm: true
    ssh_tunnel:
      host: manager.example.com
      port: 22
      remote_socket: /var/run/docker.sock
      credential: tunnel_remote_swarm
    agent_image: registry.example.com/declarack:YOUR_VERSION
    features:
    - overview
    - services
    - nodes
    - tasks
    - stacks
    - configs
    - secrets
    - networks
    - volumes
credentials:
  tunnel_remote_swarm:
    type: ssh
    username: declarack
    private_key:
      file: /run/secrets/manager_ssh_key
    known_hosts:
      file: /etc/declarack/known_hosts

The tunnel forwards the manager's Unix socket to a temporary local socket. Declarack supervises/reconnects the SSH process. The SSH user needs access to the remote Docker socket. Identity and known-hosts files must exist in Declarack; host-key verification is enabled. port defaults to 22 and remote_socket to /var/run/docker.sock. Use swarm: false and standalone features for a remote standalone engine. This is distinct from connection: ssh below.

items.title: SSH host
items.text:
targets:
  backup:
    label: Backup host
    connection: ssh
    host: backup.example.com
    port: 22
    features:
    - host_metrics
    credential: ssh_backup
credentials:
  ssh_backup:
    type: ssh
    username: declarack
    private_key:
      file: /run/secrets/backup_ssh_key
    known_hosts:
      file: /etc/declarack/known_hosts

The SSH adapter executes configured commands on that host. The built-in metrics collector requires remote python3; it is manual and does not supply an automatic environment summary. A custom inexpensive SSH operation can supply a summary.

items.title: HTTP API
items.text:
targets:
  inventory:
    label: Inventory API
    connection: http
    base_url: https://inventory.example.com/api
    features:
    - asset_inventory
    credential: token_inventory
credentials:
  token_inventory:
    type: token
    token:
      file: /run/secrets/inventory_token

base_url may have a path prefix. A binding path /assets is appended to it, giving https://inventory.example.com/api/assets. Userinfo, query strings, fragments, and whitespace are not accepted in base_url. Bearer credentials require HTTPS. An optional ssh_tunnel block uses the same SSH host/user/identity/known-hosts settings as manager tunnels, with remote_host and remote_port for the TCP upstream. They default to the URL host and HTTP/HTTPS port. The URL remains the HTTP Host/TLS identity; SSH forwards through a private local Unix socket. Direct HTTP behavior is unchanged when the block is absent. HTTPS certificate checks and the HTTPS requirement for bearer credentials remain in effect. Settings connection tests isolate temporary forwards; removed target forwards are retired on apply. See the running multi-environment lab for direct/tunneled Grafana and Prometheus configurations.

The adapter does not follow redirects. Requests default to JSON responses, have a 15-second upstream timeout, and a 2 MiB response limit. Arbitrary custom headers, OAuth login flows, and configurable TLS client certificates are not implemented.

items.title: Operations, bindings, and inputs
items.text:
An operation is a named backend capability. A feature invokes its ID; the target's provider selects a binding; the binding's executor performs the work.

operations:
  assets.inspect:
    bindings:
      http:
        executor: http.request
        method: GET
        path: /assets/{id}
        query:
          include: details
        inputs:
          id: {type: string}

bindings must be nonempty. A target exposes only the operations referenced by its enabled features, actions, selectors, detail views, workflows, or related resources. A registered operation is not automatically callable on every target. This is an installation capability boundary, not per-user role-based authorization.

items.title: Dispatch API
items.text: The UI calls POST /api/v1/targets/TARGET/operations/OPERATION/run with the input mapping as its JSON body. The response wraps executor output as {"result": ...}; JSONata feature expressions receive the inner result. State-changing HTTP requests to Declarack require X-Declarack-Action: 1, the session cookie and X-Declarack-CSRF from the auth snapshot, even when the configured upstream operation is a read. Cross-site action requests are rejected. GET /api/v1/targets exposes feature metadata to authenticated users, not connection credentials. These endpoints dispatch registered capabilities; they do not accept ad-hoc URLs, commands, or feature definitions from callers.

items.title: Request executors
items.text:
http.request and docker.request share path, method, query, body, and inputs. HTTP calls use the target's configured API; Docker calls use the selected engine. Methods are GET (default), POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE.

  • path starts with /; no origin override, dot segments, query, or fragment.
  • {name} placeholders refer to declared required inputs. Path values are encoded as individual path segments; query values are URL-encoded separately.
  • body recursively substitutes string templates. An exact '{count}' preserves the input's JSON type; 'prefix-{count}' produces a string.
  • Literal braces in templates need Python-format escaping ({{ and }}). Prefer a YAML mapping for a JSON body rather than embedding a JSON document in a string.
  • Optional inputs cannot appear in these templates: absent inputs have no implicit default. Define separate operations when request shapes differ.
  • http.request supports output: json (default), json_lines, or text through the shared decoder. Text becomes {text: ...}; JSON lines become {items: [...]}.
  • docker.request can use fields to project top-level fields and output: docker_logs to decode Docker's log framing. Its specialized projection modes are used by built-in service/node views; prefer full responses for custom views.

items.title: Input types
items.text:
All fields are required unless required: false. Unknown supplied fields fail.

Type Validation string Up to 512 characters, no NUL text Up to 700 KiB encoded text, no NUL integer Actual integer; min/max default to 0/1000 boolean Actual boolean, not the strings "true"/"false" choice String in the declared nonempty choices list list Array with at most 20 items; executor supplies any item-level checks

label supplies a human-readable action-form label. Backend schemas and executor validation remain authoritative regardless of UI confirmation or field visibility.

items.title: Command and specialized executors
items.text:
Executor Binding-specific settings ssh.exec Fixed command argument list, output; optional built-in script: host_metrics swarm.exec command, output, mount_profile, all_nodes, write, inputs.node_id swarm.update Built-in version-aware service/node updates via action swarm.workflow Registered coordinating workflow selected by handler docker.volumes Built-in volume operations selected by operation docker.compose Built-in Compose actions selected by action docker.pull Validated image pull using its reference input docker.terminal, swarm.terminal Session lifecycle selected by operation

Command templates substitute declared inputs into an argument list, not a local shell command string. SSH quotes those arguments for the remote shell. The first argument must be a fixed executable. These definitions are trusted: choosing a shell/interpreter explicitly still gives the configured code its normal authority. Command output modes are json, json_lines, text, and agent_json; results are bounded to 2 MiB. Specialized executors accept their own registered actions, not arbitrary new workflow names. Consult their bundled YAML for exact input schemas.

Swarm job mount profiles are docker_socket, host_metrics, or none. All-node jobs use all_nodes: true with string node_id (including all); single-node jobs use type: string with pattern: '[a-z0-9]{12,64}'. all_nodes with write is rejected. All-node reads have bounded fan-out and return per-node results/errors. Setting operation-level on_demand: true makes the normal feature manual; detail operations and environment summaries cannot use on-demand operations.

items.title: Features and the UI renderer
items.text:
A feature combines an operation with a generic presentation. It can be a table, a card overview, or a detail/creation workflow. The target chooses which features are visible; feature definitions themselves live at the file's top level or in an adapter.

features:
  asset_inventory:
    title: Assets
    group: Workspace
    operation: assets.list
    rows: items
    columns:
      - {label: Name, value: name, truncate: true}
      - label: State
        value: state
        badges: {ready: active, failed: destructive}
      - label: Size
        value: '$string($round(bytes / 1000000, 2)) & " MB"'
        sort_value: bytes
        optional: true
    details:
      operation: assets.inspect
      row_id: id
      input: id
      title: name
      fields:
        - {label: Name, value: name}
        - {label: Attributes, value: attributes}

This fragment requires matching assets.list/assets.inspect operations and a target that enables asset_inventory. The full example includes every required section.

Feature field Behavior title Page/navigation label group Sidebar heading; defaults to Workspace group_by_provider Provider-to-heading mapping overriding group operation Inventory/overview operation ID rows JSONata selecting table records, default $ columns Ordered table columns manual Do not automatically collect ordinary inventory on entry selector Resource selector mapping: lookup operation, input binding, labels and JSONata row/value/text expressions details Dedicated detail route, operation, identity mapping, fields cards, panels Dedicated overview-page presentation environment Cards contributed to the combined Environments page actions, workflow Action controls and optional source/lifecycle forms children, related On-demand expanded rows / associated-resource sections

description is forwarded to the frontend but is not a universal page subtitle. Not every forwarded metadata field has visible behavior in every renderer mode.

items.title: Columns, details, and overview panels
items.text:
Column value is a JSONata expression evaluated against one selected row. sort_value optionally provides a raw numeric/string sorting key, independent of formatted text. badges maps exact returned strings to active, muted, or destructive. truncate shortens long values visually. optional starts a column hidden; optional_by_provider can override that per provider.

The first visible column links to details when the row has details.row_id. details.input names the backend argument receiving that ID; details.title is a dotted result path. Detail fields use JSONata against the complete detail response. Nested values can be expanded in the shared structured-value inspector.

Ordinary tables search all mapped columns before frontend sorting and pagination. Page-size choices are 10, 25, 50, 100, and 250. Density, hidden columns, and main-table page size are browser preferences, not configurable system defaults. These controls do not implement upstream pagination: the operation still fetches its configured result.

Feature-level cards calculate value and optional caption against the whole response. A feature destination links within that target when enabled. Built-in overviews use tone names such as mint, blue, purple, and amber for styling. panels declare title, feature, JSONata rows, row_id, columns, and optional wide. Panel column tone is a JSONata expression that can return destructive. These overview cards differ from the environment.cards schema below.

Current collection inputs are intentionally limited: automatic inventory takes no inputs except the renderer's supported node_id picker; a detail page supplies its one declared identity argument. Arbitrary multi-input search forms should use an action/workflow rather than assuming generic inventory filters exist.

items.title: Three different expression mechanisms
items.text:
Location Mechanism Example Rows, values, captions, summary tones, related inputs JSONata $count(items[status = "healthy"]) Request/command templates Declared input substitution /applications/{id} Workflow bind, needs, disabled, when keys Dotted context paths form.name, results.preview.digest

Workflow when/locked rules compare values for exact equality. They are not JSONata conditions. A workflow bind value is a context path, not an arbitrary expression. Quoting expressions in YAML helps preserve punctuation, colons, and strings.

items.title: Environment summaries
items.text:
The home route #/environments gathers summaries from all configured targets. An enabled feature opts in using environment.cards and its existing operation:

environment:
  cards:
    - {label: Applications, value: '$count(items)'}
    - label: Unhealthy
      value: '$count(items[status != "healthy"])'
      caption: '"Current inventory"'
      tone: '$count(items[status != "healthy"]) > 0 ? "destructive" : null'
      feature: applications

value, caption, and tone are JSONata evaluated against the entire operation result. feature is an optional destination feature ID, not an expression. A destructive tone highlights the value. Current environment cards do not offer arbitrary color palettes or chart types. Captions describe returned data; historical comparison requires the operation to supply historical data.

Summary operations must have no inputs in their bindings and cannot be manual or on demand. Use inexpensive reads: the core does not independently prove a custom operation is read-only. Enabling a summary explicitly allows its operation to run on page entry or refresh.

Collection is bounded to four concurrent requests across cards, with a 15-second client timeout per request. Refresh can be global or per environment. There is no background polling. Client cancellation does not guarantee cancellation of remote work already in progress. Built-in summaries do not start host metrics/volume jobs.

Status Meaning Checking At least one summary is pending Loaded All configured summaries succeeded; not a workload-health guarantee Partial Some summaries succeeded and some failed Unavailable All attempted summaries failed; not a definitive host reachability test No summary No eligible summary configured; workspace links remain available

Standalone summaries are supplied by enabled Compose and image features. Swarm's overview feature supplies service/node/stack/replica summaries. Container inventory has no automatic environment summary because Swarm collection requires a node selection and may launch jobs. The same custom feature can summarize multiple HTTP or SSH environments without JSX changes.

items.title: Custom cross-target pages
items.text: Top-level pages definitions combine named operation sources across targets, with JSONata cards and tables using their shared results. They reuse existing target permissions and keep manual collectors on demand. Unlike per-target features, they can calculate totals or join rows from multiple environments. Read the custom pages guide and the complete operations dashboard preset.

items.title: Table and detail actions
items.text:
actions:
  - label: Restart application
    operation: applications.restart
    icon: restart
    help: Ask the application API to restart the selected application.
    row: {id: id}
    confirmation: Restart this application? Expect a brief interruption.
    variant: destructive

This example maps the row's id to backend input id. Other required inputs from the operation schema appear in the shared action form. row values are direct record keys, not JSONata or dotted paths. detail: true places an action in detail view instead of its list location. Without row or detail, it is a page-level action.

Action field Behavior label, icon, help Visible/accessibility label, icon, tooltip confirmation Shared confirmation modal before submitting variant Button style: usually outline or destructive immediate Execute directly; do not use for actions requiring confirmation output: json Full JSON inspector, unmasked output: FIELD Display the named result field as text output: '$' Show the serialized whole result in the ordinary action renderer presentation: {placement: row, viewer: json} Inline result beneath the originating row; also supports page/dialog and structured/text result: replace Replace displayed inventory with action result back Return to the list after a detail action visible_when JSONata against a list row; hide an irrelevant action enabled_when JSONata against a list row or detail response to enable/disable its action disabled Direct row key whose truthy/nonempty value disables the row action requires Dotted result path required for showing a detail action hidden Hide action from ordinary controls (for supporting operations)

See action output placement and viewers for stable row identity requirements, loading/error behavior, examples and placement restrictions.

Action icons currently include json, play, stop, pause, restart, trash, plus, tag, edit, terminal, logs, activity, network, and settings. The terminal configuration object wires a feature to the session renderer; use existing container/task definitions as the reference for its operation IDs and identity mapping. An icon alone does not enable a terminal.

Confirmations and disabled controls are UI behavior, not extra backend authorization. Executors must validate destructive inputs and enforce their own prerequisites.

items.title: Workflow forms
items.text:
A workflow uses a dedicated create/detail page for coordinated forms. Source settings and lifecycle actions can be separated using named sections.

workflow:
  create_label: New item
  defaults: {name: ''}
  sections:
    - {id: source, title: Source}
    - {id: deployment, title: Execution}
  fields:
    - key: name
      label: Name
      required: true
      changes_source: true
      section: source
  actions:
    - label: Save
      operation: items.save
      bind: {name: form.name}
      validate: true
      open: name
      reload: true
      primary: true
      section: source

This is a schema illustration; items.save must be defined before use. create_only: true limits the workflow to creation. Without it, details can render the workflow. defaults are merged with the current detail entry to initialize the form. summary fields use JSONata against the entry. readout can display an entry's text field or a downloadable base64 field; see config/secret feature definitions.

Workflow field options:

Field Meaning key, label, section Form key, visible name, section ID type Native input type or textarea, select, checkbox, file, selection required, description, rows Validation hint, explanatory text, textarea height choices For select: mapping of stored values to labels when Equality rules against context paths; visibility locked Equality rules against context paths; disable editing changes_source Mark dirty and invalidate stored operation results reset, reset_results Merge reset values into the form; discard named stored results when reset is applied source, warnings, item_label, empty, limit Context paths/options for a selection list

File inputs encode up to 500 KiB as base64. Selection fields return selected item objects; specialized executors validate them. Sections must match fields/actions' section values. Without sections, omit the section key on fields/actions too.

Workflow action options:

Field Meaning bind Input-name to dotted context-path mapping values Fixed input values when Equality visibility rules validate Require visible required fields and mark saved form clean after success clean Disable until source changes have been saved store Store result under results.NAME needs Require a present context value, e.g. preview digest disabled Disable if the context path has a present value confirmation Fixed confirmation text confirmation_by Choose text using field path and choices mapping output, success Display a named result field, or a success message reload, back, open Reload details, return to inventory, or open the created item's input ID reset List of form keys to restore from defaults after success primary, variant, help, icon Presentation

The context contains form, original entry, boolean creating, stored results, and provider. Hidden form fields are omitted from form-bound inputs. Workflow output is a named field; unlike ordinary actions, it is not a special JSON inspector switch. Built-in stack/Compose workflows require preview digests in the backend as well as in their UI; copying needs alone does not implement that guarantee.

items.title: Related resources and child rows
items.text:
related renders associated resources on workflow detail pages. children renders expandable inventory rows and child sections on ordinary details. Both use the shared resource renderer and declare their own operation:

related:
  title: Application resources
  operation: applications.resources
  inputs: {id: id}
  sections:
    - title: Containers
      rows: containers
      row_id: Id
      open: true
      columns:
        - label: Name
          value: '$join(Names, ", ")'
          feature: containers
          row_id: Id
        - {label: State, value: State}

Related inputs values are JSONata against the parent entry. Each section selects rows from the related operation's result. Column feature and row_id link to a destination only when that feature is enabled. route_prefix supports special routes such as terminal identities; link_when is JSONata against the child row. Sections can declare nested children using the same model. Related collection runs when its detail section or expanded row mounts and on explicit refresh. Avoid expensive operations here because these sections are not inherently manual.

Related tables provide their own search/sort/paging. Unlike main-table columns, the current related renderer sorts displayed mapped values; sort_value does not supply an alternate key there. See the built-in Compose and stack definitions for real associated-resource schemas.

items.title: A complete HTTP integration
items.text:
examples/http-environments.yaml is a complete, loadable system configuration containing:

  1. Local Docker with built-in features.
  2. Staging and production API targets reusing one custom feature.
  3. List/inspect/restart HTTP operations and typed inputs.
  4. A table, detail page, JSON inspector, confirmation action, and environment cards.

Its upstream API contract is:

GET  /applications              -> {"items": [application, ...]}
GET  /applications/{id}         -> application
POST /applications/{id}/restart -> successful JSON response, or empty success response
                                  body: {"reason": "operator-entered text"}

An application record looks like:

{
  "id": "website",
  "name": "Website",
  "status": "healthy",
  "version": "1.4.2",
  "owner": "Platform team"
}

This contract is illustrative; Declarack does not supply the example upstream APIs. Adapt paths and JSONata to your real API. No new adapter is needed for these HTTP calls. The restart button sends the configured request; the upstream implements what “restart” actually does.

items.title: Settings editing and storage
items.text: The Settings page reads the selected authoritative source, validates proposed YAML, and can test a target connection. Writes require the revision returned by the last read. A conflict requires reloading rather than overwriting another change.

items.title: What can be edited in Settings today?
items.text:
Target definitions can change through Settings, subject to storage permissions and normal validation. Changes to top-level operations, features, auth, and legacy_workspace are rejected by FileSettings.validate. The target named by legacy_workspace is also protected from Settings edits. This restriction applies to the existing single-document editor, validation, connection testing, and saving in all three storage modes. Folder-backed New file instead validates the full merged model and supports new execution/UI definitions; see the folder guide.

Execution and UI definitions can still be changed in the source file/folder through deployment, then applied using local Reload configuration. Authentication and legacy-workspace changes require restart/redeploy. “Configuration alone” means no Python/JS changes; it does not currently mean every definition can be changed through the browser editor.

The restriction is an implementation guardrail, not a YAML requirement. Custom operations may execute privileged commands or requests using the application's credentials. Authentication and some legacy-workspace globals are initialized at startup rather than safely hot-reloaded. A future full-config editor would need explicit lifecycle/restart behavior and broader validation. Target editing is also privileged; the present division is not a complete security boundary or per-user permission system. The current code does not offer a toggle to lift this restriction.

items.title: File storage
items.text:
DECLARACK_CONFIG=/etc/declarack/dashboard.yaml
DECLARACK_CONFIG_STORE=file
DECLARACK_CONFIG_EDIT=1

file is the default store. Without DECLARACK_CONFIG_EDIT=1, Settings is read-only. With it, supported changes replace the validated file atomically, retain the previous content as dashboard.yaml.previous, and update the running target model. Mount the enclosing directory writable, not a single bind-mounted file, for atomic replacement. This enables supported Settings edits, not unrestricted edits to execution definitions or auth. External file changes can use Reload configuration; authentication and legacy changes need restart.

items.title: GitHub storage
items.text:
DECLARACK_CONFIG=/etc/declarack/dashboard.yaml
DECLARACK_CONFIG_STORE=git
DECLARACK_CONFIG_GIT_REPO=your-org/your-config-repo
DECLARACK_CONFIG_GIT_BRANCH=main
DECLARACK_CONFIG_GIT_PATH=declarack/dashboard.yaml
DECLARACK_CONFIG_GIT_TOKEN_FILE=/run/secrets/config_git_token

Runtime startup still reads the local mounted file. Settings reads the configured GitHub branch/file. Saving creates a branch, file commit, and pull request; it does not merge the PR, pull the file into the container, or replace the running config. Your deployment pipeline must deliver the merged file and redeploy. Keep the mounted file and Git source aligned. Without a token, storage is read-only and only works where GitHub permits unauthenticated reads. This implementation is GitHub-specific, not a generic Git remote or repository watcher.

items.title: Swarm config storage
items.text:
DECLARACK_CONFIG=/etc/declarack/dashboard.yaml
DECLARACK_CONFIG_STORE=swarm
DECLARACK_CONFIG_SERVICE=your-stack_declarack
DECLARACK_CONFIG_SOCKET=/var/run/docker.sock
DECLARACK_CONFIG_MOUNT=/etc/declarack/dashboard.yaml

The named service must mount a Swarm config at DECLARACK_CONFIG_MOUNT. Settings reads that attachment through the selected manager socket. Saving validates the revision, creates a versioned Swarm config, and updates the service's config attachment. Swarm then redeploys Declarack. The old config remains available for Docker rollback; there is no automatic config-pruning policy. Keep your external deployment specification aligned so a later stack deploy does not restore an old attachment. The settings socket is separate from targets' connection definitions.

items.title: Authentication and credential files
items.text:
Connection credentials and optional first-account bootstrap use named credential profiles, including mounted-file references. The GUI manages profiles under Settings → Credentials and database login accounts under Settings → Administrators.

auth:
  provider: local
  bootstrap_credential: declarack_login
  session_hours: 8
credentials:
  declarack_login:
    type: basic
    username: admin
    password:
      file: /run/secrets/declarack_admin_password

Installation authentication uses database-backed local administrators and cookie sessions. provider defaults to local; bootstrap_credential optionally selects a basic profile used only when the users table is empty. session_hours defaults to 8 and accepts integers from 1 to 168. Without a bootstrap profile, use DECLARACK_ADMIN_USERNAME (default admin) and either DECLARACK_PASSWORD_FILE or DECLARACK_PASSWORD to seed the first account. Later changes to those inputs do not rotate existing passwords, and an absent bootstrap password mount does not prevent existing users from signing in.

Settings → Administrators manages database accounts separately from YAML. All administrators have full installation, credential and workload access. There are no granular roles or per-target permissions. HTTP Basic Auth is unsupported; migrate provider: basic / credential to provider: local / bootstrap_credential, and migrate clients to cookies and CSRF headers. See administrators, recovery, sessions and TLS for the complete contract, deployment examples and upgrade steps.

A credential file must contain one nonempty value; a trailing newline is accepted, embedded newline/NUL is not. Secret references are filesystem paths, not Docker secret names or automatic Docker API lookups. Mount the secret first:

# Deployment Compose/Swarm fragment, not system YAML.
services:
  declarack:
    secrets: [declarack_admin_password]
secrets:
  declarack_admin_password:
    external: true

This fragment assumes the external Swarm secret already exists. Standalone Compose has its own file-backed secret mechanism; standalone Docker Engine does not provide Swarm secret/config resources. Feature bindings enforce that distinction.

Bearer tokens, SSH keys/known-hosts, outbound HTTP Basic credentials, administrator bootstrap profiles, and the GitHub Settings token are separate credentials with separate purposes. Ordinary target metadata sent to the renderer excludes connection settings, but authenticated Settings reads show the system YAML. JSON inspection intentionally shows the full unmasked resource data. Treat the system YAML and Settings editor as administrator interfaces. Credential rotation is not file-watched. Connection credentials that are cached require activation/restart; existing login accounts require an account password reset. Inline bootstrap profile values remain in configuration history and exports.

items.title: Runtime environment variables
items.text:
DECLARACK_CONFIG_FORCE_LOAD and DECLARACK_CONFIG_WRITE_BACK accept 0 or 1 and default to 0; see database configuration.

These configure the process/deployment, not arbitrary interpolation in system YAML.

Variable Default / purpose DECLARACK_CONFIG Unset: generated local target; set: load a system YAML file or merged config folder DECLARACK_ADAPTER_DIR Extra adapter root, default /etc/declarack/adapters when loading configured targets DECLARACK_ADMIN_USERNAME admin; first-account username when no bootstrap profile is selected DECLARACK_PASSWORD_FILE Mounted first-account password file; choose this or DECLARACK_PASSWORD DECLARACK_PASSWORD First-account password fallback; bootstrap only, ignored once users exist DECLARACK_TLS off; native TLS modes files or self-signed DECLARACK_TLS_CERT_FILE Certificate PEM path, required only with TLS files DECLARACK_TLS_KEY_FILE Unencrypted private-key PEM path, required only with TLS files DECLARACK_TLS_HOSTS localhost,127.0.0.1; comma-separated self-signed DNS/IP SANs DECLARACK_TRUSTED_PROXIES Empty; explicit immediate-proxy IP/CIDR list, honoring one proto/client hop DECLARACK_MODE demo enables demo data; cannot combine demo with an explicit config file HOST Python default 127.0.0.1; runtime image sets 0.0.0.0 PORT 8080 for HTTP, 8443 for native TLS; explicit value overrides DOCKER_SOCKET /var/run/docker.sock; generated target and settings-socket fallback DECLARACK_DATA /data; default SQLite database and local working files/locks DECLARACK_DATABASE_URL Optional SQLite or PostgreSQL connection URL DECLARACK_DATABASE_URL_FILE Mounted single-line URL file; mutually exclusive with the URL variable DECLARACK_STACK_ROOT /stacks; mounted application source-folder root DECLARACK_COMPOSE_HOST_ROOT Unset; opt-in mapping for viewing reported host Compose files DECLARACK_AGENT_IMAGE Empty; fallback image for Swarm jobs DECLARACK_HOST_METRICS Enabled only by 1; fallback flag for Swarm metric jobs DECLARACK_HOST_DISK_PATH /etc; fallback worker-host path for disk measurement DECLARACK_WORKER_SOCKET /var/run/docker.sock; fallback worker-host Docker socket DECLARACK_CONFIG_STORE file; alternatives git, swarm DECLARACK_CONFIG_EDIT File-store writes enabled only by 1 DECLARACK_CONFIG_SOCKET Defaults to DOCKER_SOCKET; manager connection for Swarm Settings storage DECLARACK_CONFIG_SERVICE Required Swarm service ID/name for Swarm Settings storage DECLARACK_CONFIG_MOUNT Defaults to DECLARACK_CONFIG; service config attachment path DECLARACK_CONFIG_GIT_REPO Required owner/repository for GitHub storage DECLARACK_CONFIG_GIT_BRANCH main DECLARACK_CONFIG_GIT_PATH dashboard.yaml, relative to the GitHub repository DECLARACK_CONFIG_GIT_TOKEN_FILE Optional mounted GitHub Settings credential

Explicit Docker targets require a socket or ssh_tunnel; they do not inherit a missing socket from DOCKER_SOCKET. Per-target agent_image, host_metrics, metrics_disk_path, worker_socket, and stack_root override runtime fallbacks. With legacy_workspace, several worker fallbacks are reassigned from that target during startup, so explicitly setting worker options on each Swarm target is the clearest multi-environment setup.

DECLARACK_COMPOSE_HOST_ROOT applies to local Docker targets; tunneled targets require an explicit host_root. A local mount cannot read another server's filesystem. On native Linux, the optional deployment override maps / read-only to /mnt/host. Docker Desktop/macOS uses /Users to /mnt/host/Users instead. See host source viewing and the two compose.host-files*.yaml overrides. Viewing a file neither imports it as deployment source nor changes the Compose project.

Deployment-only names in compose.yaml, such as DECLARACK_STACKS_DIR, are Docker Compose substitution variables, not separately read backend environment variables. Registry/build secrets belong to the image build workflow, not the system YAML.

items.title: Application sources and persistent state
items.text:
The system config selects connections and capabilities; saved application sources are separate. Keep the data volume when you rely on GUI-managed sources.

State Current storage Stack source metadata, last deployment/commit and legacy encrypted PATs Target-scoped documents in the shared database Legacy PAT encryption key Binary document in the same database Saved Compose source definitions and inline YAML Target-scoped database documents; working YAML materialized locally Administrators, hashed sessions, login limits, checks, operation records and configuration revisions Framework database tables Native TLS identity Generated files under <DECLARACK_DATA>/tls, or external certificate/key mounts; outside database transfer Mounted-folder source files Configured/mounted stack_root; external to the database Table density, columns, main page size Browser local storage Terminal sessions and inventory snapshots In-memory/session state

SQLite defaults to /data/state.sqlite; PostgreSQL can be selected through DECLARACK_DATABASE_URL or DECLARACK_DATABASE_URL_FILE. See database storage and migration before upgrading an existing data volume. The import preserves historical source records and credential keys.

Named targets normally have separate logical database scopes. legacy_workspace uses the default legacy scope and bridges old bookmarks; it must name a configured Swarm target. Renaming target IDs does not automatically move stored records.

Swarm sources support inline YAML, mounted folders, general HTTPS/SSH Git sources with branch/tag/commit refs, and legacy GitHub-tag sources. General Git stores credential references; legacy PAT records remain encrypted in database documents. See source retrieval and credentials for exact storage, authentication and deployment behavior.

Standalone Compose currently supports saved inline and mounted-folder sources; it does not have the GitHub-backed stack source workflow. Reported Docker Compose file paths are discovery metadata until explicitly viewed through host_root or saved as a source. Lifecycle actions require saved sources and fresh preview digests.

Swarm config-backed system settings do not make all Declarack application state stateless. GUI-managed stack sources/PATs and saved Compose sources still need a persisted database. External source management can reduce that state, but the current implementation does not reconstruct all saved source metadata from Swarm configs.

items.title: Adapter packages and extension boundaries
items.text:
Built-in packages are discovered under /app/backend/adapters in the image. Configured installations can also load packages from the optional extra root. Each package has a manifest, trusted Python entrypoint, and optional YAML files:

id: inventory
api_version: 1
entrypoint: adapter.py:register
depends_on: [http]
operations: [operations.yaml]
features: [features.yaml]

The package may register reusable connections/executors; YAML lists define named operations/features. Dependencies load first. Duplicate IDs, unknown dependencies, cycles, invalid package-relative paths, and unsupported API versions fail startup. Packages run in the server process; mounting one is equivalent to deploying trusted application code. There is no browser plugin installer or automatic dependency installation.

Desired change Configuration sufficient? Add another existing connection type Yes, with needed mounts/credentials Reuse a feature across environments Yes Add an HTTP list/detail/action integration Yes, using http.request Change columns, JSONata, summaries, supported forms Yes, new unique feature definitions Add a command through SSH or a Swarm job Usually, within that executor's contracts Add a new transport/execution protocol Adapter code Add coordinated durable workflows Usually adapter/backend code Add a new chart type or arbitrary page layout Frontend renderer work Add continuous analytics ingestion/scheduling Not implemented by these settings Add roles, SSO, or per-user target permissions Not implemented by these settings

See ARCHITECTURE.md, action coverage, and bundled adapter YAML for resource-specific execution schemas. This guide describes implemented behavior; architectural aspirations are not additional config fields.

items.title: Troubleshooting and current limits
items.text:
Symptom Check Duplicate identifier Custom names must not collide with built-ins; use a prefix such as acme.assets Unknown/incompatible operation Enabled feature must have matching bindings for the target's provider and connection Expected standalone configs/secrets Those are Swarm resources; use Compose/application source files for standalone Missing file or socket Path must exist inside the running container with appropriate access SSH prepare fails Identity/known-hosts paths must be existing files; verify host/user/port HTTP upstream fails Check the final base URL + path, JSON response shape, HTTPS token use, and redirects Environment summary absent Enable the feature and define environment.cards; no inputs/manual/on-demand operation JSONata result empty Confirm expression context: whole response vs selected row vs detail entry Settings rejects custom definitions Edit through deployment and restart; the Settings restriction is deliberate File Settings cannot save Enable editing and mount the enclosing writable directory Git change not reflected in UI PR creation does not deploy it; deliver the merged file and redeploy Swarm Settings rollback/redeploy surprises Keep external service/stack config attachment declarations aligned Volume sizes/host metrics not automatic Collection is deliberately manual; Swarm needs a usable agent image Saved sources disappear after redeploy Persist the correct target data directory and preserve target IDs

The core validates many references and argument schemas, but it is not a complete JSON Schema validator for all YAML/UI keys. Unknown or unsupported UI fields may be ignored. Test custom integrations against representative responses and review the executor's behavior before enabling actions. There is no arbitrary JS/Python expression evaluator embedded in system YAML; use the supported JSONata mappings, input templates, and registered execution mechanisms.

See Targets, environments, and persisted checks for grouping connections and scheduled monitoring.

See Portainer parity review and volume browsing / multi-target batches.

See framework workflow extensions for typed JSON, JSONata initialization/payloads, previews and embedded resource editing.

items.title: Table tools and dashboard charts
items.text:
Features and page panels support configured filters and filtered CSV/JSON exports. Features can opt row actions into reviewed bulk execution. Custom pages can define line/bar charts and browser-driven refresh intervals. See the complete tables, bulk actions and charts reference for schemas, examples, execution guarantees, and limits.

See integration templates and dynamic form options for the Add integration workflow, adapter-owned presets, dependent dropdowns and validation.

items.title: Generic resource capabilities
items.text: See resource selectors, terminal sessions, file trees and input constraints for their schemas, adapter responsibilities and pre-release migration notes.

items.title: Container detail actions
items.text:
The built-in local-container detail page includes start, stop, restart, remove, pause/resume, rename, terminal, metrics, logs and JSON inspection. Lifecycle actions retain their confirmation dialogs. Removal returns to inventory and retains volumes; stop the container first. “Restart” restarts the same container; it does not reset its files or recreate it. In Swarm, these are manager-engine local containers, not cluster-wide task management.

Detail actions use detail: true with the same operation and row-input mapping as inventory actions. Their enabled_when expression receives the inspect response (for Docker, State.Status), whereas inventory actions receive the list row (State). Unavailable or invalid conditions disable the button.

items.title: Inventory scope and action placement
items.text:
Container and network tables show the connected engine in standalone mode. In Swarm, they collect node-local inventories across all nodes by default, with a node selector, a Node column and partial-failure reporting. Collection uses short-lived jobs from agent_image; every selected node must be able to run that image and mount its Docker socket. Offline, drained, unsupported or inaccessible nodes report errors; missing nodes are not represented as empty inventories. Declarack helper containers are excluded. Results are collected snapshots, not an atomic cluster-wide view; large responses retain the helper's explicit output limit and fail visibly rather than silently dropping rows.

Containers and local networks have node-qualified selection identities. Overlay networks can appear once per reporting node: those are sightings of the same Swarm-scoped network, not separate overlay definitions. Network inspection is pinned to the row's node, so endpoint information is local to that node. Network creation and mutation still use the connected manager. Removing a Swarm-scoped overlay affects the whole Swarm, not just one node. Manager-local detail links and lifecycle actions are shown only for manager-engine rows. Worker containers have inline inspection; running service task containers also have the existing Swarm-relay terminal action. Worker-local standalone containers currently have inspection only. Changing a Swarm service's task container directly is transient; Swarm may reconcile it. Use service actions for the desired workload state.

Services, tasks, nodes, configs and secrets use the manager's Swarm API. Volumes are inventoried and addressed per node, including the same volume name on different nodes; volume size collection remains an explicit additional action. Images and disk usage remain standalone-engine views. Image sizes are local, uncompressed sizes and use MB/GB. Pull image is the page-level creation action; Tag image edits an existing row. Image and network detail pages now expose the applicable management actions as well as inspection.

Non-destructive row forms without a confirmation (for example image tagging) open beneath that row using the same stable identity as inline inspection. Sorting and paging preserve that association; returning to the row reveals its open form. Confirmation-based writes keep their modal dialogs. Page actions stay in the toolbar and keep text labels; row actions use accessible icon buttons and hover descriptions. visible_when is a generic JSONata expression evaluated against each list row; it hides irrelevant actions. enabled_when keeps an action visible but disabled when it is inappropriate for the current state. These are UI affordances, not authorization checks; adapters still own execution scope and validation. Service replica counts display running/desired (for example 1/2), with under-replicated counts highlighted and unavailable counts shown as —.

Automatic environment summary cards no longer query the container inventory: all-node collection has node inputs and can launch helpers. Use the Swarm overview or an explicit custom page source with node_id: all when the collection is wanted. Existing custom pages calling containers.list or networks.list on a Swarm must supply node_id (a node ID or all) and map nodes.result.items; standalone calls still return the normal Docker array. Existing overrides of these built-in features must adopt the new node-qualified selection and inspection mappings.

items.title: Configuration folders and reload
items.text:
System configuration is now database-managed. A folder is imported once into logical database documents; its merge rules remain unchanged. To reimport after external edits use Settings → Review import from files, or set DECLARACK_CONFIG_FORCE_LOAD=1 for startup imports. GUI edits save database revisions and Activate configuration applies them. Enable DECLARACK_CONFIG_WRITE_BACK=1 to write files before activation. Source mounts may be read-only for DB-only editing. See authority, flags and recovery. The filesystem mechanics below describe source import/write-back and the original file provider, rather than a requirement to maintain live YAML files for DB mode.

DECLARACK_CONFIG accepts either one YAML file or a directory. A directory is simply one large configuration merge. Its files are not independent packages and their directory names have no special meaning. After merging, Declarack validates the same targets, operations, features, pages, and authentication model used by a single-file installation.

items.title: Start with the example
items.text:
The image includes /app/configurations/folder-example; the repository copy is configurations/folder-example. It contains:

folder-example/
  00-system.yaml
  10-targets/host.yaml
  20-pages/engine.yaml
  90-overrides.yaml

Use it directly in an image by setting DECLARACK_CONFIG=/app/configurations/folder-example, or copy it into an editable host directory and mount that directory:

services:
  declarack:
    environment:
      DECLARACK_CONFIG: /etc/declarack/config
    volumes:
      - ./my-config:/etc/declarack/config:ro

This is a deployment override used with the repository's base compose.yaml. Keep its password, Docker socket, and data configuration. A read-only container mount is sufficient for external file edits and Reload configuration; GUI editing or creating files additionally requires a writable mount and DECLARACK_CONFIG_EDIT=1 (see below).

items.title: Exact merge rules
items.text:
1. Find .yaml and .yml files recursively beneath the configured directory.
  2. Ignore hidden files/directories such as .git, and non-YAML files such as editor temporary files and .previous backups.
  3. Sort by relative path, case-sensitively, then load in that order.
  4. Merge mappings recursively. A later scalar, list, or different type replaces the earlier value at that key.
  5. Validate the resulting single configuration before using it.

For example:

# 10-targets/host.yaml
targets:
  host:
    label: Original label
    connection: docker_socket
    socket: /var/run/docker.sock
    features: [containers, images]

# 90-overrides.yaml
targets:
  host:
    label: My Docker host
    features: [containers]

The result retains the connection and socket, replaces the label, and enables only containers. Lists do not concatenate. Overriding columns, actions, cards, or feature lists means supplying the complete desired list.

Each file is a normal root configuration fragment. A file under targets/ still needs its targets: wrapper; no section is inferred from its filename. You can keep related target/operation/feature/page definitions together in one file or split them among several. A commented-out/empty document contributes nothing.

There is no include syntax, environment interpolation, deletion marker, or special merge directive. null is a value, not a delete instruction. Duplicate YAML keys inside one file fail; repeated keys across files follow the merge rules above. YAML << merge keys are not supported by the system-config parser. Custom IDs still must not collide with built-in adapter IDs/definitions.

Limits are 256 YAML files and 1 MiB combined source contents. File symlinks must resolve within the configured folder; symlink directories are not traversed. A dedicated config directory avoids accidentally loading unrelated YAML files.

items.title: Reload workflow
items.text:
1. Edit, add, or remove source files.
  2. Open top-level Settings.
  3. Optionally select Read source files to inspect the updated file list and merged YAML. The file selector shows each original source without flattening it.
  4. Select Reload configuration to validate and apply the current disk snapshot.

The reload action reads a fresh snapshot and submits its revision. Revisions cover filenames, contents, additions, removals, and renames. A concurrent edit detected during validation causes a conflict instead of applying the stale candidate.

If parsing or validation fails, the running model stays active. Correct the source and retry. Parse errors identify the source filename; semantic validation errors identify affected configuration IDs/references. A read failure does not erase the currently running targets or pages.

Reload supports changes to targets, operation definitions, feature definitions, and custom pages using the adapters already loaded at startup. Removed or changed SSH targets retire their old forwards. New connections are still opened lazily; a successful reload validates configuration, not upstream availability.

Changes to authentication, credential values used for installation login, or the legacy workspace identity/connection require a restart. New/changed adapter Python, process environment variables, ports, and mounts also require deployment/restart. Reload does not load new application code. Other open browser clients may need a page refresh to obtain changed navigation/feature definitions.

There is no filesystem watcher/background auto-apply in this version. Reload is explicit and revision-checked. This makes a safe foundation for a future GUI edit/validate/preview/apply workflow without adding a second configuration store.

items.title: Single-file and storage compatibility
items.text:
Existing single-file configurations keep working. Their file-store Settings editor retains its current save behavior and protected-definition policy. External edits to a local single file can also be applied with Reload configuration; unsaved browser drafts must first be saved or discarded.

Folder-backed Settings includes source browsing, merged preview, validation, connection testing, reload, and optional New file creation. Test all connections checks every target in the displayed configuration and reports each target’s pass or failure independently; testing does not save or apply the configuration. It never saves the merged document back over the source tree. Select an individual file in Configuration source to edit it when DECLARACK_CONFIG_EDIT=1 and the folder mount is writable. The merged view stays read-only.

For an existing source, use Validate file, then Save file, then Reload configuration. Saving validates the complete resulting merge, checks that the source revision has not changed, atomically replaces only that file, and retains its prior contents as <filename>.previous. It preserves file permissions and does not apply runtime changes until reload. Unsaved drafts must be saved or discarded before selecting another file or reloading. Symlink files and paths through symlink directories cannot be edited. File deletion is done on disk.

To enable creation, set DECLARACK_CONFIG_EDIT=1 and mount the configuration folder writable. In Settings, select New file, enter a relative .yaml or .yml path (nested folders are supported), and enter a root configuration fragment. Validate new file checks the entire resulting merge without writing anything. Create file validates again and atomically creates the file without overwriting an existing path. Then select Reload configuration to apply it.

Hidden paths, parent references, absolute paths, and symlink directories are rejected. The normal file-count and combined-size limits still apply. If the source revision changed, Read source files refreshes it while preserving the new-file draft. Creation requires the same authenticated action protection as other writes.

The API equivalents are POST /api/v1/settings/files/validate and POST /api/v1/settings/files, both with {path, yaml, revision}. Creation returns updated source metadata and created_path; it does not change the running model. Use PUT /api/v1/settings/files with {path, yaml, revision} to save an existing source. For a validation preview of an existing source, include existing: true when posting to /api/v1/settings/files/validate. Use POST /api/v1/settings/reload with the new revision to apply the merge.

Folders currently use local file storage. The GitHub and Swarm Settings stores continue to require a single file and retain their PR/redeployment behavior. A folder can still be delivered by your deployment pipeline from Git; that does not make it a GitHub Settings store. Packaging a folder into Swarm configs is a future capability, not an implicit behavior of this loader.

items.title: Try a new Grafana feature in the real lab
items.text:
The multi-environment lab now generates its five-target configuration under runtime/config/ and loads that directory. After building/updating its Declarack container, copy the supplied optional fragment:

cp examples/multi-environment/optional/grafana-health.yaml \
   examples/multi-environment/runtime/config/50-grafana-health.yaml

Open Settings and select Reload configuration. You get a new Grafana health feature and a Grafana status custom page, backed by the real Grafana /api/health response. No frontend rebuild is needed to load that definition. This is a complete example of one fragment adding an operation, feature, target capability, and page.

Delete that extra file and reload to remove the additions. The example's overridden Grafana feature list explicitly retains its existing dashboard inventory feature. lab.py configure regenerates the five base fragments but preserves extra files such as this one; later overrides continue to take precedence.

items.title: Reload API
items.text:
For authenticated clients:

GET  /api/v1/settings
POST /api/v1/settings/reload
     Content-Type: application/json
     X-Declarack-Action: 1
     {"revision": "revision-returned-by-the-read"}

Folder reads include ordered files (path, original yaml), merged yaml, revision, directory: true, writable: false, and reloadable: true. Reads expose administrative configuration and use the same authentication as Settings. Reload returns its accepted revision and message; errors leave the current model active.

items.title: Reviewed edits and recovery
items.text:
Settings now offers Review & save file and Review new file. Review validates the proposed full merge, shows the source-file diff and effective merged-config diff, and allows inspecting the proposed merged YAML. Saving checks the revision again; concurrent source changes require a fresh review. Saving writes the file; Reload configuration applies it separately. Authentication and legacy-workspace changes can require a restart.

Revision history keeps up to 20 source snapshots per local configuration source in the shared database (/data/state.sqlite by default, or PostgreSQL). Persist that database to retain history across container replacement; see storage. History begins with the first save through the reviewed editor, including the pre-edit content. External edits and integration-wizard writes are not independently recorded. Source snapshots include all current YAML files, but restore operates on one selected file: Restore to draft, review, save, then reload. Restored content is validated against the other files as they exist now. This is not an atomic rollback of an entire folder, and it does not remove newly added files. Git and Swarm-config providers retain their own publication/history workflows. Drafts remain in the open page; they are not persisted automatically.
