items.title: Comparing historical revisions
items.text: In Settings → History, choose a source file and saved revision to see its changes against the current saved configuration. Removed lines (−) belong to the current file; added lines (+) belong to the selected historical revision. The baseline excludes unsaved editor drafts and may differ from the active runtime configuration when saved changes have not been activated. Large diffs are bounded and explicitly marked as truncated. Comparing never saves or activates changes; Restore to draft still requires review, save and activation.

items.title: Named credentials
items.text: All runtime connection credentials live under the top-level credentials mapping. Targets, tunnels, registry host maps and Git allow-lists reference profile IDs. Mounted file paths belong on profiles too; they are not an alternative target credential mechanism. This is a breaking configuration change.

items.title: GUI workflow
items.text:
1. Open Settings → Credentials → Create credential.
  2. Choose a stable ID, optional label, and type: bearer token, username/password (including a PAT), or SSH key/known-hosts.
  3. For each secret field, choose Enter or upload value or Mounted file path. Text uploads and inline fields accept up to 64 KiB. A file reference must be an absolute path visible to the Declarack process/container. Unused file profiles can be saved before a mount is present; a connection using them must have the file available when validated/activated.
  4. Set the username for basic/SSH credentials. Set a host for Git credentials; optional hosts on other profiles restrict their destination too.
  5. Validate & review credential → Save configuration → Activate configuration. Profile edits use the same revision, source ownership, history, import and write-back workflow as other configuration documents. Split-document profiles must be consolidated in YAML first.
  6. Open Add integration, select the profile from its type-filtered credential selector, test the connection, then save and activate the target.

The editor shows which targets, tunnels, Git allow-lists, registries and login settings reference a profile. Referenced profiles cannot be removed. Removing an unused profile requires confirmation, review and save; it does not delete a mounted file. Existing connection references are edited in target YAML; Add integration selects profiles for new targets.

Entered values are stored in database configuration revisions, history and exports, and in YAML files if write-back is enabled. They are not held in a separate encrypted vault. File-backed profiles store only the path, leaving the secret outside the database. Protect the database, exports and any write-back files accordingly. Normal target metadata and setup selectors expose profile IDs and labels, not values. The administrator's YAML/configuration export remains complete. Profile IDs cannot be renamed in the form; update references in YAML when changing an ID.

items.title: Schema
items.text:
credentials:
  manager:
    type: ssh
    label: Production manager
    username: root
    private_key: {file: /run/secrets/manager_key}
    known_hosts: {file: /etc/declarack/known_hosts}
  api_token:
    type: token
    label: Inventory API
    host: inventory.example.com
    token: {file: /run/secrets/inventory_token}
  deployment:
    type: basic
    label: Registry login
    username: deploy
    password: {file: /run/secrets/registry_password}
  git_repository:
    type: basic
    username: deploy
    host: git.example.com
    password: {file: /run/secrets/git_pat}

Each secret mapping contains exactly one of file or value. For an entered secret use password: {value: "replace-with-your-secret"}, for example. SSH inline keys and known-host entries use YAML literal blocks (value: |) to preserve lines. The type, type-specific fields, optional label and optional host are the only profile keys. Unknown fields and incompatible references fail validation.

Type Required fields Used by token token: {file: ...} or {value: ...} HTTP Bearer authentication basic username, password: {file: ...} or {value: ...} HTTP Basic, registry login, HTTPS Git/PAT, first-administrator bootstrap ssh username, private_key, known_hosts (each file/value) SSH hosts, Docker/HTTP SSH tunnels, SSH Git

items.title: References
items.text:
targets:
  manager:
    connection: docker_socket
    swarm: true
    ssh_tunnel:
      host: manager.example.com
      credential: manager
    features: [services, stacks]
    registry_credentials:
      ghcr.io: deployment
    git_credentials: [git_repository]
  inventory:
    connection: http
    base_url: https://inventory.example.com
    credential: api_token
    features: []
  ssh_host:
    connection: ssh
    host: manager.example.com
    credential: manager
    features: [host_metrics, ssh_commands]

These references assume the profiles above. HTTP credentials require HTTPS, including HTTP APIs reached through SSH tunnels. SSH always verifies host keys; known-hosts content must already be trusted. Encrypted SSH private keys/passphrase prompts are not supported. An optional profile host must match the destination (hostname with optional port). Git credentials require a host and matching transport; SSH Git URLs must use the profile's username. Registry maps scope a basic profile to an explicit registry hostname; an optional profile host must match it. Reusing a profile does not make it available to a target's Git operations unless its ID is explicitly included in that target's git_credentials list.

Inline SSH material is written only to private process-lifetime files (directory 0700, files 0600) for OpenSSH and removed on normal process exit. These are reconstructable runtime files, not another persistent credential store. Registry CLI auth still uses short-lived Docker configuration; Git auth remains isolated from registry auth. File-backed registry/Git credentials are read again when used; HTTP authorization is resolved when configuration is loaded/activated. Rotate the file and activate/restart for connections that cache credential content.

items.title: Login and bootstrap
items.text:
A local-account installation can seed its first administrator from a basic profile:

credentials:
  login:
    type: basic
    username: admin
    password: {file: /run/secrets/declarack_admin_password}
auth:
  provider: local
  bootstrap_credential: login

The profile is read only when the users table is empty. It is not a recurring login credential or HTTP Basic Auth identity. Without a reference, use DECLARACK_ADMIN_USERNAME (default admin) and either DECLARACK_PASSWORD_FILE or DECLARACK_PASSWORD for that initial account. Once users exist, changing these inputs does not reset passwords, and the bootstrap password mount is no longer required. Use Settings → Administrators or the host recovery command instead. Accounts and their password hashes are stored separately from connection profiles.

Prefer mounted-file references: inline bootstrap secrets remain in system YAML, configuration history and exports even after the account is seeded. Account password changes do not rewrite that profile. See administrators, sessions and TLS for setup and recovery. Database URLs and configuration-provider Git tokens remain deployment inputs; they cannot depend on a profile inside a source that has not yet been opened.

items.title: Breaking changes
items.text:
Move SSH user, identity_file and known_hosts_file off targets/tunnels and into an SSH profile, then set credential. Replace HTTP bearer_token_file with a profile reference. Replace target-local registry profile objects with host-to-ID maps, and target-local Git profile objects with a list of allowed global IDs. Replace auth.provider: basic with local and auth.credential with auth.bootstrap_credential. Move older auth.username / auth.password_file into a referenced basic bootstrap profile or bootstrap environment variables. HTTP Basic Auth clients must migrate to login cookies and CSRF/action headers. New stack sources use general Git and a named credential; the per-stack GitHub username/PAT editor and GitHub-tag creation mode are removed. Historical legacy records may remain in storage, but no new per-stack secrets are accepted. Old configuration/history drafts using the removed fields must be converted before validation; there is no automatic runtime compatibility layer.

See database storage, Git and registry execution, and integration templates.

items.title: Custom pages across targets
items.text:
A custom page can query several configured targets and combine their responses in one layout. It uses the same named operations, JSONata mappings, shared cards, tables, badges, and detail routes as normal features. No resource-specific JSX or new adapter is needed for sources using existing execution mechanisms.

A feature describes a capability on one target. An environment summary shows feature cards grouped by target. A custom page composes named sources from multiple targets and can calculate values across them.

See the full operations dashboard preset for a Docker + Swarm + Prometheus example. The normal example config also includes a local Engine dashboard.

items.title: Page definition
items.text:
Add a pages mapping at the top level of the main system config, alongside targets, operations, and features:

pages:
  workloads:
    title: Workload overview
    description: Local containers and production services together.
    sources:
      containers:
        label: Local Docker
        target: lab
        operation: containers.list
      services:
        label: Production services
        target: production
        operation: swarm.services.list
    cards:
      - label: Total workloads
        sources: [containers, services]
        value: '$count(data.containers) + $count(data.services)'
      - label: Running local containers
        sources: [containers]
        value: '$count(data.containers[State = "running"])'
        target: lab
        feature: containers
    panels:
      - title: Production services
        sources: [services]
        rows: data.services
        target: production
        feature: services
        row_id: ID
        limit: 8
        columns:
          - {label: Service, value: Spec.Name}
          - {label: Running, value: ServiceStatus.RunningTasks}
          - {label: Desired, value: ServiceStatus.DesiredTasks}
      - title: Local containers
        sources: [containers]
        rows: data.containers
        target: lab
        feature: containers
        row_id: Id
        columns:
          - {label: Name, value: '$join(Names, ", ")'}
          - {label: State, value: State}

This fragment assumes existing lab and production targets enable the containers and services features respectively. Different target IDs and custom HTTP operations work in exactly the same way. Pages appear under the Custom pages sidebar group and have routes such as #/~pages/workloads. Settings is a global/system page and does not appear in environment navigation.

items.title: Sources and capability boundaries
items.text:
Each source declares target, operation, optional fixed inputs, optional label, and optional manual: true. Target IDs and operation IDs must already exist. Source inputs are checked against that target's binding schema at config validation and again by the operation API when executed.

A page does not grant new operation permissions. Sources must be operations used by enabled features' inventory, details, selectors, or related-resource views. Operations exposed only as action buttons cannot be used as page sources. New execution definitions still belong to the deployment-managed operations and features config, not to the page layout.

These are trusted read conventions, not proof that every custom inventory request is side-effect-free. Define custom inventory/detail operations as reads. There is no ad-hoc request URL or command field in a page source.

Operations marked on_demand, and manual feature inventory operations, are always manual on custom pages even if manual: false is supplied. For example:

# Add this source only to a page whose production target enables host_metrics.
sources:
  metrics:
    target: production
    operation: host.metrics
    inputs: {node_id: all}
    manual: true

Manual sources show a Collect control. Opening the page does not start those operations. They may create Swarm jobs only after explicit collection. Queries are independent: a source's inputs are fixed config, not dynamically derived from another source's result.

items.title: JSONata context and dependencies
items.text:
Card expressions and panel rows expressions receive this page context:

{
  "data": {
    "containers": [{"Id": "example", "State": "running"}],
    "services": []
  },
  "sources": {
    "containers": {
      "state": "ready",
      "result": [{"Id": "example", "State": "running"}],
      "checked": "2026-11-20T12:00:00.000Z"
    },
    "services": {"state": "ready", "result": [], "checked": "2026-11-20T12:00:00.000Z"}
  }
}

data.NAME contains only the result of a successful current source. Source states are idle (manual/uncollected), loading, ready, and error. Errors include error text and a check timestamp. These timestamps are client receipt times, not necessarily the upstream's measurement time.

Every card/panel can declare a sources dependency list. If omitted, it depends on all page sources. The item is evaluated only when all its dependencies are ready. A failed dependency shows unavailable; a manual/uncollected dependency prompts collection. Unknown results are not turned into a misleading zero. A successful empty result can correctly produce zero.

Declare dependencies explicitly so a failed monitoring endpoint does not hide an unrelated Docker table. The dependencies gate evaluation; they do not restrict the JSONata context. List all sources that an expression actually uses.

JSONata can join/append data as well as count it. For example, a panel can combine resource names and identify where each came from:

panels:
  - title: Workloads from both environments
    sources: [containers, services]
    rows: >-
      $append(
        data.containers.{"name": $join(Names, ", "), "environment": "Lab"},
        data.services.{"name": Spec.Name, "environment": "Production"}
      )
    wide: true
    columns:
      - {label: Name, value: name}
      - {label: Environment, value: environment}

Columns evaluate against each selected row, not the whole page context. Normalize fields in the rows expression before presenting records from dissimilar APIs.

items.title: Cards and tables
items.text:
Cards accept label, JSONata value, optional JSONata caption/tone, sources, and optional static target/feature navigation. A tone of destructive highlights an unhealthy count. A link requires a feature enabled on that destination target.

Panels accept title, JSONata rows, columns, sources, limit (1–100, default 8), and wide: true for full width. Columns support JSONata value, optional sort_value/tone, badges, and truncate. Header clicks sort all mapped rows before the display limit. These are compact dashboard panels, not upstream paging. Open the underlying feature for full search, paging, actions, and detail workflows.

A panel can set target, feature, and row_id together to link the first column to resource details. The destination is static per panel: a table that merges rows from different targets should omit that link or use separate linked panels. row_id is a direct row key. Cards and panels do not directly execute write actions.

Limits are 16 pages per config, 24 sources per page, and 24 cards/24 panels per page. There is no arbitrary grid designer, chart library, or persisted dashboard history.

items.title: Refreshing, editing, and storage
items.text:
Automatic sources load on page entry and global Refresh; individual source controls refresh only that source. Requests have bounded concurrency (four per page) and a 15-second client timeout. There is no background polling. Leaving a page cancels browser work and prevents stale updates, but cannot guarantee remote cancellation. A global refresh preserves already-collected manual snapshots on the same unchanged page definition; it does not resample them. Their receipt timestamp stays visible.

Page layout edits are accepted by the Settings storage workflow because they reuse existing target capabilities. File/GitHub/Swarm stores retain their normal write permissions and revision/deployment behavior. Changing execution definitions, authentication, or legacy-workspace settings remains deployment-managed. Removing a target requires updating any pages referencing it in the same config change.

Definitions live in system YAML; response snapshots live in browser memory. No new database is needed for this feature. Persistent health history or a scheduler is a separate capability described in HEALTH_CHECKS.md.

items.title: Global and environment placement
items.text:
Custom pages can be top-level only, limited to selected environments, or both. The reserved root environment is Home. Place pages through environment pages lists; the old top_level property is no longer accepted.

environments:
  root:
    label: Home
    pages: [overview]
    navigation:
      - {item: environments}
      - {page: overview, group: Dashboards}
      - {item: checks, label: Monitoring, group: Administration}
      - {item: operations}
      - {item: targets}
      - {item: settings}
  production:
    targets: [production_docker]
    pages: [production-summary]
    batches: [fleet-command]

This fragment assumes the referenced targets, pages and batch definitions exist. Root always exists, has no targets by default, and defaults to all defined pages when its pages list is omitted. Set pages: [] to remove those root placements. Other environments default to empty page and batch lists. Root also defaults to an empty batch list; assign both targets and batches to run fleet tools from Home.

Navigation defaults to placed pages/batches, plus installation tools in root. An explicit navigation list replaces those defaults and controls order, optional label, and optional group headings. Each entry names exactly one item, page or batch. Page and batch entries must belong to that environment. Root supports built-in items environments, targets, checks, operations, and settings; these tools remain installation-wide and cannot be placed in other environments. An empty navigation list hides all configurable links; Home and the environment selector remain available. Navigation visibility is not authorization.

Pages may be shared by several environments. Links use #/environments/<environment-id>/pages/<page-id> (including root). An unassigned page does not render in that environment. The bare application URL opens Home. The old global page route resolves against root membership.

Fleet tools use environments.<id>.batches and the environment's targets. Omit batches.<id>.targets to infer eligible targets from environments assigning that batch. Every inferred target must expose the operation with matching inputs. An explicit batch target list may further restrict eligible targets; the UI uses its intersection with the selected environment. Definitions are reusable across environments, while execution retains target selection and confirmation rules.

items.title: Database-managed documents
items.text: The environment editor now edits database-backed logical YAML documents. Save creates a pending revision; Activate configuration applies it. Source-file ownership and split-document checks operate on those logical documents, even if the original filesystem source is unavailable. Files are changed only when write-back is enabled. See storage behavior.

items.title: Editing Home and environments in the GUI
items.text:
Open Settings → Home & environments. Select Home or an existing environment, or choose Create environment and supply a unique ID and display name.

  1. Select existing targets, dashboards and fleet tools. Selecting a dashboard or fleet tool also adds its navigation link. Targets retain their own features.
  2. Arrange navigation with the up/down controls. Set optional labels and group headings, remove links, or add previously hidden links. Installation-wide tools are available only when editing root. Hiding a link does not restrict access.
  3. Choose a source file for a new or implicit definition. Existing definitions use their owning file automatically. Definitions split across files are blocked; consolidate them through the YAML editor first.
  4. Select Validate & review changes. Inspect generated YAML, the source diff, and the effective merged diff. Full configuration validation includes target, page, batch and navigation references.
  5. Save configuration, then Activate configuration to apply local changes. Saving records the same revision history as the YAML editor. Activation checks the exact saved revision; an intervening external edit must be read and reviewed again.

The form edits YAML, not a separate database model. It normalizes formatting and removes comments in the affected file; the review shows this before saving. Other sections are retained. When editing implicit environments for the first time, generated groups are materialized so adding an explicit environments section does not silently remove existing groups. IDs of existing groups are fixed; creating groups is supported, while renaming IDs and deleting definitions remain YAML operations.

Read-only configurations allow inspection and review but cannot save. Git and Swarm-config sources reuse their existing publication workflow instead of local save/reload. Review warnings and publication links remain visible. Local history and restoration are available through YAML settings & history.

items.title: Docker GUI action coverage
items.text:
Declarack exposes operations through adapter YAML, not resource-specific JSX. The table distinguishes implemented actions from candidates for broader Docker CLI coverage.

Resource Implemented Next useful actions Containers (standalone) List/inspect, create stopped from a local image, start, stop, restart, pause/resume, rename, one-shot stats, logs, remove stopped container, interactive terminal Command/env/ports/mounts/restart-policy editor, CPU/memory limits, health details, process list, filesystem changes, copy files, recreate from saved definition Images (standalone) List/inspect, local MB/GB sizes, pull by reference, add tag, non-force removal Registry credential references, push, build from Dockerfile/Git, import/export, history, explicit untag versus removal Networks Per-node Swarm inventory/inspection, manager-routed mutations; list/inspect; standalone create local bridge, connect/disconnect by container ID, non-force removal IPAM/subnet/gateway configuration, overlay creation, labels, driver options, endpoint aliases Volumes Inventory/attachments, create named local volume, remove unused volume; Swarm uses node jobs Inspect labels/options, driver configuration, backup/restore using short-lived jobs Services (Swarm) List/inspect, scale, rolling restart, logs, remove Versioned edits to image/resources/placement/update policy, rollback, create from structured form Nodes (Swarm) List/inspect, scheduling availability Labels, manager promotion/demotion, removal with quorum checks Tasks (Swarm) List/inspect Correlated logs and troubleshooting links; tasks are scheduler-owned, not directly restarted Stacks (Swarm) Source editor/preview/validation, deploy/update/prune/replace/remove and selected volume cleanup Registry credentials, deployment history and comparison Configs/secrets (Swarm) Create, inspect metadata/usage, remove; config content viewing Rotation workflow updating service references; secrets cannot be read back from Docker Engine/storage On-demand disk usage Version/info/events, filtered prune with a preview and explicit resource/data scope Hosts (SSH) On-demand metrics Explicit allowlisted host actions; Swarm never SSHs to workers

items.title: Configured actions
items.text:
An operation defines execution and validated inputs in backend/adapters/docker/operations.yaml. A feature defines its UI in features.yaml. For example:

- label: Pause container
  operation: containers.pause
  icon: pause
  help: Suspend all container processes without stopping them.
  confirmation: Suspend all container processes without stopping them.
  enabled_when: State = "running"
  row:
    id: Id

enabled_when is JSONata used for row-button availability. Docker still enforces actual state and in-use checks at execution time. icon, help, and variant control generic button presentation. Row buttons use accessible labels and native tooltips; detail and create-page buttons retain visible text. Destructive actions use variant: destructive and a modal confirmation showing the target resource. Dialogs focus Cancel initially, contain keyboard focus, and support Escape before execution. Creation uses dedicated pages. workflow.create_only keeps create forms separate from inspect pages.

Enabled features determine the backend operation allowlist. An action can be removed by overriding its feature definition in deployment configuration; hiding a button alone is not authorization. Internal terminal transport operations are explicitly listed as hidden feature actions so they remain part of that allowlist.

items.title: Interactive container terminals
items.text:
Open Containers → Open terminal. Select /bin/sh, /bin/bash, or /bin/ash (it must exist in the image) and optionally an exec user. Connect runs docker exec -it against the selected target's Unix socket or managed tunnel. The default user is the container's configured user, with no privileged exec flag. The shell does not change the container's main command.

The bundled Docker CLI and Python's POSIX PTY support provide the backend; xterm.js renders the shell. Authenticated same-origin operations carry input, resize events, and bounded output over short HTTP polls, preserving the existing Waitress server. Output stays in memory and is not written to application logs. There are at most eight terminals per process, with five-minute cleanup after the last input/resize. Disconnect and navigation close the local CLI connection; background commands started inside the container may continue. There is no session reconnection or cross-instance session sharing. Multi-replica deployments require sticky routing. Demo mode refuses terminal and image-pull execution.

On a Swarm target, Local containers terminals access containers visible to the connected engine. For worker tasks, use Open node terminal from Tasks or the service child rows. The Swarm adapter uses the relay described below; it never SSHs into workers.

items.title: Scope and verification
items.text:
Container creation currently uses the image's default command, creates the container stopped, and requires an image already present. Pull the image first. Image pull uses target-scoped registry credential files and has a 120-second timeout. Configure registry profiles through Settings; see registry credentials and Git sources. Without profiles, the CLI uses /etc/declarack/docker. Network creation defaults to a local bridge for standalone Docker and an overlay for Swarm; it is sent to the connected engine or manager. Removal never forces deletion and container removal never deletes its volumes.

Unit tests exercise non-force requests, terminal command arguments, limits, socket isolation, binary output, input size bounds, and versioned service restart. Live smoke tests use disposable Alpine containers to verify interactive exec, resize, and disconnect. Existing workloads are not used for mutation tests.

items.title: On-demand volume sizes
items.text:
In Volumes, choose Collect volume sizes to fetch inventory plus disk usage. Inventory loads automatically when the Volumes page opens and when the top-level Refresh button is pressed. Size measurement remains an explicit action. Docker disk usage likewise loads automatically when its page opens. Sizes use Docker's /system/df?type=volume response and display decimal MB/GB with the collection timestamp. A measured empty volume shows 0 MB; missing/unsupported usage shows Unavailable, while inventory-only results show Not collected. No size is inferred from a mount path, and unavailable values are never treated as zero. Refreshing inventory clears the previous size snapshot.

On Swarm, collection runs as a read operation through the existing short-lived node jobs, for one node or all selected nodes. Each result retains node identity; node errors remain visible alongside successful results. Publish and configure the updated image for both the dashboard and DECLARACK_AGENT_IMAGE before using this new node-agent operation. No worker SSH is used.

The generic action renderer supports immediate: true for input-free read actions and result: replace to render their response using the feature's existing YAML mapping. Failed size collection preserves the previous snapshot.

items.title: Compact inventories, paging, and full inspection
items.text:
Inventory tables default to compact spacing. Use Compact / Comfortable to change density and Columns to reveal optional columns; preferences persist in this browser. Resource names link to dedicated detail pages. Detail summaries use a compact grid, and nested objects/arrays expand without crowding basic fields.

Tables page on the frontend with 10, 25, 50, 100, or 250 rows per page (default 25). Search filters the complete fetched inventory before paging. Changing search or page size returns to page one; pages clamp when results shrink. First/previous/ next/last controls and a visible row range show which results are displayed. The full inventory is still fetched from Docker; pagination reduces rendering, not backend payload size.

Inspect JSON explicitly fetches the complete, unprojected Docker inspect response for containers, images, networks, volumes, services, nodes, tasks, configs, and secrets. JSON is unmasked, including environment variables, labels, and driver options. Docker itself does not return secret payloads. The summary APIs retain their projections. JSON inspection is a configured, on-demand action, subject to the enabled feature allowlist. Volume inspect in Swarm uses a single-node job.

The explorer supports expandable nested trees, key/value search, expand/collapse, plain JSON text, clipboard copy, and local JSON download. Copy/download always include the entire response, even when the tree is filtered. No external JSON viewer or new backend dependency is required. Swarm volume inspection requires publishing the same updated image for the dashboard and its node jobs.

items.title: Inventory sorting
items.text:
Click a data-column header to sort ascending; click it again for descending. Headers show a direction arrow and expose aria-sort for assistive technology. Sorting applies after full-inventory search and before pagination, and returns the table to page one. Missing values stay at the bottom in either direction. Names use natural ordering (for example, node-2 before node-10).

Columns can define a JSONata sort_value separately from their displayed value. Image/volume size columns sort by raw byte counts rather than their MB/GB labels. Run the frontend sorting checks with node --test frontend/src/lib/sort-rows.test.mjs.

items.title: Stack associations and service child rows
items.text:
Swarm stack detail pages include collapsible sections for services, tasks/container identities, networks, configs, secrets, and declared volume references. Networks, configs and secrets include both resources labeled with the stack namespace and external resources referenced by its deployed service specs. Failures fetching one resource group are shown without hiding successful groups. Volume references do not assert that a local volume exists on a particular node; use node inventory.

Services expand into child rows in both the service inventory and stack resource sections. Children are loaded only when expanded. They use Swarm task records to show container IDs, node placement, slot, current and desired state, and errors, including historical and pending tasks. IDs link to task details; the manager API does not proxy inspect/exec for worker containers. No worker SSH is used.

Features declare children and related definitions containing an operation, JSONata input mapping, rows and columns. Related sections can declare their own children. These operations are included in the feature allowlist and checked for provider compatibility. The renderer is generic; stack association logic stays in the Swarm backend. Related tables support search, sorting, and paging.

items.title: Standalone Compose projects
items.text:
Standalone targets can enable features: [compose, containers, images, networks, volumes, disk_usage]. The default target and example config include Compose. Discovery uses docker compose ls --all --format json, with a Docker project-label fallback if the CLI is unavailable. Stopped projects are included. Project detail pages show related containers, networks and volumes, followed by source settings and lifecycle controls, using the same YAML-driven renderer as stacks.

Save an inline Compose file or choose an explicitly mounted folder beneath stack_root (or DECLARACK_STACK_ROOT). Preview resolves Compose configuration and supplies a digest; up/update, start, stop, restart and down refuse a stale digest. Up and down optionally remove orphaned project containers. Down retains volumes and saved sources. Source files are private files under the target's data directory. GitHub-backed Compose sources and a destructive clear-volumes workflow are not implemented in this version.

Docker's ConfigFiles label reports paths on the original Docker host. These are metadata, not proof the dashboard can read those files. Existing projects can be viewed without importing their sources, but lifecycle actions require an explicitly saved accessible source. Relative bind mounts resolve from the dashboard's source path; use matching absolute paths on the Docker host (or absolute bind paths in the Compose file). External resources without project labels are not enumerated by the project resource view. The runtime image includes the Compose CLI plugin. BuildKit-only Compose build features require a separately mounted Buildx CLI plugin; it is not bundled in the small default runtime. Standard deployments using published images do not need that plugin.

items.title: Swarm worker terminal adapter
items.text:
Configure a Swarm target's agent_image to the same published image/digest as the dashboard. Nodes must be able to pull it, including registry authentication where needed. Open a running task's terminal through Tasks or a service/stack child row.

The swarm.terminal executor verifies the task is running, resolves its actual container and node on the manager, and creates two per-session replicated jobs: a socket-mounted relay pinned to the target node, and a socket-free bridge pinned to the connected manager. They use an encrypted, internal, non-attachable overlay with no published ports. A random session token authenticates the bridge to the relay. The dashboard execs into the manager-local bridge; the bridge streams input, output and resize events to the worker relay. No worker SSH, worker Docker TCP listener, permanent agent, public callback, or WebSocket dependency is required.

The selected node and connected manager must both be ready, active Linux nodes; a drained manager cannot schedule the temporary bridge. There are at most four Swarm terminal sessions per dashboard process (within the generic eight-terminal limit), five-minute input/resize idle cleanup, and a fifteen-minute relay lifetime. Disconnect/error removes both jobs and retries overlay removal after endpoints are released. Expiry labels allow the manager job cleanup loop to remove expired services/networks after a dashboard restart. Shell processes/background commands inside the target container can outlive a dropped exec connection. Multi-replica GUI deployments require sticky sessions because sessions are in memory.

Live tests validated Compose lifecycle on disposable projects and the two-job terminal transport, authentication path, input/output, resize and cleanup on the local single-node Swarm. Separate physical worker hosts were not available for a multi-host integration test; unit tests verify distinct worker/manager placement and scope validation. Normal Swarm encrypted-overlay connectivity is required.

items.title: Viewing discovered host Compose files
items.text:
An optional read-only host mount enables View host Compose files on discovered project pages. Set DECLARACK_COMPOSE_HOST_ROOT=/mnt/host, or host_root per target. A reported /srv/app/compose.yaml maps to /mnt/host/srv/app/compose.yaml. Discovery checks file metadata; file contents are read only by the explicit viewer action. The viewer handles multiple reported config files without importing or deploying them. Original files and the project's saved source remain unchanged.

Native Linux can use compose.host-files.yaml to bind / read-only at /mnt/host. Docker Desktop macOS should use compose.host-files.macos.yaml, which preserves /Users/... paths under /mnt/host/Users/.... Binding Desktop's / exposes the Linux VM root and does not provide the original macOS Compose paths.

The reader confines resolved paths to the configured mount, opens components without following replacement symlinks, permits regular UTF-8 files only, and bounds each file to 512 KiB and combined content to 2 MiB (up to 16 reported files). Missing files and read errors are returned per file. Remote SSH engine targets never inherit the local global filesystem mapping; configure their own matching mount explicitly. Host-root mounts are opt-in and may be narrowed to project roots.

items.title: Real two-Swarm lab
items.text:
The multi-environment lab runs two independent Docker-in-Docker Swarms with one manager and worker each. It exercises manager SSH tunnels, actual worker-scheduled services, host standalone inventory, Prometheus/Grafana direct and SSH access, node-local volume jobs on all four nodes, and an interactive terminal into a worker task through Swarm relays.

Container and network inventories now aggregate selected/all Swarm nodes through same-image jobs. Node-qualified row identity keeps duplicate names separate. Worker rows offer node-pinned inspection and, for running task containers, the Swarm terminal relay. Direct worker lifecycle mutations remain unavailable. Manager-engine lifecycle actions are confirmed and refreshed in place; use service actions for durable Swarm workload changes. Non-confirmation row forms stay beneath their resource, while destructive confirmations remain modal. See the scope and placement contract.

items.title: Task identity and relationships
items.text: Task lists and details resolve service names and node hostnames through batched manager lookups. They show the task attempt, slot, image, container identity and state; full IDs remain available in details and optional columns. Removed services or nodes are labeled explicitly, and unavailable name lookups retain the task with a context warning. Declarack helper tasks are excluded from the list. Inspect container reads from the owning node through a short-lived job; an old task can reference a container Docker has already removed. This action may report unavailable rather than return container data. Task JSON inspection continues to return the original manager task response.

items.title: Targets, environments, and persisted checks
items.text:
A target is a connection with its enabled interactive features. An environment groups targets and optionally links to custom pages. A target can belong to several environments or none. Environment membership does not grant or restrict execution permissions.

Without an environments section, each target is presented as its own environment alongside the reserved root (Home) environment. An explicit environments: {} leaves only root. Root never implicitly includes targets. The installation-wide Targets page lists all connections. Root navigation controls links to Targets, Settings, Checks, Operations and the environment directory. Other environments place their own pages and fleet tools.

targets:
  host:
    connection: docker_socket
    socket: /var/run/docker.sock
    features: [containers, images, volumes]
  public_api:
    connection: http
    base_url: https://status.example.com
    features: []

environments:
  local:
    label: Local infrastructure
    targets: [host]
    # pages: [operations]  # Optional IDs of existing custom pages.

operations:
  website.health:
    check_safe: true
    bindings:
      http:
        executor: http.request
        path: /health

checks:
  docker:
    title: Docker connection
    target: host
    every: 60s
    failure_threshold: 3
    recovery_threshold: 2
  public-api:
    title: Public API readiness
    target: public_api
    operation: website.health
    healthy: 'status = "ok"'
    every: 30s
    failure_threshold: 2
    recovery_threshold: 1
    enabled: true

The public API target is ungrouped and enables no visible features, but checks can still use it. Environment groups keep their targets' features; they cannot define or override features themselves. Grouped pages reference existing custom pages.

items.title: Where checks are stored
items.text:
Definitions live in system YAML, including configuration folders. You can create/edit check fragments in Settings, save them, then reload configuration. They are backed up and deployed using the same workflow as the rest of the config. There is no separate database copy of check definitions or check builder UI.

Runtime monitoring state lives in the shared database: /data/state.sqlite by default, or configured PostgreSQL. It stores current state, consecutive result counters, last collection/success, next due time, operator pauses and recent results. Persist the database to retain this information; YAML definitions remain separate. See storage setup and legacy import.

The scheduler runs in the backend, even when no browser is open. Each check is scheduled again from completion time. A missed interval during downtime is not replayed; an overdue check runs after restart. Runs are serialized in this first version, so long upstream operations can delay other checks. Adapter transport and command timeouts still apply; there is no per-check timeout override or cron syntax. JSONata evaluation has a 1-second evaluation guard, stack depth 100, and sequence limit 10,000; these are interpreter guards, not process isolation.

Only one scheduler acquires the filesystem lock in a shared data directory. Deploy one Declarack replica for monitoring in this version. Separate data volumes create independent schedulers; SQLite and a file lock are not a distributed coordination service. Use a local persistent filesystem with working file locks.

items.title: Check behavior and limits
items.text:
• Omit operation for an adapter connection probe. This tests connectivity, not overall workload health. The HTTP probe tolerates many non-server-error HTTP responses; use an explicit health operation when response content matters.
  • An operation check executes a compatible inventory/detail read, or a custom operation explicitly marked check_safe: true. This is an administrator's assertion about custom operation behavior, not a sandbox. Do not mark modifying commands safe. Non-GET/HEAD HTTP/Docker bindings cannot be scheduled.
  • Checks do not need the operation's feature enabled on the target. This does not enable that operation in the general target operation API.
  • inputs uses the operation's existing input schema. healthy is JSONata evaluated directly against the operation result. It must return a boolean. Omission means a successful operation is healthy. Errors, missing/non-boolean results, and evaluation failures count as failed results.
  • every accepts integer seconds or an integer duration ending in s, m, or h; minimum 10 seconds, maximum 24 hours. It defaults to 60 seconds.
  • Failure/recovery thresholds are consecutive results, each 1–100 (default 1). Counters reset on the opposite result. The initial state is unknown; it changes only after the corresponding threshold is reached. A prior healthy state can remain healthy while failures are still below threshold; the latest result and failure counter remain visible.
  • enabled: false disables the check through configuration. Operator Pause/Resume is persisted separately. Paused/disabled checks cannot be run manually. A run already in flight may finish when Pause is pressed.
  • Check or target definition changes reset the current evaluation state and due time. Runtime pause remains. Previous history remains visible. Removed checks are no longer scheduled; stale in-flight results from changed/removed checks are discarded.
  • At most 256 checks; at most 100 results per check and 25,600 results globally. Operation response bodies are not stored in monitoring history.

items.title: Alarms and the UI
items.text:
Checks shows current alarm state, latest result, last success, schedule, and consecutive result counts. Select a check for its dedicated history page. Run now, Pause, and Resume use authenticated action endpoints. The page refreshes state every 10 seconds without triggering extra check executions.

A transition into failing is a local alarm; a transition into healthy records recovery. This release persists/displays transitions but does not send webhook, email, or other outbound notifications. Maintenance windows, alert acknowledgments, notification adapters/delivery retries, uptime percentages, and a public status page are future extensions.

API endpoints:

  • GET /api/v1/checks: configured checks and persisted status.
  • GET /api/v1/checks/<id>: status plus up to 100 recent results.
  • POST /api/v1/checks/<id>/run: run now and persist its result.
  • POST /api/v1/checks/<id>/pause and /resume: persist an operator pause.

Writes require the usual authentication and X-Declarack-Action: 1 header. The real lab includes grouped environments and manager/Grafana connection checks. Copy examples/multi-environment/optional/checks.yaml into its runtime config folder for a JSONata Grafana database check using an additional ungrouped target.

Custom pages can be global, environment-only, or both: see page placement. Environment pages and batches lists place tools in selected groups; root controls Home and installation-wide navigation.

items.title: Reusable workflows for resource management
items.text: This expansion closes management gaps through reusable framework capabilities. Docker resource rules remain in adapter executors and feature/operation YAML; the React workflow renderer does not contain service, node, or network update logic.

items.title: What the built-in Docker configurations now provide
items.text:
• Swarm service editing: image, environment, service/container labels, entrypoint, arguments, mounts, published ports, network attachments, resource constraints, placement, restart/update policy, health-check settings, logging, and existing config/secret reference objects.
  • Version-checked service rollback to Docker's previous specification.
  • Version-checked node role, availability and labels editing; the adapter refuses demotion of the last manager. Existing availability actions remain available.
  • Network creation defaults to overlay in Swarm and bridge in Standalone. Driver, internal and attachable controls combine with expert JSON for IPAM, labels, driver options, IPv6 and other supported network-create properties.
  • Container creation accepts expert Docker create options, including environment, command/entrypoint, ports, mounts, resource limits, restart policy, labels, health-check configuration and network attachments. Name/image stay dedicated fields, and the image field takes precedence over options.Image.

The advanced JSON fields expose Docker structures rather than a guided editor for every Docker option. Standalone container edit/replace/duplicate now uses tracked server-owned plans, structured row editors, and retained backups. Creating a container does not automatically start it or pull a missing image. Swarm engine-level container creation still acts on the manager engine. Service creation, private registry credential management and GitOps remain gaps.

items.title: Typed operation inputs and defaults
items.text:
Operation schemas support type: object alongside existing types. Objects must be JSON-serializable, finite JSON under 700 KiB; the HTTP request body limit also applies. A schema default supplies an omitted input, is validated at configuration load, and is copied for each call. An explicitly supplied invalid value is not replaced by a default. Lists retain their default 20-item limit unless a validated max_items (1–1000) overrides it.

inputs:
  options: {type: object, default: {}}
  attachable: {type: boolean, default: false}

items.title: JSONata request bodies
items.text:
HTTP and Docker request bindings can use a JSONata body_expression instead of a body template. The evaluation root is the validated input object. This allows config authors to merge optional structured settings without adding executors. Both mechanisms cannot be supplied together. Expressions are parsed on config load; evaluation uses a 1-second guard, depth 100, and sequence limit 10,000.

executor: docker.request
method: POST
path: /containers/create
query: {name: '{name}'}
body_expression: '$merge([options, {"Image": image}])'

The existing body template syntax remains supported. These mapping guards are not process isolation and assume trusted configuration authors.

items.title: Workflow building blocks
items.text:
Setting Purpose initial Field-key to JSONata-expression mapping evaluated against the inspected entry. defaults Initial field values; JSON fields implicitly default to an object/array. defaults_by_provider Provider-specific defaults, before entry and initial values. Field type: json Editable typed structured input with parse/type errors. Field json_type: object/array Expected root JSON shape; default object. Action map Input-name to JSONata-expression mapping evaluated against workflow context. review Context path to a {before, after, version, warnings} preview object. embedded: true Render the workflow within a normal detail page, preserving its actions and resource sections. Section collapsible / collapsed Native collapsible groups, optionally initially closed.

Context contains form, entry, results, creating, and provider. In action mappings, form JSON fields are parsed objects/arrays, not textarea strings. Malformed, non-finite or incorrectly shaped JSON prevents workflow execution. Missing/null initialized JSON objects/arrays use the configured empty defaults. Values are merged in this order: implicit structured defaults, workflow defaults, provider defaults, inspected entry, then defined initial results.

Action values are built from static values, then JSONata map, then path-based bind. Mappings are awaited before execution. Existing binds still work, including nested paths such as entry.Version.Index. Ordinary row actions also support nested row bindings. The generic action dialog and batch page accept object inputs.

review displays changed paths, including absent values and array replacements. The apply confirmation repeats the reviewed diff. Editing a field invalidates the preview and marks the form dirty; reviewed values must be previewed again. For other workflows, changes_source retains its existing invalidation behavior. An action with reload: true can set reload_on_error: false to preserve its draft on failure; reviewed Swarm editors use this behavior. Refresh explicitly when a version conflict requires a fresh inspection. Backend executors still enforce concurrency and allowed mutations: a client-side diff by itself does not authorize or validate a write.

items.title: Add a guided field without a new React component
items.text:
This is a configuration fragment for an existing standalone Docker target. It reuses shipped operations to turn a friendly memory field into Docker's byte count. No new Python executor or JSX branch is required. Enable container_launcher in the target's feature list (lists replace earlier lists when merging).

features:
  container_launcher:
    title: Container launcher
    operation: containers.list
    columns:
      - {label: Name, value: '$join(Names, ", ")'}
      - {label: State, value: State}
    workflow:
      create_only: true
      create_label: Create container
      defaults: {memory_mb: 64, env: []}
      fields:
        - {key: name, label: Name, required: true}
        - {key: image, label: Local image, required: true}
        - {key: memory_mb, label: Memory MB, type: number, required: true}
        - {key: env, label: Environment variables, type: json, json_type: array}
      actions:
        - label: Create stopped container
          operation: containers.create
          bind: {name: form.name, image: form.image}
          map:
            options: '{"Env": form.env, "HostConfig": {"Memory": $number(form.memory_mb) * 1000000}}'
          validate: true
          back: true
          primary: true

items.title: Swarm review/apply behavior
items.text:
The swarm.manage adapter executor uses YAML-defined editable paths and value kinds. Preview reads the current specification, requires the explicit inspected version, copies it, and changes only declared fields. Unedited and unknown fields are retained. Structured fields replace their selected subtree, so editing a labels object intentionally replaces that labels map; deleted keys appear in the diff.

Preview returns the reviewed changes, current version, full before/after specs, warnings and a digest. Apply re-reads the resource and validates both the version and digest before submitting an optimistic Docker update. No-op previews are identified and do not issue updates. Docker may still reject policy/shape/resource constraints: preview is not a Docker dry-run or an image-availability check.

A changed version requires refreshing details and previewing again. Docker can change a service version as update/rollback status evolves, so a conflict can occur without another person editing it. Apply and rollback acknowledge the Docker API request, not eventual task convergence; inspect tasks and errors afterward.

For stack-owned services, the adapter warns that later Compose deployment can overwrite direct edits. Update the source configuration too. Config/secret fields refer to existing IDs; they do not create secrets or reveal secret contents. Rollback requires PreviousSpec and uses Docker's rollback=previous behavior, including its previous-spec registry-auth reference. This does not add a registry credential UI.

items.title: Generic resource capabilities
items.text: Declarack's core renders resources, executes declared operations and manages bounded sessions. Adapters own system-specific commands, transports and resource semantics. These capabilities use the same renderer for HTTP applications, Docker resources and SSH hosts.

items.title: Resource selectors
items.text:
A feature can obtain choices from a read operation, map its response with JSONata, and bind the selection to a declared string/choice input of its inventory operation:

features:
  tutorial.team-applications:
    title: Applications by team
    operation: tutorial.team-apps.list
    rows: items
    selector:
      operation: tutorial.teams.list
      input: team
      label: Team
      rows: items
      value: id
      text: name
    columns:
      - {label: Application, value: name}
      - {label: Status, value: status}

The operation names are declared by the API tutorial. To try this, copy selectors.yaml into the folder from the dashboard tutorial, read source files and reload. Open Training API → Applications by team. Platform returns Catalog API and Queue worker; Product returns Customer portal. Changing the selection clears old rows and selection. Automatic inventory reloads; manual inventory waits for Collect.

selector.inputs supplies optional constant lookup inputs. rows, value and text are JSONata expressions. Choices must have unique nonempty string or safe integer identities (converted to strings for the selected operation input). At most 1,000 choices are loaded. An invalid lookup is shown as an error.

Use all: {value: all, label: All nodes} only when the inventory operation implements that value. A provider's published feature omits this option if its input constraints reject the value. The renderer does not implement aggregation; that belongs to the operation executor. Lookup operations cannot be on-demand or use mutating HTTP methods. The lookup must be available on the target for its selector to appear.

Workflow fields use the existing type: select and options_from contract. There is no separate node-picker component. Provider-conditional fields only grant their lookup operations on the matching provider.

The same table renderer now uses Team rather than a built-in Node picker. Switching to Product loads its application automatically. Select the image for full size.

items.title: String constraints
items.text:
Operation input schemas use generic types and constraints:

inputs:
  resource:
    type: string
    pattern: '[a-z0-9]{12,64}'
  project:
    type: string
    min_length: 2
    max_length: 40

Patterns match the entire string. Length constraints are 0–512 characters; the default upper bound is 512. Constraints and default values are checked when loading configuration and submitted values are checked before execution. Docker/Swarm adapters declare their identifier constraints in their own operation YAML and check required executor constraints at registration. They are not core input types.

items.title: Interactive terminals
items.text:
An action opts into the generic terminal view and declares its transport operations:

actions:
  - label: Open terminal
    operation: ssh.terminal.open
    icon: terminal
    terminal:
      title: SSH terminal
      description: Open an interactive session as the configured SSH user.
      read: ssh.terminal.read
      write: ssh.terminal.write
      resize: ssh.terminal.resize
      close: ssh.terminal.close
  - {label: Terminal read, operation: ssh.terminal.read, hidden: true}
  - {label: Terminal write, operation: ssh.terminal.write, hidden: true}
  - {label: Terminal resize, operation: ssh.terminal.resize, hidden: true}
  - {label: Terminal close, operation: ssh.terminal.close, hidden: true}

The built-in ssh_commands feature includes this action. Enable that feature on an SSH target to use it. The session runs as the configured SSH user, with the mounted identity and known-host validation already used by the SSH adapter. Shell choices are declared in the open operation's schema; opening a terminal is manual.

The renderer builds connection fields from the open operation's inputs, using label, default, choices, placeholder, numeric bounds and required state. action.row maps resource identity fields when needed. Remaining input fields become connection controls. cols and rows are reserved for terminal geometry. No shell, user, container-name or Docker path is built into the terminal component.

All five operations must be declared and enabled on the same feature/target:

Operation Protocol Open Identity/connection fields plus cols, rows; returns session Read session; returns base64 data and boolean closed Write session, UTF-8 data Resize session, cols, rows Close session; closes the process and provider cleanup callback

Adapters construct argument arrays and pass an ownership scope to backend.terminal_sessions.Terminals. The PTY manager never constructs Docker or SSH commands. Docker scopes include target identity and connection; SSH scopes include target identity and SSH arguments. A session cannot be accessed through a different target. Input/output, concurrent sessions and idle time remain bounded. Swarm task terminals keep their node-local relay and cleanup inside the Swarm adapter; they do not SSH into workers.

items.title: File browsing
items.text:
An action maps any required resource inputs and binds a list operation plus file_browser.read. Both operations must be declared as feature actions. The shared view understands file-tree responses rather than Docker volume records. file_browser.title customizes its heading.

List responses contain:

{
  "path": "",
  "items": [{"name":"hello.txt","path":"hello.txt","kind":"file","size":12,"mode":"-rw-r--r--"}],
  "total": 1,
  "offset": 0,
  "previous_offset": 0,
  "next_offset": null,
  "capabilities": {"read_only":true,"max_file_bytes":65536,"symlinks":false}
}

Read responses contain path, name, size, optional UTF-8 text and base64 base64. Pagination follows provider offsets. The view displays advertised limits; the executor must enforce them. The shared backend.file_tree.browse(root, ...) helper is descriptor-relative and refuses traversal, symlinks, devices and files over its 64 KiB bound. An adapter supplies the root; Docker mounts a volume at /volume in a short-lived helper. This refactor does not add SSH file browsing or file writes.

items.title: Related rows and collection status
items.text:
children.expand_label supplies an expansion button label; children.identity is a JSONata expression for its parent title. Defaults say “Show related resources.” No Docker Spec.Name or container label is inferred by the shared row component.

A feature with per-resource collection results can map a status summary:

collection_status:
  title: nodes
  rows: nodes
  label: node_name
  error: error

The result shape belongs to the operation. Another adapter can use rows: hosts, label: hostname, and error: failure without changing the renderer.

items.title: Adapter ownership and schema changes
items.text:
Docker/Swarm services are grouped by responsibility: stack sources/deployment in adapters/swarm/stacks.py, node jobs in adapters/swarm/jobs.py, inventory in adapters/docker/resources.py, and overview dispatch in adapters/swarm/workflows.py. The runtime module composes those services. They are exposed through an adapter blueprint and adapter executors. The HTTP host retains authentication, settings, operation dispatch, check/run endpoints and static assets. Stack databases and encryption keys continue using the configured data directory and target scope.

Connectors can supply bind(state, target_id, config) when registering their connection. It returns the target-specific runtime state; the core does not know how an adapter partitions its storage.

This is a pre-release schema cleanup. Update custom definitions directly:

  • Replace docker_id and volume_name with type: string and the desired pattern.
  • Replace a bare selector operation string with the selector mapping above.
  • Replace type: node-picker with type: select and options_from.
  • Import the generic PTY manager from backend.terminal_sessions and supply a command explicitly; use backend.file_tree for the rooted file helper.
  • Rebuild and load the same updated agent image on Swarm nodes when updating the controller. Node helpers must have the matching module paths.

Feature navigation icons use an explicit icon setting (for example server, layers, drive, activity or file) rather than interpreting feature IDs.

No runtime package dependencies or Docker image stages were added.

items.title: Health checks in Declarack
items.text: Declarack displays upstream health data and runs configured scheduled checks with persisted state/history. Outbound notifications are not implemented.

items.title: Health information available today
items.text:
• Docker inspect data exposes configured health checks and their results when the engine supplies them. A running container is not automatically healthy.
  • Swarm overviews highlight services below desired replicas and report ready nodes. Replica convergence and node readiness differ from application readiness.
  • Connector tests probe configured connections on demand. A successful probe does not prove that every workload or resource operation is healthy.
  • The Prometheus preset displays target health and active alerts from an existing Prometheus server. Prometheus owns that data's collection, rule evaluation and retention.
  • Configured scheduled checks evaluate a connection or eligible read operation, with JSONata conditions and consecutive failure/recovery thresholds.

items.title: Persisted checks
items.text:
Definitions live in system YAML. The shared database stores current state, recent results and operator pauses (SQLite by default, or PostgreSQL). The Checks page provides Run now, Pause, Resume and dedicated history pages. A browser does not need to stay open for the controller's scheduler to run.

Read targets, environments and checks for the schema, interval/retention limits and reset behavior, or follow the scheduled-check tutorial. A missing sample starts as unknown; it is not counted as healthy or as an invented numeric zero.

items.title: What remains outside the implementation
items.text:
The current scheduler is a local single-controller service, not distributed coordination across replicas. Local alarm/recovery transitions do not send email, webhooks or messages. Notification delivery/retries, maintenance windows, alert acknowledgments, uptime percentages and public status pages remain future work.

Chart refresh does not store history. Use an upstream time-series query for chart samples, or the existing check history for check-specific results. No general log ingestion or DuckDB analytics pipeline is implied.

items.title: Portainer parity review: Docker Standalone and Swarm
items.text:
Reviewed 2026-11-20 against Portainer's current online Docker documentation and Declarack's adapter definitions, execution code, and UI. This is a capability review, not a claim that every supported operation has a dedicated end-to-end integration test. Portainer documentation spans Community and Business features; items explicitly documented as Business-only are noted. Kubernetes, Podman, and Edge fleet management are outside this Docker/Swarm comparison.

Conclusion: Declarack does not have full Portainer parity. It covers common inventory, inspection, lifecycle operations, Compose/stack management, and remote Swarm terminals. Advanced deployment editors, cluster-wide engine-resource management, registry workflows, GitOps automation, and multi-user governance are substantial gaps. Recent additions include a read-only volume file browser, configurable multi-target operation pages, and reviewed service/node editing built on reusable workflow extensions. Network and container creation now accept structured options. These improvements do not make the overall product equivalent to Portainer.

Legend: Covered = a shipped operation/UI handles the stated scope; Partial = narrower scope or less complete UI; Missing = no first-class shipped workflow. A Docker API endpoint being technically callable from custom YAML does not count as a finished management feature.

items.title: Docker Standalone
items.text:
Portainer reference: Docker resource overview, container details, advanced container settings, edit/duplicate, statistics.

Capability Declarack Actual scope / remaining gap Container inventory, details, full inspect JSON Covered Config-defined tables, detail fields, JSON inspection, search, sorting, page-size selection. Start, stop, restart, pause, resume, rename, remove Covered Individual container actions with confirmations for destructive actions. Create a container Partial Name/image fields now combine with typed expert Docker create JSON. Creation stays stopped and does not pull missing images. Advanced create settings Partial — expanded Typed create-options JSON now supports command, env, ports, mounts, restart/logging policies, limits, devices, DNS, capabilities and health checks. Dedicated guided controls for all options are still missing. Edit/replace or duplicate an existing container Partial — implemented Reviewed standalone cloning/replacement, retained backups, explicit recovery and tracked runs. Fresh-storage duplicate defaults; advanced JSON for many settings. Compose and Swarm use their deployment workflows. See limits. Interactive container console Covered Shell/user selection, interactive I/O and resize through Docker exec. Attach to the primary container process Missing Exec terminal is not process attachment. Container logs Partial Fetchable output, not a full live-tail/filter/download log viewer. Container statistics Partial Snapshot operation / raw data; not equivalent to live CPU, memory, network, I/O charts and process listings. Container health Partial Inspect state exposes Docker health and health-check output; no full health-check editor or historical charts. Commit a running container into an image Missing No shipped commit workflow. Container webhooks Missing No external lifecycle/redeploy webhook endpoint.

Portainer reference: images, image building, pruning, networks, volume browsing.

Capability Declarack Actual scope / remaining gap Image list, inspect, size display Covered Sizes formatted in MB/GB while sorting uses underlying bytes. Pull, tag, remove images Covered Shipped standalone workflows/actions. Build images from Dockerfile, upload, or Git Missing No image build UI or build-context management. Import/export images Missing No archive workflow. Push images / authenticated registry selection Missing No first-class registry credentials/push management. Detect newer image versions Missing No registry comparison indicator. Prune dangling/unused images and build cache Missing Disk usage is visible; individual removal does not equal reviewed bulk pruning. Network inventory, inspect, remove Covered Engine-scope resources. Network creation Partial Driver/internal/attachable fields, bridge default on Standalone, overlay default in Swarm; expert JSON supports IPAM, labels, options and IPv6. No fully guided editor for every property. Connect/disconnect containers to/from networks Covered Individual network actions. Volume inventory, inspect, attachments Covered Local volume inventory with references to attached containers. Volume size measurement Covered Explicit collection; unavailable data remains unavailable rather than zero. Create/remove volumes Partial Basic local-driver creation; no general storage-driver/options editor. Browse volume directories Partial — added Read-only directory navigation, file preview, and bounded downloads. No host-root mount is required. Upload, rename, edit, delete volume files Missing Portainer provides upload/download/rename/delete. Declarack intentionally ships read-only browsing first. Host system/device/filesystem management Partial Disk usage and configurable metrics; no general host device browser or root-filesystem management.

Portainer's volume browser requires Swarm or its Agent according to the linked documentation. Declarack uses short-lived helpers on Standalone and node-pinned jobs in Swarm. Their deployment requirements and writable capabilities differ.

items.title: Compose projects
items.text:
Portainer reference: stack deployment, stack inspection/editing, migration/duplication/rename.

Capability Declarack Actual scope / remaining gap Discover existing Compose projects Covered Docker Compose project discovery, project containers and source metadata. View Compose YAML from host Partial Requires accessible reported host paths through an explicitly configured host mount, or a saved source. Docker labels do not contain the full Compose file. Inline or mounted-folder Compose sources Covered Saved source, preview/validation, reviewed apply. Start, stop, restart, up, down, remove orphans Covered Config-defined project workflow. Git-backed standalone Compose projects Missing Current standalone editor supports inline/folder sources, unlike the Swarm GitHub stack workflow. Arbitrary Git providers/branches, multiple Compose overlays Missing No equivalent of Portainer's broader source/ref/multiple-file deployment UI. Dedicated .env editing/import and deployment-variable management Missing Not a first-class project settings workflow. Automatic Git polling and redeploy webhooks Missing Deployments remain explicit. Scheduled checks do not redeploy applications. Template catalog, deploy-from-template, save-as-template Missing Example system configurations are not an application-template catalog. Cross-environment migration/duplicate/rename wizard Missing No purpose-built transfer workflow or persistent-data migration.

items.title: Docker Swarm
items.text:
Portainer reference: services, service configuration, tasks, Swarm node details, cluster visualizer, configs, secrets.

Capability Declarack Actual scope / remaining gap Services, nodes, tasks inventory and inspect Covered Tables, details, raw JSON, desired/running replica visibility. Expand services into task/container rows Covered Task-based worker/container associations. Scale, force restart, remove a service Covered Versioned service updates for supported actions. Service logs Partial Fetchable output; not a complete live log/statistics experience. Create a service with a dedicated form Missing Deploy through Compose stacks instead. Edit service image, env, labels, mounts, ports, networks, secrets/config attachments Partial — added Version-checked YAML-defined editor with typed structured fields, preview and apply. Includes command/args, logging and health settings. More guided fields and remaining container-spec settings are still gaps. Service resources, placement, update/restart policies Partial Live editor now supports placement, resource, restart/update-policy JSON with preview; not a guided control for every subfield. Service rollback Covered — added Explicit-version rollback, previous-spec check, confirmation, Docker server-side rollback. Service redeploy webhooks Missing No external webhook trigger. Node availability (active/pause/drain) Covered Versioned node availability action. Node role promotion/demotion and label editing Covered — added Version-checked role/labels/availability editor with preview; last-manager demotion is refused. Initialize/join/leave Swarm, token/CA/autolock management Missing No complete cluster-administration interface. Cluster topology/task placement visualizer Missing Tables/relations are available; no equivalent visualizer. Remote worker container terminal Covered Task identity resolves node/container; same-image node-local relay jobs. Worker SSH is not used. Cluster-wide container/image/network lifecycle management Partial Generic Docker API operations target the manager engine. Task associations and worker terminals do not make every engine resource/action cluster-wide. Swarm overlay network creation/settings Partial — added Correct overlay default, driver and attachable controls, and expert create JSON. Existing networks still follow Docker’s immutability limits. Configs and secrets list/create/remove/inspect Covered Swarm only. Docker does not return secret contents. Neither appears as native standalone Docker resources. Per-node volume inventory/sizes/create/remove Covered Node-selected or aggregated reads through jobs. Writes select one node. Per-node volume file browsing Partial — added Explicit single-node read-only job mounts the selected volume. No writable file manager. On-demand node metrics Covered Same-image jobs aggregate node snapshots; no worker SSH or continuous metrics retention by default. Host disks/PCI devices/root filesystem Missing No full host-management interface.

items.title: Swarm stacks and source persistence
items.text:
Portainer reference: stack sources, deployment options and GitOps.

Capability Declarack Actual scope / remaining gap Inline YAML, mounted folder, GitHub source Covered Stack workflow separates source settings from deployment. Private GitHub username/PAT Covered Source metadata and encrypted token/key are target-scoped records in the shared SQLite/PostgreSQL database; redeploy retrieves the saved source and credential. See storage migration guidance. Arbitrary Git ref/branch/provider support Partial Current checkout resolves tags (refs/tags/<tag>); do not advertise general ref support. Deploy/update/remove/replace, selected volume cleanup, orphan cleanup Covered Reviewed source digest, deployment and cleanup workflow. Stack services/tasks/networks/configs/secrets/volume references Covered Related-resource views distinguish ownership/references; declared volume references are not physical node inventory. Private image registry authentication Missing GitHub PAT source access does not authenticate container registries. Automatic GitOps, webhooks, deployment windows Missing Explicit deploy only; checks scheduler is not a GitOps controller. Relative Git-repository bind mount provisioning Missing No equivalent of Portainer's documented Business-only relative-path provisioning. Application templates and cross-target migrations Missing Examples/config merging are different capabilities.

items.title: Platform and governance gaps
items.text:
References: registries, Business RBAC, authentication.

Declarack has database-backed local administrator accounts, cookie sessions with CSRF protection, native file/self-signed TLS, Docker-secret/file credential references, configuration editing and reload, target/environment separation, custom multi-target pages, persisted checks, and now bounded multi-target operation pages. These do not provide Portainer's user/team resource ownership, granular RBAC, LDAP/AD/OAuth, registry credential lifecycle, Business registry browsing/management, access-policy administration, or audit-log governance. All administrators have full installation, credential and workload access; environment grouping is not authorization. Settings supports create/disable/enable/password reset/session revocation, but no account deletion, signup or role selection. Recorded operation plans include metadata.actor, including through batch fan-out. Bounded account activity records creation, password reset, disable/enable, session revocation and host recovery, with actor identity and no secrets (1,000 retained; newest 100 available read-only). These account events and plan metadata are not a complete generic resource audit log; simple direct calls do not all produce recorded plans. HTTP Basic Auth is unsupported. TLS has no ACME, automatic renewal or redirect listener. Demo bypasses login and explicitly disallows user management. See administrators and TLS. No full Portainer Server backup/restore wizard, licensing system, Edge Agent/tunnel fleet provisioning, offline snapshots, or remote agent lifecycle management is claimed.

items.title: Recommended next work
items.text:
1. Extend the new reviewed service editor with more guided field types and remaining service settings (for example user, working directory, hostname/DNS), then add a dedicated service creation flow. Rollback and basic editing are now shipped.
  2. Expand guided controls on the shipped standalone edit/replace/duplicate flow; retain its explicit data/network handling and recovery checks.
  3. Introduce registry credential references usable by image and stack deployment; separate registry authentication from Git authentication.
