  4. Make container/image/network node scope explicit everywhere; add selected-node operations before claiming cluster-wide engine management.
  5. Add reviewed pruning with resource counts and storage estimates, without automatically deleting attached volumes or active build caches.
  6. Add generic Git refs/providers, standalone Git Compose sources, and deployment webhooks before a full GitOps controller.
  7. Expand the file browser to writable operations only with clear permissions, overwrite checks, confirmations, and backup expectations.
  8. Build team authorization and audit history before marketing multi-tenant access.

A single percentage would hide material differences. Track individual workflows, node scope, source modes, and governance separately.

items.title: Repository evidence
items.text:
• backend/adapters/docker/{features,operations,compose-features,compose-operations}.yaml
  • backend/adapters/docker/{adapter,compose,volume_files}.py
  • backend/adapters/swarm/{features,operations,workspace-features,workspace-operations}.yaml
  • backend/adapters/swarm/{adapter,inventory,terminal,terminal_relay}.py
  • backend/adapters/ssh/{adapter.py,features.yaml,operations.yaml}
  • backend/server.py (source persistence, Docker requests, job lifecycle)
  • backend/{terminal_sessions,file_tree,batches,checks}.py and backend/adapters/docker/node_agent.py
  • frontend/src/{configured,workflow,terminal,related-resources,file-browser,batch-page}.jsx

See framework workflow extensions for the reusable capabilities behind these additions.

Recent framework additions: reviewed bulk actions, filters, CSV/JSON export, opt-in refresh and multi-source charts. These do not add continuous statistics history, bulk rollback or unrestricted node scope.

items.title: Registry/Git follow-up (2026-11-21)
items.text: Target-scoped registry credential files now support image pulls, standalone Compose CLI operations, Swarm stack deployment with worker auth forwarding, and service edits. Swarm stacks gain general HTTPS/SSH Git URLs with branches, tags and full commit IDs. General Git uses saved metadata plus reusable mounted credential references; legacy GitHub tag/PAT storage remains available. This supersedes the missing-registry and tag-only rows above for these scopes. Registry browsing/push, standalone Git Compose sources, automatic GitOps, webhooks and repository bind-mount provisioning remain gaps. See setup and persistence.

items.title: Inventory scope update
items.text: Containers and networks now use node-local Swarm jobs for selected/all-node inventory, with node-qualified identities and partial failure reporting. Worker inspection and running task terminals are available directly from container rows. Direct worker lifecycle/network mutation is still not covered: those actions use the connected manager engine, with service actions governing desired task state. This expands inventory coverage without implying that every Docker action is cluster-wide. See the scope contract.

items.title: Registry credentials and Git stack sources
items.text: Define reusable credentials through Settings → Credentials, then reference IDs in targets. Both entered values and mounted-file paths use the same profiles; see credential management. Target registry settings map hosts to basic profile IDs, and git_credentials lists allowed basic/SSH profile IDs. Save and activate configuration before use. Registry and Git authentication remain separate execution scopes even when profiles are reused.

items.title: Configure target credentials
items.text:
targets:
  production:
    label: Production Swarm
    connection: docker_socket
    socket: /var/run/docker.sock
    swarm: true
    features:
    - overview
    - services
    - nodes
    - tasks
    - stacks
    - configs
    - secrets
    - networks
    - volumes
    registry_credentials:
      ghcr.io: registry_ghcr.io
      registry.example.com:5000: registry_registry.example.com_5000
    git_credentials:
    - company_https
    - company_ssh
credentials:
  registry_ghcr.io:
    type: basic
    username: example-user
    password:
      file: /run/secrets/ghcr_token
  registry_registry.example.com_5000:
    type: basic
    username: deploy
    password:
      file: /run/secrets/registry_password
  company_https:
    type: basic
    username: deploy
    host: git.example.com
    password:
      file: /run/secrets/git_token
  company_ssh:
    type: ssh
    username: git
    host: git.example.com
    private_key:
      file: /run/secrets/git_key
    known_hosts:
      file: /etc/declarack/git_known_hosts

Replace target IDs, addresses and usernames, and mount the referenced files before using the credentials. Include a port in the Git credential host when the URL uses one. HTTPS tokens and SSH keys are different profile types; SSH URLs must include the remote user, for example ssh://git@git.example.com/team/app.git. SSH requires an explicit identity and known-hosts profile. HTTPS repositories without authentication can leave the credential field empty.

Profiles are scoped to one target. A Git credential can only authenticate to its configured host and transport; redirects are refused. Registry credentials apply by image hostname. For Docker Hub use docker.io; it is normalized to Docker's https://index.docker.io/v1/ authentication key. Include a port for a non-default registry port. Do not put paths or embedded credentials in registry hostnames. Registry TLS/trust and any insecure-registry policy remain Docker engine/client configuration; this feature does not disable certificate verification.

items.title: Registry execution
items.text:
Configured credentials are available to standalone image pulls, existing standalone Compose deployment workflows, Swarm stack deployments, and reviewed Swarm service edits. Compose and stack commands receive a target-scoped temporary Docker config.json, removed after the command finishes. Swarm stack deployment adds --with-registry-auth so workers can pull private images. Service edits send a matching X-Registry-Auth header. Rollback retains Docker's previous-spec auth.

Credential files are read when an operation runs, so replacing a mounted token file does not require saving every stack again. Existing running services do not receive rotated credentials until an update/deploy forwards them. All configured registry files for a target must be readable for a Compose up or stack deploy. Read-only previews and stop/remove operations do not load registry credentials. When no registry profiles are configured, CLI workflows use the existing /etc/declarack/docker config-directory convention.

Registry authentication is separate from source-repository access: a Git PAT does not authenticate an image pull. There is no registry catalog browser, image-push workflow or credential-value editor in this change.

items.title: Use a general Git source for a Swarm stack
items.text:
1. Open Stacks → New stack, or edit a saved source.
  2. Select Git repository (HTTPS / SSH).
  3. Enter the repository URL, ref and relative Compose path.
  4. Select a configured Git credential, or leave it empty for public HTTPS.
  5. Save source, preview, validate, then deploy through the existing confirmation.

Refs can be HEAD, a branch such as main or release/next, a tag, full refs/heads/main / refs/tags/v1.2.0, or a full commit ID. Use full refs when a branch and tag share a name. The server must permit fetching the selected ref or commit; this is not a full-history clone. The default Compose path is compose.yaml; set docker-compose.yml or a nested path explicitly when needed.

Source retrieval uses Git's HTTPS/SSH protocols, rather than a provider-specific archive API. This supports GitHub, GitLab, Gitea/Forgejo and other compatible Git servers. Submodules, Git LFS materialization and symlinks are not supported. Retrieval uses isolated Git configuration, bounded commands and a bounded regular- file archive. Relative Compose config/secret files resolve from the selected Compose file's directory. Bind-mounted host paths still need to exist on the Docker nodes; downloading a repository does not provision files onto workers.

Preview reports the resolved commit and Compose digest. Deploy retrieves the source again and refuses to proceed if the ref moved or the reviewed content changed. Preview again to deploy a new revision. This is explicit deployment, not an automatic GitOps reconciler or webhook integration.

items.title: Persistence and redeploy
items.text:
The saved Swarm source record stores git_url, ref, git_path and the credential profile ID in target-scoped documents in the shared database. It stores the last deployed commit too. General Git source records store only the profile ID. The profile stores either a mounted-file reference or an entered value in system configuration. Redeploy reads the saved metadata, resolves that target's allowed named profile and reads its current credential source. Persist the configured database to retain saved source records; keep configuration and secret mounts available after container replacement.

The older GitHub tag creation mode and per-stack PAT editor have been removed. Legacy stored records may remain as historical data. Its username/PAT storage still uses an encrypted per-stack token and target encryption key, both retained in the configured database (and copied by legacy import). New Git sources use named inline/file-backed profiles instead.

General Git sources are currently offered for Swarm stacks. Standalone Compose retains inline and mounted-folder source modes; it gains registry credentials but not the new Git source editor in this change.

The live two-node lab verified private SSH retrieval, a worker deployment, and ref-change rejection. This saved source remains available for preview after its temporary workload was removed.

items.title: Upgrading to Declarack
items.text: Declarack is the new name for the application and its configurable administration framework. Existing Docker/Swarm features remain part of Declarack. There is no separate framework package to install.

items.title: New names
items.text:
Interface Current name Product, login realm, HTTP user agent Declarack Repository daniellmorris/declarack Published image path for subsequent builds ghcr.io/daniellmorris/declarack Runtime variable prefix DECLARACK_ Default config/adapter/CLI credential directory /etc/declarack Compose service / logical data volume declarack / declarack-data Current database state.sqlite by default, or PostgreSQL; legacy stack databases require import Action request header X-Declarack-Action: 1 New job labels / names io.declarack.worker-job, declarack-*

The main YAML can still be named dashboard.yaml. Its keys (targets, features, operations, auth, legacy_workspace) and resource routes have not been renamed. DOCKER_SOCKET, HOST, and PORT remain unchanged.

items.title: Existing settings and data
items.text:
Legacy SWARMDECK_* process variables are accepted as fallbacks. If both prefixes are present, the explicit DECLARACK_* value wins, including an empty value. New deployment templates use only the new names. Docker Compose's own substitution now expects the new names; backend fallbacks do not rewrite your Compose .env file.

Current releases use the shared storage service, defaulting to state.sqlite. Stop the controller and explicitly import an old data directory before using it. Legacy import reads swarmdeck.sqlite when declarack.sqlite does not exist, copies encrypted PATs and credential.key into database documents, and preserves the original files. If both old names exist, declarack.sqlite wins; investigate before combining data. Target IDs continue to determine source scopes.

Browser preferences are copied from old keys when a matching new key is absent. The legacy action header remains accepted during upgrades; new clients send the Declarack header. Existing worker labels remain recognized for resource filtering and expired-job/network cleanup. New jobs use Declarack labels.

items.title: Docker Compose upgrade
items.text:
Renaming a Compose service does not rename an existing running container or volume. Before switching, inspect your existing deployment and identify its actual data volume name. Stop the old dashboard service to release port 8080, then deploy the new service with the same data volume explicitly attached. Do not remove that volume. For example, an additional override can reuse a volume already present:

volumes:
  declarack-data:
    external: true
    name: YOUR_EXISTING_DATA_VOLUME_NAME

Use the exact name from docker volume ls/the existing container's mount inspection. The logical volume name in the new Compose file is declarack-data; Docker's actual volume name may be project-prefixed. Without a reuse mapping, a renamed deployment can create a fresh empty volume. Keep the previous volume and a backup until verified.

Update environment names, service references in overrides, image names, mounted /etc/declarack paths, and any DECLARACK_CONFIG_SERVICE references. Paths explicitly stored in your YAML can remain old paths if you keep mounting files at those paths; the application does not automatically rewrite target configuration files.

Rebuild/publish the renamed image and update Swarm agent_image references to the same build, preferably by digest. Renaming a GitHub repository does not move old GHCR packages. Previous image names/digests are not deleted or republished as part of the source rename. Update deployment automation and image-pull credentials as needed.

The active local checkout directory is not moved while Codex is using it. Its Git remote can point to the renamed repository independently of the checkout folder name.

items.title: Source-based forms and tracked operation plans
items.text: Declarack's core supplies reusable form controls, source mapping, reviewed actions, and durable operation records. Docker-specific recreation rules live in the Docker adapter, not the React renderer. This is the first built-in consumer of the plan runner; YAML does not yet provide an arbitrary background workflow language.

items.title: Structured form fields
items.text:
Workflows support these field types in addition to ordinary inputs and JSON:

fields:
  - key: labels
    label: Labels
    type: key-value
    max_items: 100
  - key: env
    label: Environment
    type: string-list
  - key: ports
    label: Ports
    type: collection
    item_fields:
      - {key: port, label: Container port, type: number, integer: true, min: 1, max: 65535, required: true}
      - key: protocol
        label: Protocol
        type: select
        default: tcp
        choices: {tcp: TCP, udp: UDP}

Each control can switch between rows and advanced JSON. Maps reject duplicate or empty keys and non-string values. Collections retain unknown row properties, so editing known columns does not discard future API fields. Numbers, bounds, required columns and select choices are checked before requests are submitted. Operation schemas and adapter validation remain authoritative on the server. The default row limit is 256. A key-value field can specify key_pattern.

Swarm service labels, environment, commands and ports use these controls; Docker container forms reuse them. Advanced API structures remain available as JSON.

items.title: Seeding and dependent defaults
items.text:
initial maps source fields into form fields. seed.expression selects the base object before initial mappings; seed.omit removes dot-separated paths from a copy. Without a seed expression, the source entry is the base as before.

seed:
  expression: config
  omit: [identity, metadata.version]
initial:
  source_id: Id
fields:
  - key: mode
    label: Operation
    type: select
    choices: {duplicate: Duplicate, replace: Replace}
    reset_map:
      name: 'form.mode = "duplicate" ? entry.editor.copy_name : entry.editor.name'
      start: 'form.mode = "replace" and entry.editor.running'
    changes_source: true

The selected value is already in form when reset_map runs. JSONata expressions also receive the usual workflow context. changes_source invalidates the preview. A feature can use workflow_by_provider to replace its workflow for a particular provider. All variants are validated; only the selected variant's operations are exposed for that target. This keeps standalone replacement off Swarm task pages.

items.title: Server-owned execution
items.text:
Adapter executors can submit ordered Step instances to operation_runs() from the backend services dictionary. Each step has an ID, title, callable, optional condition and descriptive retry_safe flag. The runner records pending, running, completed, skipped and failed steps. If execution fails, it runs the explicitly declared recovery steps in order, attempting remaining recovery steps even when one fails. A retry-safe declaration does not cause automatic retries.

A workflow action consuming the resulting {run_id: ...} uses:

await_run: true
open_result: container_id

The browser follows the run through GET requests and opens the returned resource when complete. Closing the browser stops watching; execution continues on the server. The global Operations page lists recent runs and displays step results, recovery failures and metadata. APIs are GET /api/v1/runs and GET /api/v1/runs/<id> under the existing application authentication.

Records live in the shared database. Resource/run lock files remain local to the runtime data directory. Persist the database to retain records. The latest 1,000 terminal records are retained, and the list returns the latest 100. Step results are bounded at 128 KiB. A resource lock serializes plans against the same daemon/container, including aliases targeting the same engine; it does not lock external Docker CLI users or every ordinary lifecycle action.

Runs are process-owned. After backend termination, an abandoned run is marked interrupted when read. It is never silently resumed or replayed. Inspect Docker resources, completed step results and recovery metadata before taking manual action. This implementation requires a single controller with a local data volume; it is not a distributed job queue or a high-availability scheduler.

items.title: Standalone container duplicate and replace
items.text:
Open an unmanaged standalone container's dedicated detail page. Choose Duplicate or Edit / replace, adjust the fields, then preview and confirm. The preview freezes the submitted request; source fingerprints and preview digests reject stale edits. The image must already exist locally.

  • Duplicate starts with a new name, stopped state, no published host ports and fresh anonymous local volumes. Source bind mounts are omitted. Copied static IPs and network aliases are removed. Explicit controls allow source mount sharing and port publication, with warnings about writers and port conflicts.
  • Replace checks dependencies, stops the source if running, disables its automatic restart policy, renames it to declarack-backup-..., releases network endpoints, creates the new container, reconnects additional networks, optionally starts it and verifies state/health. Actual named and anonymous volume identities, bind settings, declared network aliases/static IPs, limits and restart settings are preserved in normalized create configuration. Editing advanced JSON can intentionally change them.
  • Failure retains a stopped new container as declarack-failed-..., then disables its restart policy and attempts to restore the original name, network attachments, restart policy and running state. If replacement shutdown and restart isolation cannot be confirmed, the original stays stopped for manual recovery. Any recovery failure remains visible. Preflight failures do not mutate the source.

No container or volume is automatically deleted. Retained backups and failed containers consume storage and may still reference volumes; remove them manually only after verifying the result. A replacement creates a fresh image-based writable layer: files changed outside mounts are not copied. Recovery restores configuration, not application data modified on shared storage. This is not a filesystem snapshot.

Swarm tasks must be managed through services/stacks. Compose replacement must use the Compose project (duplicates drop Compose ownership labels). Replacement of the active controller, auto-remove sources, shared container namespaces, dependent namespace consumers and legacy links is refused. SELinux-relabeled bind mounts and unsupported mount kinds require deployment-managed recreation. Dependency scanning is bounded to 256 containers. There is no automatic image pull, cancellation, automatic retry, or crash recovery. Existing rename/network-connect/start actions and the retained run metadata support explicit manual recovery after inspection.

Implementation examples: backend/adapters/docker/recreate-operations.yaml, backend/adapters/docker/features.yaml, backend/adapters/docker/recreate.py, and backend/operation_runs.py.

items.title: Action output placement and viewers
items.text: Actions can display a result beneath the resource that produced it, in the page, or in a dialog. This is a shared renderer contract: Docker, Swarm, SSH and HTTP adapters return data; feature YAML chooses the presentation. No adapter-specific React component is needed.

items.title: Configure an inline row result
items.text:
Add a stable identity and an output action to an existing feature:

features:
  applications:
    title: Applications
    operation: apps.list
    rows: items
    selection_key: id
    columns:
      - {label: Name, value: name}
    actions:
      - label: Metrics
        operation: apps.metrics
        row: {id: id}
        immediate: true
        output: $
        presentation:
          placement: row
          viewer: structured
      - label: Inspect JSON
        operation: apps.inspect
        row: {id: id}
        immediate: true
        output: json
        presentation: {placement: row, viewer: json}

This is a feature fragment. Define the apps.list, apps.metrics and apps.inspect operations with bindings for your adapter, then enable applications on the target. List results in this example have an items array with unique string or integer id fields. The two action operations accept id. See the API interface tutorial for connection and operation setup.

Synthetic HTTP example: the result belongs to Alpha, rather than the page header.

Clicking Metrics opens the result directly underneath that application's row. Inspect JSON replaces that row's metrics panel. Another row can have its own independent result open at the same time. A close control hides each panel.

items.title: Contract
items.text:
Setting Values / behavior presentation.placement row, page (default), or dialog presentation.viewer structured, json, or text; default is json for output: json, otherwise text output: '$' Pass the entire returned value to the viewer, preserving types output: json Pass the entire returned value; defaults to the searchable JSON inspector output: FIELD Pass a direct result property to the viewer; this is not JSONata immediate: true Execute directly when clicked, using configured row/selection inputs

structured shows top-level fields and expandable nested values. json reuses the searchable tree/text inspector with copy and download controls. text preserves text formatting and serializes objects as JSON. Viewers grow with their content up to 80% of the viewport height, then scroll. Use Expand height to show the complete result at its natural height, and Limit height to restore the scrollable limit; they do not mask fields or truncate the returned payload. Missing or empty text output is reported explicitly, rather than inventing data.

For a page result, use presentation: {placement: page, viewer: text}. For an output dialog, use presentation: {placement: dialog, viewer: json}. Placement does not change the adapter operation, authorization or confirmation requirements. An output dialog is a result viewer, not an extra confirmation step.

items.title: Row identity and lifetime
items.text:
A row result requires row input bindings and a stable identity supplied by selection_key, details.row_id, or children.row_id (in that order). Identity paths support dotted fields and must resolve to a unique nonempty string or a safe integer. Zero is a valid identity. For node-local resources, use a key containing both node and resource identity; a volume name alone is not unique across nodes.

Sorting, filtering and pagination do not reassign results to another row. Hidden rows retain their result while you navigate the same loaded inventory. A fresh inventory collection, selector change or route change clears results. Closing a panel or starting a different output action for the same row invalidates older responses, so a slow response cannot reopen or overwrite it. Closing hides the result; it does not undo or cancel a server-side operation already submitted.

Loading and action failures appear in the row panel. An inline read does not block actions on other rows. It does not trigger an automatic inventory reload. Existing related-resource expansion remains available independently.

Row placement is for list actions. It cannot be combined with detail: true, back, result: replace, bulk actions, terminals or file browsers. Page and dialog placement are available for ordinary output actions, including detail views. Every explicit presentation requires output. Invalid settings are rejected when configuration is loaded.

Actions without presentation retain page-level output. Dedicated resource detail pages remain accessible through resource links. Confirmed actions still use their declared confirmation; do not set immediate on actions that require confirmation.

items.title: Bundled usage
items.text: Container stats use structured inline output. List-row Inspect JSON actions for containers, images, networks, volumes, Swarm services, nodes, tasks, configs and secrets use inline JSON output. Detail-page inspection stays in the page. Volume keys retain node ownership, and Swarm child-container expansion is independent of action output.

items.title: Row forms and conditional actions
items.text:
A row action without confirmation opens its input form directly below its row when the feature declares a stable identity. Forms retain the target and resource label from the configured table or detail fields. They use the same row slot as inline results, so editing a tag and inspecting JSON do not move the user to an unrelated page-top panel. The open form and its in-memory field values remain associated with that identity through sorting, filtering and paging; they are discarded when the form is cancelled or successfully submitted. Features without stable row identity retain the page form. Confirmation-based actions keep modal dialogs.

Use visible_when for a JSONata row condition that hides an irrelevant action, and enabled_when to disable a visible action for the current state. Neither replaces backend authorization or adapter scope checks. Main resource tables also honor column tone and link_when, matching the shared row mapping used elsewhere. A feature may offer multiple terminal transports with different row identities; the session renderer selects the transport matching the encoded identity, rather than assuming the first terminal action applies to every row.

items.title: Active system configuration
items.text:
The database is now authoritative for system configuration as well as runtime state. Individual YAML documents retain their original text and folder paths in immutable revisions under the framework.configuration document namespace. A small state record points to the saved and active revisions. Saving a GUI draft does not change the running system; Activate configuration does. A restart loads the active database revision, including when import files are absent. Pending saved changes remain available after restart but are not applied silently.

environment:
  DECLARACK_CONFIG: /etc/declarack/config
  DECLARACK_CONFIG_FORCE_LOAD: "0"
  DECLARACK_CONFIG_WRITE_BACK: "0"
  DECLARACK_CONFIG_EDIT: "1"
volumes:
  - declarack-data:/data
  - ./config:/etc/declarack/config:ro

This is a deployment fragment; retain your normal authentication and target mounts.

Setting Behavior Both flags off (default) Import the configured source only when the database has no configuration; later starts use the active database revision. GUI saves stay in the database. DECLARACK_CONFIG_FORCE_LOAD=1 Validate and import the configured source on every startup. Files take precedence over both saved and active GUI revisions. Invalid/unreadable source fails startup without replacing the previous active revision. DECLARACK_CONFIG_WRITE_BACK=1 Before activating a GUI revision, write its documents back to the local configured file/folder. Requires an existing source, writable directory mount and appropriate permissions. Saving alone does not write files. Both flags on Startup loads files; GUI activation writes changes back so the next startup imports them. DECLARACK_CONFIG_EDIT=0 Disable GUI document editing. Editing defaults to enabled for database-managed configuration.

The two import/write-back flags require an explicit DECLARACK_CONFIG path. Without one, first startup seeds the database with the detected local Docker/Swarm configuration and exposes logical documents to the GUI. Importing a single YAML file preserves single-document editing; importing a folder retains folder-style editing and Add integration. Mounting source files read-only does not prevent DB-only GUI editing; set DECLARACK_CONFIG_EDIT=0 when that is desired.

Settings shows saved/active revisions and pending activation. Review import from files → Import & activate explicitly replaces database configuration after a source diff and revision check. Export documents returns JSON containing each logical path and its original YAML text, plus the saved revision. To recreate a folder, write each document's yaml to its relative path. Export never includes contents of externally referenced secret files. Restoring revision history still loads a draft, which must be reviewed, saved and activated.

The source snapshot used for import is retained as the write-back baseline. External edits cause a conflict rather than an overwrite. Multi-document write-back uses a database journal and atomic replacement of each file; it is not an atomic filesystem/database transaction. Interrupted publication retains the old active revision and retries on activation or startup before any forced import. If a file contains an external edit, recovery stops: reconcile each affected file to its pre-activation or proposed contents, then retry. Fix mount/permission errors before retrying. Do not run another controller against a partially published tree. File deletions during write-back are unsupported; GUI operations currently add or update documents. Writable directory mounts are required even for a single file, so atomic replacement works. Concurrent external filesystem writers still require operator coordination; filesystems do not provide the database's compare-and-swap.

Configuration snapshots retain 20 historical revisions per installation source. Immutable document revisions referenced by that history, the active/saved pointers, or the import/recovery baseline are retained; unreferenced ones are pruned.

Git and Swarm-config providers remain import/publication sources. Publish to source provider uses their existing pull-request or service-config workflow. Publication does not replace the local active pointer. Import the updated source explicitly or use startup force-load. Automatic WRITE_BACK is supported only for local file/folder sources, so publishing a PR cannot be mistaken for updating its branch. Authentication/legacy workspace changes still require restart with an appropriate source import. None of this enables multiple active controllers.

For normal DB-managed operation, back up the database plus mounted credentials and external application folders. YAML import files are useful exports/seeds; they are no longer required for restart unless force-load/write-back is enabled. An older database with no configuration record imports its source once at next startup; the prior configuration history and runtime records are retained.

Declarack uses SQLAlchemy Core and Alembic with two supported backends:

  • SQLite by default: one controller, /data/state.sqlite, no database server.
  • PostgreSQL when configured: the same stores and operations, using psycopg.

PostgreSQL is tested alongside SQLite in CI. Other SQLAlchemy dialects are not currently supported or advertised. No ORM or external queue is required.

items.title: Select a backend
items.text:
SQLite requires no new setting. The repository Compose deployment persists its /data directory using the declarack-data volume. DECLARACK_DATA changes the runtime directory. An explicit SQLite URL must use an absolute path:

DECLARACK_DATABASE_URL=sqlite:////data/state.sqlite

For PostgreSQL, set one of these bootstrap environment variables:

DECLARACK_DATABASE_URL=postgresql+psycopg://user:password@database:5432/declarack
DECLARACK_DATABASE_URL_FILE=/run/secrets/declarack_database_url

The second option reads a mounted single-line file containing the URL; it does not put database credentials in system YAML. URL-encode reserved characters in a username or password. The connection-string setting is deployment configuration, not a live-editable Settings field. Restart the controller after changing it or its mounted URL file. Both drivers ship in the application image. Provision the PostgreSQL database and account first. Use your normal PostgreSQL TLS options in the URL and grant schema/table migration permissions.

For example, an override for the repository Compose deployment can contain:

services:
  declarack:
    environment:
      DECLARACK_DATABASE_URL_FILE: /run/secrets/declarack_database_url
    secrets:
      - declarack_database_url
secrets:
  declarack_database_url:
    file: ./secrets/database-url

This example expects an existing reachable database; it does not install one. Keep the base deployment's authentication, socket and application source mounts. For Swarm, provision the URL as a Docker secret using the same container path.

items.title: What the database owns
items.text:
State Representation Administrators and scrypt password hashes users Hashed opaque session tokens and expiry user_sessions Serialized account-write coordination auth_control Hashed username/client login-throttle buckets login_limits Bounded account audit events Generic documents in framework.auth.audit; newest 1,000 retained, newest 100 exposed by the activity API Check state, pauses and bounded results checks, check_history Multi-step operation/recovery records operation_runs Configuration editor source snapshots configuration_snapshots Swarm source metadata and legacy encrypted PATs Documents in swarm.stacks, scoped by target Legacy PAT encryption keys Binary documents in swarm.credentials, scoped by target Standalone Compose source definitions and inline YAML Documents in docker.compose, scoped by target Adapter-owned small files/documents Namespaced versioned binary documents, maximum 2 MiB each

Keys for legacy encrypted PATs now travel with those records in database backup and transfer. Database access therefore protects both ciphertext and its key; this is not encryption independent of database access. New Git/registry profiles continue to reference external files/secrets instead of copying their values into source records.

The database does not own Docker's volumes or application data. It also does not replace mounted system configuration, Git configuration publication, Swarm config attachments, external Compose folders, auxiliary files or mounted credential sources. Back up those resources separately.

Inline Compose YAML is materialized into a local working file as needed. Deleting that cache does not delete the saved source. Mounted-folder sources still need their referenced filesystem available on the controller. Git checkouts and registry auth files remain temporary. Arbitrary host files and large backups are not implicitly uploaded to the document store.

items.title: Upgrade an existing data directory
items.text:
Existing databases are never silently ignored or overwritten. Stop the old controller, back up the complete data directory, then import its previous stores into an empty destination using the new image/environment:

python -m backend.storage import-legacy --source /data

--source is the old directory. The destination is selected by DECLARACK_DATABASE_URL / _FILE, or defaults to /data/state.sqlite. Use --data /another/runtime-directory if needed. The import reads old SQLite files and Compose source files, copies their records and encryption keys in one database transaction, and leaves the originals unchanged. It supports the historical swarmdeck.sqlite filename too. Missing optional stores are allowed; malformed records fail the import and roll back copied data. Existing destination records cause refusal, rather than merging or overwriting.

For a named-volume Compose deployment, after building the new image and stopping the controller, a one-off container with the same volume and environment can run that command. Keep the old files until backups and application verification are complete. The controller detects legacy files without an import marker and tells you to import before using storage; this prevents an accidental empty-state upgrade.

On ordinary startups, embedded Alembic migrations upgrade the selected schema. Migration 0002 adds users, user_sessions, auth_control and login_limits; first-account bootstrap runs only if the users table is empty. Account passwords use scrypt:32768:8:3; sessions store token hashes, not raw cookie tokens. Accounts are independent of YAML revisions and target credential profiles. The operator can also run:

python -m backend.storage upgrade

Future schema changes belong in new migration revisions. Review migrations and back up state before upgrading an installation.

items.title: Move between SQLite and PostgreSQL
items.text:
Stop the controller and ensure both databases are backed up. Put the full source and destination URLs in mounted single-line files, then run:

python -m backend.storage transfer \
  --source-url-file /run/secrets/source_database_url \
  --destination-url-file /run/secrets/destination_database_url

The command copies every framework table, including versioned binary documents, source records, encryption keys and all four authentication tables, into an empty destination transaction. Account hashes, session expiries, login limits and retained account audit documents travel with the transfer; private TLS files do not. The command preserves check-history sequence IDs and prepares the PostgreSQL sequence for subsequent inserts. The source remains unchanged. Identical URLs and nonempty destinations are refused. Change the controller's database setting only after successful transfer, then verify account login, checks, source previews and history. This is an offline data transfer, not live database replication or continuous synchronization.

items.title: Adapter storage contract
items.text:
Adapters receive a storage factory in services['storage']. It returns a framework-owned Storage with SQLAlchemy Core connection/transaction access and documents(namespace, scope). Domain-specific records and behavior remain in the adapter. For example:

storage = services['storage']()
files = storage.documents('example.adapter', target['_storage'] or '__default__')
revision = files.put_json('source', {'repo': 'example/project'}, expected_revision=None)
source = files.get_json('source')
files.put_json('source', {**source, 'ref': 'main'}, expected_revision=revision)

Namespaces and target scopes isolate records. expected_revision=None requires a new document; an existing revision requires a matching saved version. Conflicts return an operation error instead of overwriting another editor's changes. Documents expose binary content and metadata; adapters should serialize only what they own, and avoid storing temporary files or credential values unnecessarily. Operations can participate in a shared transaction through the provided connection. Framework relational tables use Core expressions; migrations retain explicit schema snapshots.

items.title: Execution and availability boundaries
items.text:
Both modes currently support one active controller. An external database does not coordinate schedulers, operation ownership, terminals or local locks across replicas. Checks and multi-step runs still have process/local-directory ownership; restart inspection marks abandoned runs interrupted rather than resuming their side effects automatically. Terminal sessions, tunnels and in-memory previews remain ephemeral.

With PostgreSQL, /data can be ephemeral for the database-backed records above; it still holds local working files, locks and generated TLS identity. Persist /data/tls/cert.pem and /data/tls/key.pem in self-signed mode so restart does not change client trust. File-mode TLS certificates/keys remain external mounted files. TLS identity is not stored in the database or copied by database transfer. Persist or remount anything operator-managed there, such as custom folder sources. System configuration, external secrets and Docker state keep their own persistence requirements.

Back up SQLite while stopped or with a consistent SQLite backup procedure. Back up PostgreSQL using PostgreSQL tools. A database outage stops durable operations; the application does not silently fall back to a fresh local SQLite database.

items.title: Storage verification
items.text:
CI starts a disposable PostgreSQL service and runs the same repository contracts against SQLite and PostgreSQL. Locally, set DECLARACK_TEST_POSTGRES_URL only to a dedicated disposable test database, then run python -m unittest backend.tests.test_storage. These integration tests clear that database's framework tables; never use an installation database for them.

Existing configuration revisions remain available for restoration into a draft after migration.

items.title: Credential profiles
items.text: Named credential definitions are part of configuration documents. Entered values therefore persist in the database, history, exports, and optional write-back files. Mounted-file profiles persist only references. Inline SSH keys/known-hosts are materialized privately under temporary directories for OpenSSH and are disposable. Environment bootstrap inputs remain deployment settings. A named bootstrap profile is configuration and shares its history/export behavior; it is used only to seed the first administrator, not to rotate existing account passwords. See credential management.

items.title: Authentication and TLS backups
items.text: Back up authentication tables with the database; they include administrator password hashes, hashed sessions and throttle state. The generic documents table also holds bounded framework.auth.audit account events without secrets; these are included in database backup/transfer, not YAML exports. Protect restored copies as installation-wide credentials. Restore generated self-signed TLS files separately from <DECLARACK_DATA>/tls (normally /data/tls); the private key must remain 0600. File-mode TLS keys/certificates and credential secret mounts also need separate backup/rotation. Database-backed configuration exports contain inline bootstrap profile values but never the contents of externally referenced files. See account recovery and TLS lifecycle.

items.title: Reusable tables, bulk actions, refresh and charts
items.text: These capabilities belong to the framework. Features and adapters supply data, expressions, input schemas and operations; the renderer contains no resource-type switches. Built-in Docker/Swarm configurations demonstrate them, and custom HTTP or SSH features use the same definitions.

items.title: Inventory filters, exports and refresh
items.text:
A feature or custom-page panel can define up to 12 filters. Each filter maps a row with JSONata, then compares its string value to the selected choice. Filters combine with text search and sorting. Empty selection means all values.

filters:
  - key: state
    label: State
    value: State
    choices: {running: Running, exited: Stopped, created: Created}

Inventory tables and custom-page panels export all currently filtered/sorted rows, including rows beyond the current page. CSV includes the visible columns (panel columns for custom pages). Values are quoted and spreadsheet formula prefixes are neutralized. JSON contains full mapped row objects with original value types; it is unmasked. Hidden columns affect CSV only. Exports are browser downloads and do not write application storage. Related-resource tables retain their existing UI.

Custom-page panels now have search, filters, sorting and page-size controls rather than truncating results permanently. Their limit remains the initial page size (1–100). Inventory selection supports up to 100 resources across pages. Select-all selects only the current page, within that cap. Refresh clears selection; auto refresh pauses while resources are selected.

Feature and page refresh_interval defaults to 0 (off), or can be 5–3600 seconds. The UI offers an independent, session-only interval selector. Hidden browser tabs start no new refreshes, missed ticks do not queue, and refreshes do not overlap. Inventory refresh pauses during actions, confirmation, bulk selection and loading. Detail editors and on-demand/manual features do not refresh automatically. Custom-page refresh collects only non-manual sources; manual metrics remain explicit. This is browser-driven polling, not a background scheduler. Checks remain separate.

items.title: Reviewed bulk actions
items.text:
Opt existing row actions into bulk execution:

selection_key: id
operation: applications.list
rows: items
actions:
  - label: Restart application
    operation: applications.restart
    row: {id: id}
    enabled_when: state = "running"
    bulk: true
    confirmation: Restart these applications? Expect brief interruptions.

selection_key is a stable unique row field path, defaulting to details.row_id. Values must be strings or safe integers; map other identities to strings. Composite identities can be created by the feature's rows mapping: the built-in volume table uses node ID plus volume name. Bulk actions require a confirmation, row-bound inputs and a stable key. They reuse ordinary operation schemas/defaults; shared inventory inputs such as selected node scope supply matching action inputs. Actions needing additional user-entered values are skipped if their required inputs cannot be supplied. Terminals and file browsers cannot be bulk actions.

The browser submits selected keys and the action's operation name, not arbitrary execution definitions. The server verifies that the feature/action is enabled on the target, re-reads inventory, maps rows and checks enabled_when, disabled and operation arguments. Missing/ineligible resources are listed as skipped. Ambiguous inventory keys are rejected. The confirmation shows eligible count, keys and skips. Confirmation requires a digest of this preview; a fresh inventory read must still produce the same eligible inputs before execution starts.

Eligible operations execute sequentially once each, in selection order. A failed resource does not stop remaining resources. The parent run is failed if any step fails, and the Operations page preserves each result. Nested asynchronous runs are watched by their run ID (up to one hour); timeout does not cancel the child. There are no automatic mutation retries or bulk rollback. Inventory/action state can still change after preview: adapters/remote APIs must enforce their own constraints. A per-target/feature bulk lock prevents overlapping bulk runs of that feature; it does not lock external clients or every individual action.

Bulk execution uses the same durable run store and interruption rules described in operation plans. Closing the browser does not stop server execution. Normal mutations stop if their journal cannot be written; explicit recovery safety steps remain best effort when storage fails.

API routes (under existing authentication and action-request protection):

  • POST /api/v1/targets/<target>/features/<feature>/bulk/preview
  • POST /api/v1/targets/<target>/features/<feature>/bulk/run

Both receive {operation, keys, inputs}; run additionally requires digest and confirmed: true. Selection is limited to 100 keys and inventory to 10,000 rows.

Built-in opt-ins: container start/stop/restart/pause/resume/remove, image removal, network removal, volume removal, and service restart/removal. Docker still rejects in-use resources. Bulk availability follows enabled operations and target scope; it does not turn manager-local Docker operations into cluster-wide operations.

items.title: Multi-source dashboard charts
items.text:
Custom pages can contain cards, panels, charts, or any combination. Chart rows receives {data, sources}, exactly like cards and panels. x and each series value receive one mapped row. For example:

pages:
  workloads:
    title: Workloads
    refresh_interval: 30
    sources:
      containers: {target: local, operation: containers.list}
      services: {target: production, operation: swarm.services.list}
    charts:
      - title: Workloads across targets
        type: bar
        sources: [containers, services]
        rows: >-
          [{"target":"Local Docker","count":$count(data.containers)},
           {"target":"Production Swarm","count":$count(data.services)}]
        x: target
        series:
          - {label: Workloads, value: count}
      - title: Service replicas
        type: bar
        sources: [services]
        rows: data.services
        x: Spec.Name
        series:
          - {label: Running, value: ServiceStatus.RunningTasks}
          - {label: Desired, value: ServiceStatus.DesiredTasks}

Sources must already be enabled inventory/detail/related reads. Existing target and environment page placement rules apply. type is bar or line; a page can have up to 24 charts, each with 1–8 series. limit is 1–200 (default 100), selecting the last mapped rows. Input order is preserved: sort timestamp rows in JSONata for line charts. wide: true spans both columns on wide screens. Native SVG tooltips show full labels/values. No new chart runtime dependency is needed.

Only finite numeric values are plotted. Missing/null/string values remain gaps, not fabricated zeros; unavailable sources show an unavailable state. Negative and zero values are supported. Charts show the returned snapshot/query data and retain no historical samples. To show time series, query a source that supplies history, such as a Prometheus range query. No DuckDB/log ingestion is implied.

The complete operations dashboard configuration includes two charts, filters, paging and an opt-in 30-second refresh interval.

items.title: Row action results
items.text: Use action output presentation to expand structured data, JSON or text beneath the originating row. Placement and viewers are configured in YAML and shared across adapters. Related-resource expansion remains separate.

items.title: Integration templates and dynamic form options
items.text: Declarack can generate an integration from an installed template and populate form choices from configured operations. These are reusable framework capabilities: adapter folders and trusted configuration supply the definitions; the frontend has no Docker/Grafana/SSH setup branches.

items.title: Add an integration
items.text:
Open Targets → Add integration (also available from Settings).

  1. Choose a template and enter a unique target ID, display name and connection settings.
  2. Optionally choose an environment ID or type a new one. Blank leaves the target ungrouped. Existing environments retain their current targets and page assignments.
  3. Review the generated YAML. Declarack validates the complete merged configuration, including operation references, connection settings and source-file ordering.
  4. Optionally test the draft connection. This runs the connector's ordinary probe; it does not save the target or verify every resource permission/API endpoint.
  5. Save the integration as a new configuration fragment, then Reload configuration. Use Edit saved YAML to open that exact source file in Settings.

Saving requires a writable folder-backed configuration and DECLARACK_CONFIG_EDIT=1. Catalog browsing is available for read-only deployments. The wizard does not write single-file, Git-backed, or Swarm-config-backed settings; existing editing workflows for those modes are unchanged.

Installed templates cover local Docker, Docker through SSH, Swarm through SSH, SSH host metrics, Grafana, Prometheus and a custom HTTP JSON API. Each HTTP template also has an SSH-tunneled variant. These connect to existing systems; they do not provision Docker engines, Swarm clusters or monitoring servers. SSH keys, known_hosts and optional bearer-token files must already be mounted in Declarack. HTTP bearer/basic credentials require HTTPS, as they do for manually configured targets.

Generated operation and feature IDs use the new target ID as a namespace, allowing multiple copies of an integration. Existing targets, files, operation definitions and feature definitions are never overwritten. Sequential default filenames such as zz-integrations/000001-staging.yaml preserve the order of successive additions. If another later source overrides the target or environment membership, review fails with a filename-ordering error rather than silently losing the new target.

Review/save use the source revision and a digest. Any intervening source edit requires a fresh review. Saving does not reload configuration or run deployment operations. A failed connection test can still be saved for an offline target. Installed templates select named credentials from Settings → Credentials; profiles can hold entered values or mounted file references. The generated fragment remains ordinary editable configuration.

items.title: Supply a new template
items.text:
An adapter manifest can list template files:

integration_templates: [integration-templates.yaml]

Those files contain an integration_templates mapping, just like adapter operation and feature files. Trusted system configuration can also add templates under the same top-level key. Duplicate IDs are rejected. Changes to deployment-managed single-file template definitions follow the same restrictions as operation/feature definitions; folder configuration authors can edit their source files and reload.

Here is a complete additional template fragment, using the installed Docker adapter:

integration_templates:
  company.docker-readonly:
    title: Docker inventory
    description: Start with a small inventory view of an existing engine.
    fields:
      - key: socket
        label: Mounted Docker socket
        default: /var/run/docker.sock
        required: true
        pattern: '^/'
    document:
      targets:
        '{{id}}':
          label: '{{label}}'
          connection: docker_socket
          socket: '{{socket}}'
          features: [disk_usage]

id and label are common fields supplied by the framework; environment placement is handled separately. Template fields support text, number, checkbox and static select controls, defaults, required, pattern, max_length, numeric min/max/integer, and JSONata syntax validation with format: jsonata. Up to 24 custom parameters are supported. Installed SSH presets demonstrate integer ports and mounted paths.

The document is a YAML/JSON tree. {{field}} as an entire value preserves the parameter's type. Embedded placeholders interpolate text, including mapping keys such as {{id}}.resources. YAML is serialized after expansion; parameter text is never evaluated as YAML, shell commands or JavaScript. Empty optional mapping values are omitted; false and 0 are preserved. A template must create exactly the requested target ID. It may additionally add namespaced operations, features, pages, checks or batches. It cannot modify auth or configuration-storage settings.

Installed definitions are examples under backend/adapters/{docker,swarm,ssh,http}/integration-templates.yaml. Templates are trusted configuration, not remotely downloaded packages or an installer mechanism. The HTTP API preset supplies a generic one-column JSON view; customize the saved feature columns, actions and mappings in YAML to fit the actual API.

API endpoints use existing application authentication/action-request protection:

  • GET /api/v1/settings/integrations: templates, environments and source revision.
  • POST /api/v1/settings/integrations/preview: validate and return generated YAML.
  • POST /api/v1/settings/integrations/test: validate and probe the draft target.
  • POST /api/v1/settings/integrations/save: revalidate and create the new file.

POST bodies contain template, values, optional environment/path, and revision. Save also requires the reviewed digest.

items.title: Dynamic select fields
items.text:
Use options_from on a workflow select field:

- key: image
  label: Image
  type: select
  required: true
  allow_custom: true
  options_from:
    operation: images.list
    rows: '$distinct(RepoTags[$ != "<none>:<none>"])'
    value: '$'
    label: '$'
    limit: 200

The standalone container form uses this image picker and an optional primary network picker. A blank network keeps Docker defaults or advanced create options. The selected network is mapped into HostConfig through workflow JSONata, not JSX. Image loading does not pull an image or start a container.

options_from.operation must be a declared inventory, selector, detail or related read with a binding compatible with the workflow target. The workflow grants this read without requiring its resource to appear in navigation. Actions are refused as option sources. Config authors remain responsible for assigning genuine reads as inventory operations: an arbitrary external command/API cannot be proven read-only by its name. Manual/on-demand inventory requires manual: true, which shows an explicit Load options button and never auto-collects after dependency changes.

rows maps the operation result. value and label map each returned row. Values must be unique strings or safe integers; the select submits strings. Duplicate identities produce an error. The default limit is 200, configurable from 1–1000; truncation is shown in the UI. Refresh options explicitly re-reads the source. Without allow_custom, unavailable values/loading errors prevent selecting an invalid choice. Existing values remain visible, never silently replaced by the first option. allow_custom: true offers suggestions and permits manual text when an API is unavailable or an existing value is not returned.

items.title: Dependent fields
items.text:
Inputs are JSONata expressions evaluated against the workflow context (form, entry, provider, creating, results). Declare parent fields explicitly:

fields:
  - key: project
    label: Project
    type: select
    required: true
    options_from:
      operation: projects.list
      rows: items
      value: id
      label: name
  - key: deployment
    label: Deployment
    type: select
    required: true
    options_from:
      operation: deployments.list
      depends_on: [project]
      inputs:
        project_id: form.project
      rows: items
      value: id
      label: name

The example operation names must be defined as compatible reads in your own features. Missing parent values block collection. Changing a parent clears its transitive dependents and invalidates reviewed results. Reset maps also clear fields depending on the values they change. Unknown parents and dependency cycles are rejected at configuration load. Query input changes start a fresh read; unrelated edits do not restart an identical request. Aborted or stale responses cannot replace options for a newer query. Form unmount cancels browser reads; it does not promise to cancel work already running on the remote system.

Scalar validation is shared with the setup form: required values, choices, patterns, lengths, finite numeric bounds/integer constraints and optional JSONata syntax. Zero and false remain valid values. These are authoring/UX checks; operation schemas and adapter validation remain authoritative for actual changes.

items.title: Users, sessions and TLS
items.text:
Declarack uses local, database-backed administrator accounts and a dedicated login page. Every administrator has full access to the installation, credentials and workloads. Environments and navigation groups do not restrict that access. There are no teams, resource ownership rules, granular roles, signup, SSO or API keys. Login accounts are separate from target, Git and registry credential profiles.

Sign in with a local administrator account.

items.title: First administrator
items.text:
The optional system configuration block is:

auth:
  provider: local
  bootstrap_credential: installation_bootstrap
  session_hours: 8
credentials:
  installation_bootstrap:
    type: basic
    username: admin
    password: {file: /run/secrets/declarack_admin_password}

local is the only provider and the default. bootstrap_credential is optional and must reference a basic profile. session_hours is an integer from 1 to 168, defaulting to 8. The profile's username/password seed the first administrator only when the users table is empty. This does not enable HTTP Basic Auth.

Without that reference, first startup uses DECLARACK_ADMIN_USERNAME (default admin) and either DECLARACK_PASSWORD_FILE or DECLARACK_PASSWORD. Choose one password source; a mounted file is preferable. The file contains a single value; a trailing newline is accepted. These variables are bootstrap inputs, not live account settings. Startup without any initial password fails when no users exist.

Once accounts exist, changing bootstrap environment values or profile secrets does not change their passwords. The bootstrap password mount may be absent on later starts: it is not reread for existing users. Keep a referenced profile's configuration valid. Manage existing passwords through Administrators or host recovery instead of rotating bootstrap inputs. Accounts are database rows, not YAML documents. A profile with inline {value: ...} still leaves that bootstrap secret in configuration revisions, history and exports; prefer file references.

items.title: Manage users
items.text:
Open Settings → Users (#/settings/~users) for the account list. Click a username or Manage to open that user's dedicated detail page. The You badge identifies your own account. The top-level Refresh reloads the list, account summary and activity; there are no separate card refresh buttons.

Choose Create user to open #/settings/~users/~new. Enter a username and password, then submit. Success opens the new account's detail page; Cancel returns to the list without saving. Usernames are immutable, 1–64 ASCII characters: the first must be a letter or number; subsequent characters may also be _, ., @ or -. Names are canonicalized to lowercase and unique. New and reset passwords must contain 12–1024 characters. The login form does not apply the new-password minimum to password entry. Every created account currently has full administrator access; role-based restrictions are not implemented.

Details use #/settings/~users/USER_ID and separate Account summary, Password, Access, Sessions and Activity. Password fields appear only after Reset password. Disabling, enabling, resetting a password or signing out sessions requires a confirmation. Disabling an account or resetting its password revokes its sessions; Sign out all sessions also signs out all its sessions. Resetting your own password or signing out your own sessions signs you out immediately. You cannot disable yourself, and the backend protects the last enabled administrator. There is no account deletion or role selector. Navigating away clears password fields.

Global activity is collapsed on the list. User details filter the latest 100 installation events to the selected account; this is not an exhaustive per-user history. Account events are retained up to the existing 1,000-event bound and exclude passwords/session tokens. Accounts remain database rows, separate from YAML configuration.

The authorization design proposal describes possible roles and operation-scoped permissions; it does not describe current enforcement.

Demo mode returns an authenticated demo session and bypasses login. Administrator management is explicitly unavailable in both backend and static demo modes.

items.title: Recover access from the host
items.text:
Run this from an environment with the same database selection and access as the controller, with a file containing the new 12–1024 character password:

python -m backend.auth reset-password USER --password-file FILE

Replace USER with an existing username and FILE with its container/host-visible password file. This host-only command resets the password, reenables the account and revokes all its sessions. It does not create a missing user and has no HTTP recovery endpoint. Keep database access and recovery files restricted to operators. Changing DECLARACK_PASSWORD will not recover an existing account.

items.title: Sessions and API clients
items.text:
Passwords use scrypt:32768:8:3 hashes. Login creates an opaque random session cookie; the database stores its SHA-256 hash, not the bearer token. Sessions have a fixed expiry (8 hours by default), with at most 20 concurrent sessions per user. The header shows the signed-in username and Sign out control. Signing out, reaching the session expiry timer, or receiving an API 401 unmounts protected UI and returns to login, preventing stale sensitive views from remaining visible. Login failures are throttled by username and client address: 10 failures block further attempts until the five-minute bucket expires.

The declarack_session cookie is HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, and scoped to /. It is Secure when Declarack observes HTTPS, either natively or through an explicitly trusted proxy. Plain HTTP remains allowed for local development; it does not set Secure. Use HTTPS for remote access.

Endpoint Behavior GET /api/v1/auth/session Public session discovery; anonymous response is {"authenticated":false,"demo":false} POST /api/v1/auth/login JSON username and password; sets cookie and returns authenticated snapshot POST /api/v1/auth/logout JSON {}; revokes current session and clears cookie GET /api/v1/users Administrator list and current_user_id GET /api/v1/users/activity Read-only account activity: {"events":[...]}, newest 100 retained events first POST /api/v1/users Create with username and password PATCH /api/v1/users/ID Change password or boolean disabled POST /api/v1/users/ID/revoke-sessions JSON {}; revoke all sessions for the account

Authenticated snapshots include authenticated, demo, user, csrf_token and numeric Unix expires_at. Anonymous protected API reads return JSON HTTP 401, not a Basic Auth challenge. Writes must send X-Declarack-Action: 1; authenticated writes, including logout, must also send X-Declarack-CSRF with the snapshot's csrf_token and the session cookie. Login needs the action header but has no existing-session CSRF token. Cross-site writes are rejected; a supplied Origin must match the request origin. Non-browser clients may omit Origin but must supply the required action/CSRF headers. Keep the cookie jar and token private. A 401 requires a fresh login; refreshing session discovery supplies the current snapshot and token.

Account writes revalidate the caller's actual session hash, expiry and enabled account under the database account lock, after any password hashing. A session revoked while an account creation or password reset is queued cannot finish that write using its earlier request authentication.

Revocation prevents subsequent API access; it does not cancel work already accepted by an adapter or roll back a running operation. Existing terminal idle cleanup still bounds abandoned PTYs.

items.title: Account activity and audit scope
items.text:
Settings → Administrators → Recent account activity is read-only. Account events are stored as generic documents in framework.auth.audit; the newest 1,000 are retained, and GET /api/v1/users/activity returns the newest 100 in {"events":[...]}. The endpoint requires an authenticated administrator and is unavailable in demo mode, like the rest of account management.

Recorded actions are user.created, user.password_reset, user.disabled, user.enabled, sessions.revoked and user.recovered. Events include the action, target user_id, Unix timestamp at, and actor identity (id, username and role for an administrator, or a type marker of bootstrap / host-operator). They contain no passwords, session tokens or other secrets. Account mutation and its audit event share the database transaction; older events are pruned rather than retained as an unlimited history.

Recorded operation plans separately include the actor in metadata.actor (id, username, role, or a system marker for non-user work). Batch fan-out propagates ContextVars into worker threads so those recorded plans preserve the initiating actor. Bounded account activity and plan metadata do not form a complete generic resource audit log or audit governance system; simple direct resource calls do not all produce recorded plans.

items.title: Native TLS
items.text:
The process serves one HTTP or HTTPS listener through Cheroot. TLS is deployment configuration, independent of system YAML:

Variable Default / purpose DECLARACK_TLS off; accepts off, files, self-signed DECLARACK_TLS_CERT_FILE Certificate PEM path; required in files mode DECLARACK_TLS_KEY_FILE Unencrypted private-key PEM path; required in files mode DECLARACK_TLS_HOSTS localhost,127.0.0.1; comma-separated DNS/IP SANs for self-signed HOST 127.0.0.1 in Python; Docker image sets 0.0.0.0 PORT 8080 with TLS off, 8443 with TLS enabled; explicit value overrides DECLARACK_TRUSTED_PROXIES Empty: trust no forwarded headers; explicit comma-separated IP/CIDR list

The following commands assume an existing administrator database or the first-account bootstrap inputs, and valid target configuration/mounts. For a certificate issued by your CA, set:

export DECLARACK_TLS=files
export DECLARACK_TLS_CERT_FILE=/run/secrets/declarack_cert.pem
export DECLARACK_TLS_KEY_FILE=/run/secrets/declarack_key.pem
python -m backend.server

Mount those paths before startup. TLS requires a valid, currently usable matching certificate/key pair and TLS 1.2 or later. Encrypted private keys are unsupported. Certificate/key variables are accepted only in files mode. If you use containers, update the published port to the selected listener; an existing 8080:8080 mapping does not expose the default TLS listener on 8443.

For a locally trusted development/lab certificate:

export DECLARACK_TLS=self-signed
export DECLARACK_TLS_HOSTS=localhost,127.0.0.1
python -m backend.server

First startup generates a 365-day certificate and an unencrypted key at <DECLARACK_DATA>/tls/cert.pem and key.pem (normally /data/tls). Generated files start with mode 0600; the private key is enforced as 0600 on reuse. The pair is persisted and reused, not regenerated on every restart. Trust the certificate explicitly on clients. Persist it even when the database is external PostgreSQL.

Certificates load at startup. Replace files and restart to reload; there is no ACME integration, automatic renewal, hot reload, or HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect listener. An expired pair fails startup. A changed DECLARACK_TLS_HOSTS must be covered by the existing SANs; to generate a replacement, stop the controller, back up and remove both generated files, then restart with the new hosts. Reestablish client trust. An incomplete persisted pair fails startup rather than replacing one half.

items.title: HTTPS reverse proxies
items.text:
You may terminate TLS at a reverse proxy and keep DECLARACK_TLS=off internally. Set DECLARACK_TRUSTED_PROXIES to the immediate proxy's actual IP or CIDR. Only requests from those peers honor one rightmost X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-For hop. The proxy must overwrite or append its observed scheme and client address. Forwarded host, port and URL prefix are never honored; preserve the public Host header and deploy at the origin root. Arbitrary forwarded headers from untrusted peers cannot mark an HTTP request secure.

Without proxy trust, HTTPS termination appears as HTTP to Declarack, affecting Secure cookies and Origin verification. Keep the internal listener reachable only by intended peers and configure the proxy and explicit trust list together.

items.title: Upgrade from Basic Auth
items.text:
This is a breaking configuration and client change. Replace auth.provider: basic with local and rename auth.credential to auth.bootstrap_credential. Older auth.username / auth.password_file fields must also move into a referenced basic bootstrap profile or the bootstrap environment variables. Import the updated configuration under the normal configuration authority rules. A restart alone retains the active database revision. To apply changed authentication bootstrap/settings from files, publish/export the intended documents and restart once with DECLARACK_CONFIG_FORCE_LOAD=1, then remove that flag.

No HTTP Basic Auth requests are supported. Browser Basic Auth and scripts using curl -u must migrate to login, cookies and CSRF/action headers. On an installation with an empty users table, the bootstrap seeds the first account; thereafter manage it in the database. See credentials for outbound HTTP Basic, Git and registry profiles, which remain separate supported uses of basic.

items.title: Volume browsing and multi-target operation pages
Read-only volume file browser
items.text:
Open a Docker target's Volumes, collect inventory, then select Browse files on a volume row. Swarm rows retain their node ID, so identical local volume names on different nodes remain distinct. Browsing opens a dedicated page, not a modal.

Directories support navigation, Up, refresh, and pages of 200 entries. Selecting a regular file previews UTF-8 text when possible and offers a binary-safe download. The first version is deliberately read-only: there is no upload, file write, rename, mkdir or delete API. Files larger than 64 KiB cannot be previewed/downloaded; directories larger than 5,000 entries return an explicit limit error. Permission errors remain errors. Symlinks, devices and FIFOs are not followed. Relative paths are resolved by directory descriptors with no-follow opens rather than trusting a string prefix. Data never needs to be exposed by mounting the host root into the GUI container.

The target must supply agent_image, or the process must supply DECLARACK_AGENT_IMAGE, naming the same Declarack image version as the backend:

targets:
  docker:
    connection: docker_socket
    socket: /var/run/docker.sock
    agent_image: ghcr.io/daniellmorris/declarack:latest
    features: [volumes]

Use a pinned release/digest in production and make it available on the relevant engines. The helper path does not perform an implicit image pull. Driver-backed volumes must be mountable by Docker; this is not a host-path fallback.

  • Standalone: inspect the existing volume, create a temporary same-image container with only that volume mounted read-only, no network, a read-only root filesystem, dropped capabilities, and no-new-privileges. Collect its result and remove the helper. This also works through a managed manager/host SSH tunnel.
  • Swarm: first inspect the volume on the selected node through a socket job, then run a node-pinned job mounting only that volume read-only. No worker SSH is used, and the file-reading job does not receive the Docker socket. The image must be present/pullable on the selected node. Jobs use the existing lifecycle cleanup.

Inspection prevents normal accidental creation of nonexistent volumes. Docker volume mounting and inspection are separate requests: a concurrent external volume deletion/recreation is not an atomic storage snapshot. Do not remove or replace a volume while browsing it. A failure after helper creation, or a process crash, can require normal Docker cleanup; browser helpers carry the label io.declarack.volume-browser=1.

The feature YAML declares a file_browser action and hidden read operation. The generic browser receives those operation names; Docker-specific execution and node selection remain in the adapter. Operations are volumes.files.list and volumes.files.read, with name, optional path/offset, and a required node_id in Swarm. They are on demand and never scheduled from an environment summary.

items.title: Configured multi-target batches
items.text:
A batches section defines top-level pages that run one enabled operation against several targets. This is generic orchestration, not a new pseudo-SSH target. SSH remains responsible for connecting, executing commands and collecting metrics. Target/environment membership remains independent.

targets:
  server_a:
    connection: ssh
    host: server-a.example.com
    features:
    - host_metrics
    - ssh_commands
    credential: ssh_server_a
  server_b:
    connection: ssh
    host: server-b.example.com
    features:
    - host_metrics
    - ssh_commands
    credential: ssh_server_a
environments:
  servers:
    label: SSH servers
    targets:
    - server_a
    - server_b
    batches:
    - metrics
    - command
batches:
  metrics:
    title: Fleet metrics
    operation: host.metrics
    columns:
    - label: CPU percent
      value: result.cpu
    - label: Memory available MB
      value: $round(result.memory.MemAvailable / 1000000, 1)
    - label: Disk available GB
      value: $round(result.disk.available / 1000000000, 2)
  command:
    title: Fleet command
    operation: ssh.command
    confirmation: Run this command on all selected SSH hosts?
    columns:
    - label: Output
      value: $substring(result.text, 0, 500)
credentials:
  ssh_server_a:
    type: ssh
    username: operator
    private_key:
      file: /run/secrets/ssh_key
    known_hosts:
      file: /etc/declarack/known_hosts

Save and reload configuration. Open the SSH servers environment to access its batches. Select a subset of that environment’s hosts, fill the operation's declared inputs, and run. Command batches show a confirmation dialog including the hosts and input values. There is no scheduling, automatic retry or transaction rollback for batch changes. Metrics run only when requested. SSH Linux metrics require remote python3 and readable /proc; commands use the configured SSH account's permissions, not an implicit sudo/root escalation.

Each host returns its own success/error and duration. One host failure does not cancel the others. Output tables use JSONata against {target, label, ok, result, error, duration_ms}; Full result expands the structured response. These are execution results, not historical monitoring records. Use checks for persisted monitoring. A successful command exit does not prove its intended external effects.

Limits: 32 batch pages, 1–32 targets per page, four concurrent executions per run, and 64 KiB of result per target. Commands run through the existing 20-second SSH command timeout and output cap; supplied ssh.command input is additionally limited to 4096 bytes.
