Nonzero exit and transport failures are isolated error rows; failed-command stdout/stderr is not currently returned. No automatic retry is made because a failed connection can leave a remote command's outcome uncertain.

The same operation must be enabled on every configured target, with identical input schemas. This does not grant access to disabled target operations or arbitrary unconfigured hosts. Actions require a configured confirmation message; read-style primary operations can omit one. A custom read operation is an administrator's assertion about its behavior, not an automatic safety classification. Do not use a modifying operation as an unconfirmed read.

POST /api/v1/batches/<id>/run accepts {targets, inputs, confirmed}. targets can only narrow the configured list. Actions require confirmed: true in addition to the standard authenticated X-Declarack-Action: 1 protection.

items.title: Real lab example
items.text:
The engine image now includes Python for SSH metric collection. Existing engines need that package installed, or a rebuild through the lab's normal up workflow. Copy examples/multi-environment/optional/tools.yaml into the runtime config folder and reload. It adds two explicit SSH manager-host targets, a group, and command and metric batch pages. Swarm worker access still uses jobs exclusively. Because this lab uses DinD containers on one Docker host, host /proc measurements are not independent physical machines.

The current development lab also has a dedicated sample volume named declarack-browser-demo-20261120 on standalone Docker and Swarm A's worker. Its documents/hello.txt is a safe fixture for testing navigation and previews.

items.title: Real multi-environment lab
items.text:
Start two independent Docker Swarms inside Docker, each with one manager and one worker, actual running services, Prometheus, Grafana, and Declarack. Declarack also connects to the outer host Docker engine using its standalone feature set.

This uses four privileged Docker-in-Docker engine containers. It requires a local Docker Engine/Docker Desktop that permits privileged Linux containers, Docker Compose, Python 3 (standard library only), and the host's OpenSSH client/keygen. It was exercised on Docker Desktop with Docker 29.5.2 nested engines. The nested nodes share the outer Linux kernel; they are not separate VMs or physical hosts. Allow a few GB of free disk and memory for images and persistent engine volumes.

The outer host's existing Swarm membership is left unchanged. No host Swarm init, join, or leave command is executed. Selecting standalone features for the host is a Declarack view choice, not a change to the daemon's actual operating mode.

items.title: Start
items.text:
From the repository root:

python3 examples/multi-environment/lab.py up --http-mode ssh

The script builds the engine/app/Declarack images, creates local credentials, starts the containers, initializes two distinct Swarms, joins exactly one worker to each, loads job/app images into all four engines, deploys services, provisions monitoring, creates runtime Declarack configs, and verifies real responses. First startup downloads Grafana/Prometheus images and can take several minutes.

The fixed Compose project is declarack-lab. Re-running up reuses its data and keys, verifies membership, reloads local images, and updates its sample services. Image changes may recreate engine containers and roll the sample services; their volumes preserve cluster identity while workloads reconverge. It refuses to reset a manager that is unexpectedly joined as a worker elsewhere. Do not point these commands at an unrelated remote Docker context.

items.title: Optional host Compose file access
items.text:
The base deployment does not mount the host filesystem. To let the standalone Host Docker target view Compose YAML at the paths reported by Docker, select an optional read-only mount when starting the lab:

# Docker Desktop on macOS: /Users -> /mnt/host/Users (read-only)
python3 examples/multi-environment/lab.py up --http-mode ssh --host-files macos

# Native Linux: / -> /mnt/host (read-only)
python3 examples/multi-environment/lab.py up --http-mode ssh --host-files linux

Both overrides set DECLARACK_COMPOSE_HOST_ROOT=/mnt/host. The macOS version preserves /Users/... paths recorded in Compose labels; it does not mount the Docker Desktop VM root. Enable Docker Desktop file sharing for the source path if Docker reports a mount denial. Paths outside /Users need a separate explicit mapping; missing or inaccessible files remain unavailable in the project view. These mounts expose host files read-only to the controller, not remote Swarm or SSH filesystems. They are not needed for Docker volume browsing.

Pass the same --host-files option to later up or configure commands, or set LAB_HOST_FILES=macos / LAB_HOST_FILES=linux in your shell. none is the default and explicitly disables the override on the next controller recreation.

To enable the mount on an already running lab without rebuilding or restarting its Swarm nodes and monitoring services, use the matching Compose override:

docker compose -f examples/multi-environment/compose.yaml \
  -f examples/multi-environment/compose.host-files.macos.yaml \
  up -d --no-deps declarack

On Linux replace the second file with compose.host-files.yaml. The macOS file is compose.host-files.macos.yaml. These commands operate the lab controller and its configured LAB_DECLARACK_PORT (default 9080); they do not modify a separately launched preview container.

items.title: What runs
items.text:
Environment Engine/node layout Workloads Swarm A swarm-a-manager + swarm-a-worker lab-web: 2 worker replicas; lab-heartbeat: 1 manager replica Swarm B swarm-b-manager + swarm-b-worker Same services, independently scheduled Host Docker Your outer Docker daemon Contains the lab infrastructure plus your existing containers Prometheus Separate outer container Scrapes four Docker engines, two routed web services, and itself Grafana Separate outer container Provisioned Prometheus data source and live lab dashboard

Each nested engine has its own /var/lib/docker volume. The managers and workers use separate bridge networks per Swarm for their underlay. Managers also join the access network for SSH and monitoring. Worker SSH servers are not started. The Docker API listens on Unix sockets, not a published unauthenticated TCP port.

items.title: Open the applications
items.text:
All published ports bind to host loopback:

Application URL / port Declarack custom page http://127.0.0.1:9080/#/~pages/lab Declarack environments http://127.0.0.1:9080/#/environments Grafana live dashboard http://127.0.0.1:9300/d/declarack-lab Prometheus targets http://127.0.0.1:9090/targets Swarm A application http://127.0.0.1:18081/health Swarm B application http://127.0.0.1:18082/health Manager A SSH 127.0.0.1:2221 Manager B SSH 127.0.0.1:2222

Declarack username is admin. Retrieve its generated password locally:

cat examples/multi-environment/runtime/declarack_password

Grafana permits anonymous Viewer access for this local lab. To administer it, log in as admin with runtime/grafana_password. Prometheus is unauthenticated inside the lab. Keep the loopback bindings when using these settings.

Ports can be overridden with exported environment variables before every lab command: LAB_DECLARACK_PORT, LAB_GRAFANA_PORT, LAB_PROMETHEUS_PORT, LAB_SSH_A_PORT, LAB_SSH_B_PORT, LAB_WEB_A_PORT, and LAB_WEB_B_PORT. Defaults are those in the table. Changing published ports on an existing lab needs up, not just configure. The primary app already running on port 8080 is unaffected.

items.title: SSH from your host
items.text:
Keys are generated locally under the ignored runtime/ directory. SSH host keys are read from each manager through Docker and recorded in a dedicated known-hosts file; host verification stays enabled. Your personal SSH config/keys/known-hosts files are not changed.

ssh -F /dev/null \
  -i examples/multi-environment/runtime/client_key \
  -o UserKnownHostsFile=examples/multi-environment/runtime/known_hosts \
  -o StrictHostKeyChecking=yes \
  -p 2221 root@127.0.0.1

Use port 2222 for manager B. Inside either manager:

docker node ls
docker service ls
docker service ps lab-web
docker info

Only manager SSH ports are published. Declarack reaches workers through the manager API and node-pinned Swarm jobs, including volume inventory and terminals. The Declarack job image is loaded into every nested engine so these operations do not depend on GHCR credentials or an external registry.

items.title: Direct HTTP versus SSH tunnels
items.text:
Both monitoring containers are reachable from either manager's access network. The default Declarack configuration uses manager A as the SSH hop for Prometheus and manager B for Grafana. Docker manager targets always use SSH; the host target uses the mounted socket.

Switch just the monitoring targets to direct container-network HTTP:

python3 examples/multi-environment/lab.py configure --http-mode direct
python3 examples/multi-environment/lab.py verify

Switch back to SSH:

python3 examples/multi-environment/lab.py configure --http-mode ssh
python3 examples/multi-environment/lab.py verify

configure recreates the runtime base config from the checked-in template and updates only Declarack. It overwrites local runtime config edits; copy your custom version elsewhere before regeneration. The Swarms, workloads, and monitoring keep running.

An HTTP target's optional tunnel block is:

grafana:
  connection: http
  base_url: http://grafana:3000
  ssh_tunnel:
    host: swarm-b-manager
    user: root
    identity_file: /run/lab/client_key
    known_hosts_file: /run/lab/known_hosts
    remote_host: grafana
    remote_port: 3000
  features: [grafana.dashboards]

Omit ssh_tunnel for direct access. The remote destination is resolved/reached from the SSH manager; the URL host remains the HTTP Host/TLS identity. The backend opens private Unix listening sockets and supervises the forwards. No local TCP forwarding ports need to be published for Declarack's internal tunnels. HTTPS verification, redirect restrictions, and the existing HTTPS requirement for bearer tokens remain. SSH encrypts to the manager; HTTPS is needed when the onward hop also needs TLS.

You can also create browser-facing forwards from your host's terminal. For Grafana through manager A:

ssh -F /dev/null -N \
  -i examples/multi-environment/runtime/client_key \
  -o UserKnownHostsFile=examples/multi-environment/runtime/known_hosts \
  -o StrictHostKeyChecking=yes \
  -L 127.0.0.1:19300:grafana:3000 -p 2221 root@127.0.0.1

Then open http://127.0.0.1:19300. For Prometheus, use -L 127.0.0.1:19090:prometheus:9090 and open http://127.0.0.1:19090. Either manager (2221 or 2222) can forward either service. Stop the SSH command with Ctrl-C. These user-managed browser forwards are separate from Declarack's managed internal tunnels.

items.title: Configuration files
items.text:
• declarack.yaml: complete checked-in config for all five targets, existing monitoring features, and a cross-target custom page.
  • runtime/declarack.ssh.yaml: generated container config with managed HTTP tunnels.
  • runtime/declarack.direct.yaml: generated container config with direct HTTP.
  • runtime/declarack.yaml: merged single-file copy of the selected transport.
  • runtime/config/: five ordered YAML base fragments, loaded by the container. Extra user fragments are retained by regeneration; base fragments are rewritten.
  • runtime/declarack.host.yaml: generated variant for running the Python backend on your host, with loopback SSH ports and absolute key/password paths.

The host-side variant can be used with DECLARACK_CONFIG and a different PORT; it does not require shutting down the lab's Declarack container. Its data directory is selected separately with DECLARACK_DATA. Never commit runtime credentials. Settings can browse the individual files and merged config, then explicitly reload external edits. Folder GUI writes are not enabled yet. Try the optional Grafana extension by copying one fragment into this folder and reloading.

items.title: Verify and stop
items.text:
python3 examples/multi-environment/lab.py verify
python3 examples/multi-environment/lab.py status
python3 examples/multi-environment/lab.py down

Verification checks host SSH, distinct Swarm IDs, exactly one ready manager and worker per cluster, service replica convergence, each cluster's HTTP workload, all seven Prometheus scrapes, Grafana dashboard inventory, and the host Docker inventory through Declarack. It does not treat an HTTP 200 from Declarack alone as proof that every environment works.

down removes only this Compose project's containers/networks and retains its named volumes and local runtime credentials. Your existing host containers and Swarm membership are unaffected. A destructive reset is a separate explicit operator action: remove only the declarack-lab volumes after stopping, and remove its runtime directory if you want new client credentials. Keeping Grafana's data volume preserves its existing admin password, so keep its password file with it.

Node-local volume jobs were verified on both nodes of each Swarm. An interactive terminal into a worker task was also verified through manager SSH and the Swarm relay network. This is a real multi-node DinD test; independent physical-machine validation is still a separate deployment concern.

items.title: Environment groups and persisted monitoring
items.text:
The generated folder includes 60-environments.yaml and 70-checks.yaml. Environment groups collect the two Swarms, local Docker, and monitoring targets. The top-level Targets page remains the complete connection inventory. Checks run on the server and keep their state/history in the existing Declarack data volume.

For a check-only target without an environment or interactive features:

cp examples/multi-environment/optional/checks.yaml \
   examples/multi-environment/runtime/config/75-monitoring-checks.yaml

In Settings, reload configuration, then open Checks. The optional check queries Grafana's real /api/health endpoint and evaluates database = "ok" with JSONata. See monitoring documentation for persistence, thresholds, single-replica deployment, and the current local-only alarm scope.

items.title: Optional volume browsing and SSH fleet pages
items.text: optional/tools.yaml adds two SSH host targets and batch pages for on-demand metrics and reviewed commands. Copy it into runtime/config/80-tools.yaml and reload. SSH metrics require Python 3 on those hosts; new lab engine builds include it. The standalone Docker override points volume helpers to declarack-lab:local. See volume/fleet documentation.

items.title: Environment-only custom pages
items.text: Copy optional/environment-pages.yaml into runtime/config/85-page-placement.yaml and reload Settings to add Local engine overview only within Local Docker. It is excluded from the global Custom pages section. The existing lab overview remains global and linked in the Swarm groups, demonstrating shared placement.

items.title: Root and fleet navigation
items.text: Home is the reserved environments.root. Configure its navigation to order or hide installation-wide links. Custom page placement uses environment pages lists; set root pages explicitly when a dashboard should appear only elsewhere. The optional SSH tools are assigned to ssh-hosts.batches and infer their hosts from that environment's targets, rather than repeating a host list in each tool. Open the SSH hosts environment to select hosts and collect metrics or confirm a fleet command. See navigation configuration.

items.title: Documentation training API
items.text:
A standard-library HTTP API used by the documentation tutorials. It binds only to 127.0.0.1 and needs no Docker engine. Data and restart counters are in memory. The restart endpoint changes example data; it never restarts a real process.

python3 examples/tutorial-api/server.py

Start a second independent instance for the multi-target tutorial:

python3 examples/tutorial-api/server.py --port 9011 --label Staging

Run Declarack as a host Python process with declarack.yaml; its loopback URLs are intentionally host-process URLs, not container-network addresses. The full tutorial explains prerequisites, startup, actions and dependent form fields. The dashboard tutorial and checks tutorial use the extra fragments.

The API provides GET /, /health, /apps, /apps/<id>, /teams, and /teams/<id>/apps, plus POST /apps/<id>/restart. Stop with Ctrl+C. Do not use this unauthenticated training server as a production management API.

items.title: Work with a configuration folder
items.text:
For the model, hierarchy diagrams and a complete example, start with How configuration fits together. For environment forms, use Settings → Home & environments and follow the structured editing workflow.

Use a folder when you want editable source files and guided integration setup. It is one system configuration assembled from ordered fragments, not a collection of independent plugin installations.

items.title: Current save and activation behavior
items.text: The database owns configuration. The file/folder below seeds an empty installation; GUI edits save logical documents in the database, then Activate configuration applies them. Use Review import from files after external edits, or set DECLARACK_CONFIG_FORCE_LOAD=1 to import at each startup. Enable DECLARACK_CONFIG_WRITE_BACK=1 for GUI activation to update local files. Both flags default off. A writable source mount is only required for write-back, not DB-only editing. See storage and recovery. The older screenshots show the former source-file Save/Reload labels; the same review workflow now saves and activates database revisions.

items.title: Start from the supplied example
items.text:
From the repository root:

cp -R configurations/folder-example my-config

Create a deployment override named compose.local-config.yaml:

services:
  declarack:
    environment:
      DECLARACK_CONFIG: /etc/declarack/config
      DECLARACK_CONFIG_EDIT: '1'
    volumes:
      - ./my-config:/etc/declarack/config

Start it alongside the base Compose file, which supplies the password, socket and persistent data volume:

export DECLARACK_PASSWORD='choose-a-strong-local-password'
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.local-config.yaml up -d --build

Open the GUI on port 8080. Settings should list source files and show New file, file editing and Reload configuration. If the directory is mounted read-only, external edits/reload still work but GUI saves do not.

items.title: Add an integration
items.text:
1. Open Targets → Add integration.
  2. Choose the transport/system template. Enter a unique target ID and display name.
  3. Supply paths as seen inside the Declarack container. Mount SSH keys, known_hosts and credential files before referencing them.
  4. Select an existing environment ID, enter a new ID, or leave it blank.
  5. Review the generated YAML and optionally test the connection.
  6. Save, then reload. Edit saved YAML opens the new fragment directly in Settings.

The wizard adds a new file and preserves existing source files. A failed connection test does not prevent storing an intentionally offline target. Review and save still require a valid merged configuration. Single-file, Git and Swarm-config storage retain their existing editing workflows; wizard saves currently require a folder.

items.title: Walk through a Custom HTTP API integration
items.text:
These captures use the local training API on your host and the folder-backed tutorial instance. Choose Custom HTTP API and use training-copy, Training copy, origin http://127.0.0.1:9010, endpoint /apps, rows items, and environment tutorial. This adds a separate connection to the same synthetic API. In a container deployment, use an address reachable from that container instead of this host-process loopback address.

Start at Targets → Add integration. Choose the template that matches the connection you want to create. Select the image to open it at full size.

Enter a unique Target ID, display name, API origin, endpoint and JSONata rows expression. The target ID also appears in the proposed new file path. Select the image to open it at full size.

Review configuration validates the full merge. Test connection checks reachability; a passed test does not save or apply the target. Select the image to open it at full size.

Save integration creates the fragment. Choose Reload configuration to apply it, or Edit saved YAML to inspect it in Settings. The default custom API template starts with a generic Resource column; customize its YAML columns for your API. Select the image to open it at full size.

items.title: Understand the merge
items.text:
Paths sort case-sensitively. Mappings merge recursively. Lists and scalar values are replaced by later values. For example, a later features: [containers] replaces an earlier feature list; it does not append to it.

A simple convention is system settings first, targets next, pages/checks afterward, and deliberate overrides last. Generated integration files use sequential names under zz-integrations/ to preserve successive environment membership updates.

items.title: Edit and reload deliberately
items.text:
• Edit a selected file, then choose Save file. The prior source is retained as .previous; saving does not apply it.
  • Choose Reload configuration to validate the entire source and apply it.
  • If another writer changed a file, read source files again before retrying a save.
  • Authentication and legacy-workspace changes require restart. Adapter code changes also require restart; ordinary YAML definitions can be reloaded from the folder.

The merged preview is read-only because its values may come from several files. A .previous file is a preceding-source backup, not a full revision history/rollback UI.

Select a source file rather than Merged configuration. Editing creates a draft; Review & save file opens a diff before Save file writes it. This example only changes the comment above the tutorial check. Select the image to open it at full size.

The save status confirms the disk write. The running configuration is unchanged until you reload. Select the image to open it at full size.

Reload configuration validates and applies the full folder. Settings returns to the merged read-only preview. Select the image to open it at full size.

items.title: Create another file
items.text:
Choose New file, provide a relative .yaml path and enter a configuration mapping. Review new file validates the entire proposed merge and displays source and effective-config diffs. Save file writes it without overwriting an existing path; reload afterward to apply it. The empty mapping shown below is a harmless starting point; replace it with your actual definitions before creating a useful feature, page or check.

New file operates on the configuration folder. Cancel exits without creating a file. Select the image to open it at full size.

items.title: Test all targets
items.text:
Choose Test all connections to see a separate Passed/Failed result for every target in the displayed configuration. Testing does not save or apply changes.

Each row includes both the target label and ID, plus the connection result. This capture follows the extra training-copy integration above. Select the image to open it at full size.

Exact merge and save rules · Template and form reference

items.title: Review and restore revisions
items.text:
Select a source file and choose Review & save file after editing. Inspect the source diff, expand Effective merged configuration diff, or inspect Preview merged configuration. Choose Back to editing to adjust the draft, or Save file and then Reload configuration to apply it.

Open Revision history, choose an earlier snapshot, and select Restore to draft. This loads the selected file without writing or applying it. Review and save it through the same flow. Local history retains 20 snapshots per source and needs a persistent data directory. See the recovery rules for retention and provider limits.

The screenshots above show the earlier editor; the current editor inserts the review step between editing and saving.

The current editor shows both the exact file change and its effect after all fragments merge.

items.title: Start from an example
items.text:
Open Example snippets in Settings to search by task or filter by category. Examples cover targets, custom API tables, confirmed actions, environment groups, multi-target dashboards, checks, and SSH fleet operations. The right pane explains what to adapt and links to prerequisite examples. Copy YAML copies the selected fragment; it does not change the editor or the running configuration. Paste into New file or merge it into an existing draft, then review, save and reload. Prerequisites belong in separate source files unless their mappings are explicitly merged. The snippet library publishes the same YAML in the docs.

Search examples or filter by category. Each snippet includes prerequisites, adaptation notes and copyable YAML.

items.title: Deployment and persistence
items.text: The application image contains Python, the built frontend and required Docker/SSH clients. The documentation site is a separate static build; none of its packages are installed in the runtime image.

items.title: Production essentials
items.text:
Use a strong first-administrator bootstrap password, persist the database and required local files, and mount only the sockets/files your targets need. The repository Compose file binds HTTP port 8080 to loopback. For remote access use native TLS or an HTTPS reverse proxy with explicit immediate-proxy trust. HTTP remains available for local development.

Local administrators sign in with cookie sessions; all have full installation, credential and workload access. Environment groups do not supply per-user permissions. SSO, teams and granular RBAC are not implemented. Bootstrap inputs seed an empty user database only; later password changes belong in Settings → Administrators or host recovery.

See administrators, sessions and TLS for first-account files, recovery, cookie/CSRF clients and the breaking Basic Auth migration. Native TLS uses DECLARACK_TLS=files with mounted certificate/key paths, or DECLARACK_TLS=self-signed with persisted /data/tls identity. The default TLS port is 8443, so adjust container port mappings. Certificates load on restart; there is no ACME or automatic renewal. Behind a TLS proxy, configure DECLARACK_TRUSTED_PROXIES with explicit IPs/CIDRs to recognize HTTPS and set Secure cookies. Only one forwarded proto/client hop is trusted; host/prefix are not.

items.title: Match the controller and node image
items.text:
In Swarm, publish the same image for the controller and node-local jobs. Set DECLARACK_AGENT_IMAGE to that reference, preferably an immutable registry digest. Every participating node must be able to pull it. The build workflow reports the published digest; a controller-local image alone is not a registry deployment.

Node jobs require compatible Linux engines and eligible ready/active nodes. Metrics remain on demand by default. Worker SSH is not part of Swarm collection.

items.title: What to persist
items.text:
State Location / requirement System configuration Active/saved database revisions; mounted files or other providers are import/publication sources Administrators, hashed sessions, login limits, Stack/Compose sources, checks, operations and configuration revisions Shared database: SQLite /data/state.sqlite by default, or configured PostgreSQL Git/registry and first-account bootstrap credential references Mounted files or Docker secrets; existing users do not depend on bootstrap password files Native TLS identity Persist /data/tls for self-signed mode; remount certificate/key files for files mode, including with PostgreSQL Table preferences Browser storage; separate from server backups

Database setup, legacy import and backend transfer explains what is stored, how to upgrade previous installations, and what remains external. Back up the database, system configuration and operator-managed mounts together. Stop SQLite writers or use a consistent SQLite backup method; use PostgreSQL backup tools for PostgreSQL. The legacy encryption keys are included in the new database, alongside the encrypted source credentials.

items.title: Configuration storage choices
items.text: Folder storage supports atomic GUI source-file saves and new integration fragments. File storage supports its existing restricted settings edits. Git storage opens configuration pull requests; merging does not itself update a running mount. Swarm config storage updates the controller service's config attachment and redeploys it. Their bootstrap requirements and edit restrictions are in the system reference.

items.title: One controller for local persisted services
items.text:
Checks and operation plans are process-owned, with SQLite or PostgreSQL storage. Do not treat multiple controllers sharing a data volume as a distributed scheduler or queue. A backend restart marks abandoned plans interrupted when inspected; it does not resume them automatically. Inspect resources and run metadata before retrying.

Existing health sources and persisted checks are distinct from outbound alerting: Declarack currently records local alarm/recovery state but does not send notifications.

Runtime variable reference · Upgrade compatibility

items.title: Manage Docker and Swarm
items.text: Choose the connection and feature set that matches the engine. A standalone view of an engine does not initialize, leave or otherwise change its Swarm membership.

items.title: Scope matters
items.text:
Workflow Standalone Docker Swarm Application deployment Compose projects Stacks and services Native configs/secrets Not available Swarm resources Container and network inventories Connected engine Selected/all node jobs with Node column and partial failures Container lifecycle / network mutations Connected engine Connected manager engine; worker task management uses services Images and disk usage Connected engine Use a separately configured standalone-engine target Volumes and host metrics Local helper operations Selected-node or aggregated Swarm jobs Container terminals Docker exec on the engine Task placement plus same-image node relay jobs

A worker terminal is not SSH into that worker. Declarack connects to the manager, resolves the task's node/container and runs a node-local relay job. An SSH tunnel may connect the controller to the manager without changing this rule.

items.title: Services and stacks
items.text:
Service detail pages support reviewed specification edits, version checks and rollback where Docker has a previous specification. Stack workflows handle inline, folder, general HTTPS/SSH Git sources and legacy GitHub tags, plus deploy/update/remove/replace and explicit cleanup choices. Update the stack source for stack-managed services so a later redeploy does not undo direct edits.

A GitHub source credential authenticates source retrieval. It does not authenticate image pulls from a private container registry. Review the current source/ref limits in the coverage review before planning GitOps.

items.title: Standalone replacement and duplication
items.text:
Open a container's dedicated detail page, select Edit / replace or Duplicate, adjust fields, then review and confirm. Dynamic image suggestions use local image inventory; they do not pull missing images. New-container forms can select a primary network through the same generic option mechanism.

Replacement retains the original as a stopped backup with automatic restart disabled. Failure recovery attempts to restore the original; uncertain replacement shutdown leaves the original stopped for inspection. Duplicates default to stopped state, fresh storage and no published host ports. Neither flow automatically deletes containers or volumes. Writable-layer changes are not copied, and shared-data changes cannot be rolled back by restoring a container specification.

Read recreation guarantees and limits before using this workflow on persistent applications.

items.title: Bulk actions and storage
items.text:
Select rows, choose a bulk action and inspect eligible/skipped resources before confirming. The server re-reads inventory and runs eligible operations once each. Failures are recorded separately; there is no automatic bulk rollback or mutation retry. Docker continues to enforce in-use resource constraints.

Volume file browsing is read-only and node-specific. Size collection is explicit; unavailable measurements remain unavailable. Missing values must not be interpreted as zero. File and fleet workflows describe helper requirements and limits.

Full action matrix · Real manager/worker lab

Swarm stack sources now also support general HTTPS/SSH Git URLs with branches, tags or commit IDs and target-scoped credential references. Registry credentials can be forwarded to workers for private images. See registry credentials and Git sources for configuration and limits.

items.title: Configuration snippet library
items.text:
In Declarack, open Settings → Example snippets to search these examples and copy YAML. These are fragments: add prerequisites as separate YAML files first, adapt placeholders and IDs, then review, save and reload. Files merge in filename order. Lists replace earlier lists. Copying an example does not save or apply configuration.

SSH examples need mounted identity and known-hosts files. Checks start scheduling after reload; persist the data directory for history.

items.title: Standalone Docker
items.text:
Targets — Connect to a local Docker socket, including Compose projects.

Mount the Docker socket into Declarack. This grants control of the engine. Replace example_docker if you already have a local target.

Suggested filename: 10-local-docker.yaml.

targets:
  example_docker:
    label: Example local Docker
    connection: docker_socket
    socket: /var/run/docker.sock
    swarm: false
    features: [compose, containers, images, networks, volumes, disk_usage]

items.title: Swarm manager over SSH
items.text:
Targets — Reach a remote Swarm through an SSH tunnel to its manager.

Replace the manager hostname and user; mount existing SSH key and known-hosts files. The SSH user needs Docker access. Swarm node-local work uses jobs, not SSH to workers.

Suggested filename: 10-remote-swarm.yaml.

targets:
  example_swarm:
    label: Example Swarm
    connection: docker_socket
    swarm: true
    ssh_tunnel:
      host: manager.example.com
      remote_socket: /var/run/docker.sock
      credential: tunnel_example_swarm
    agent_image: ghcr.io/daniellmorris/declarack:latest
    features:
    - overview
    - services
    - nodes
    - tasks
    - stacks
    - configs
    - secrets
    - networks
    - volumes
credentials:
  tunnel_example_swarm:
    type: ssh
    username: declarack
    private_key:
      file: /run/secrets/manager_ssh_key
    known_hosts:
      file: /etc/declarack/known_hosts

items.title: Linux host over SSH
items.text:
Targets — Collect on-demand Linux host metrics and expose command execution.

Replace the hostname and user; mount existing SSH key and known-hosts files. Metrics require python3 on the remote host; commands run as the configured user.

Suggested filename: 10-ssh-host.yaml.

targets:
  example_ssh:
    label: Example Linux host
    connection: ssh
    host: host.example.com
    features:
    - host_metrics
    - ssh_commands
    credential: ssh_example_ssh
credentials:
  ssh_example_ssh:
    type: ssh
    username: declarack
    private_key:
      file: /run/secrets/host_ssh_key
    known_hosts:
      file: /etc/declarack/known_hosts

items.title: Custom HTTP API
items.text:
Targets — Define an HTTP target that a custom feature or check can use.

Replace base_url with your API. This target intentionally has no navigation features until the table snippet is added. The examples assume JSON responses.

Suggested filename: 10-http-api.yaml.

targets:
  example_api:
    label: Example application API
    connection: http
    base_url: https://api.example.com
    features: []

items.title: API table with filters and details
items.text:
Features — Map a JSON items array into a searchable resource table with detail pages.

Assumes GET /items returns {"items":[{"id":"1","name":"Example","status":"running"}]} and GET /items/1 returns one item. Adapt paths and JSONata mappings. The features list replaces the earlier list.

Requires: Custom HTTP API (including their prerequisites), or equivalent existing definitions.

Suggested filename: 20-api-table.yaml.

operations:
  example.items.list:
    bindings:
      http:
        executor: http.request
        path: /items
  example.items.inspect:
    bindings:
      http:
        executor: http.request
        path: /items/{id}
        inputs:
          id: {type: string}
features:
  example.items:
    title: Example items
    group: Applications
    operation: example.items.list
    rows: items
    columns:
      - {label: Name, value: name}
      - label: Status
        value: status
        badges: {running: active, stopped: muted}
    filters:
      - key: status
        label: Status
        value: status
        choices: {running: Running, stopped: Stopped}
    details:
      operation: example.items.inspect
      row_id: id
      input: id
      title: name
      fields:
        - {label: Name, value: name}
        - {label: Status, value: status}
targets:
  example_api:
    features: [example.items]

items.title: Confirmed row and bulk action
items.text:
Actions — Add a restart action with an icon and confirmation to the example table.

Assumes POST /items/{id}/restart. This performs a real mutation when clicked; adapt it to your API. The actions list replaces any earlier actions list.

Requires: API table with filters and details (including their prerequisites), or equivalent existing definitions.

Suggested filename: 30-api-action.yaml.

operations:
  example.items.restart:
    bindings:
      http:
        executor: http.request
        method: POST
        path: /items/{id}/restart
        inputs:
          id: {type: string}
features:
  example.items:
    actions:
      - label: Restart item
        icon: restart
        operation: example.items.restart
        row: {id: id}
        bulk: true
        confirmation: Restart the selected items?

items.title: Group targets into an environment
items.text:
Environments — Show Docker and an application API together in one environment.

Targets carry their features. An environment groups targets and can also reference custom pages. Replace IDs to group your existing targets.

Requires: Standalone Docker, Custom HTTP API (including their prerequisites), or equivalent existing definitions.

Suggested filename: 30-environment.yaml.

environments:
  example_workspace:
    label: Example workspace
    targets: [example_docker, example_api]

items.title: Dashboard across Docker and Swarm
items.text:
Dashboards — Combine sources from two engines into cards, tables and a chart.

Sources are queried on page load. JSONata expressions refer to source results by name. Replace target IDs to use existing engines.

Requires: Standalone Docker, Swarm manager over SSH (including their prerequisites), or equivalent existing definitions.

Suggested filename: 40-cross-target-dashboard.yaml.

pages:
  example_operations:
    title: Example operations dashboard
    sources:
      local:
        target: example_docker
        operation: containers.list
      swarm:
        target: example_swarm
        operation: swarm.services.list
    cards:
      - label: Running local containers
        value: $count(data.local[State = "running"])
      - label: Swarm services
        value: $count(data.swarm)
    panels:
      - title: Swarm replicas
        sources: [swarm]
        rows: data.swarm
        target: example_swarm
        feature: services
        row_id: ID
        columns:
          - {label: Service, value: Spec.Name}
          - label: Running / desired
            value: '$string(ServiceStatus.RunningTasks) & "/" & $string(ServiceStatus.DesiredTasks)'
            sort_value: ServiceStatus.RunningTasks
            tone: 'ServiceStatus.RunningTasks < ServiceStatus.DesiredTasks ? "destructive" : "active"'
    charts:
      - title: Workloads by target
        type: bar
        rows: '[{"target":"Docker","count":$count(data.local)},{"target":"Swarm","count":$count(data.swarm)}]'
        x: target
        series:
          - {label: Workloads, value: count}

items.title: Environment-only custom page
items.text:
Dashboards — Limit the example dashboard to a specific environment.

Root pages are explicitly empty. The team environment includes the page. This controls page placement, not user authorization.

Requires: Dashboard across Docker and Swarm (including their prerequisites), or equivalent existing definitions.

Suggested filename: 50-page-scope.yaml.

environments:
  root:
    pages: []
  example_operations_team:
    label: Example operations team
    targets: [example_docker, example_swarm]
    pages: [example_operations]

items.title: Scheduled connection check
items.text:
Checks — Check a target connection with failure and recovery thresholds.

No operation means connector-level connection testing. Scheduled checks begin after the configuration is applied. Persist /data for check history.

Requires: Custom HTTP API (including their prerequisites), or equivalent existing definitions.

Suggested filename: 30-connection-check.yaml.

checks:
  example_api_connection:
    title: Example API connection
    target: example_api
    every: 60s
    failure_threshold: 3
    recovery_threshold: 2

items.title: Scheduled JSON health check
items.text:
Checks — Evaluate a JSON readiness response with JSONata.

Assumes GET /health returns {"status":"ok"}. Adapt the path and healthy expression. Use eligible reads for scheduled operations; persist /data for history.

Requires: Custom HTTP API (including their prerequisites), or equivalent existing definitions.

Suggested filename: 30-http-health-check.yaml.

operations:
  example.health:
    check_safe: true
    bindings:
      http:
        executor: http.request
        path: /health
checks:
  example_api_health:
    title: Example API readiness
    target: example_api
    operation: example.health
    healthy: status = "ok"
    every: 30s
    failure_threshold: 2
    recovery_threshold: 1

items.title: Metrics across SSH targets
items.text:
SSH fleets — Aggregate Linux host metrics across a selected set of SSH targets.

Add more SSH target IDs to the targets list. Metrics are requested on demand, not continuously collected.

Requires: Linux host over SSH (including their prerequisites), or equivalent existing definitions.

Suggested filename: 30-ssh-fleet-metrics.yaml.

batches:
  example_fleet_metrics:
    title: Example fleet metrics
    operation: host.metrics
    columns:
      - {label: CPU percent, value: result.cpu}
      - label: Available memory MB
        value: $round(result.memory.MemAvailable / 1000000, 1)
      - label: Available disk GB
        value: $round(result.disk.available / 1000000000, 2)

environments:
  example_fleet_metrics:
    label: Example SSH metrics
    targets: [example_ssh]
    batches: [example_fleet_metrics]

items.title: Command across SSH targets
items.text:
SSH fleets — Run an operator-supplied command on selected SSH hosts with confirmation.

Add more SSH target IDs to the targets list. Commands run with the configured SSH user privileges; this is interactive fleet execution, not a scheduled check.

Requires: Linux host over SSH (including their prerequisites), or equivalent existing definitions.

Suggested filename: 30-ssh-fleet-command.yaml.

batches:
  example_fleet_command:
    title: Example fleet command
    operation: ssh.command
    confirmation: Run this command on every selected SSH host as its configured user?
    columns:
      - label: Output
        value: $substring(result.text, 0, 1000)

environments:
  example_fleet_command:
    label: Example SSH command
    targets: [example_ssh]
    batches: [example_fleet_command]

items.title: Registry credentials for Docker
items.text:
Credentials — Registry credentials for Docker. File-backed references keep credential values outside the configuration.

Mount the registry token file first. Credentials apply to this target’s image pulls and Compose operations by image hostname. Use docker.io for Docker Hub; Git tokens are separate.

Requires: Standalone Docker (including their prerequisites), or equivalent existing definitions.

Suggested filename: 20-registry-credentials.yaml.

targets:
  example_docker:
    registry_credentials:
      ghcr.io: registry_ghcr.io
credentials:
  registry_ghcr.io:
    type: basic
    username: example-user
    password:
      file: /run/secrets/ghcr_token

items.title: Git and registry credentials for Swarm
items.text:
Credentials — Git and registry credentials for Swarm. File-backed references keep credential values outside the configuration.

Mount referenced files and replace hosts/users. In the stack editor choose Git repository, enter HTTPS or ssh:// URL and a branch/tag/commit, then select the credential. Registry auth is forwarded to workers during deployment.

Requires: Swarm manager over SSH (including their prerequisites), or equivalent existing definitions.

Suggested filename: 20-swarm-source-credentials.yaml.

targets:
  example_swarm:
    registry_credentials:
      ghcr.io: registry_ghcr.io
    git_credentials:
    - example_https
    - example_ssh
credentials:
  registry_ghcr.io:
    type: basic
    username: example-user
    password:
      file: /run/secrets/ghcr_token
  example_https:
    type: basic
    username: deploy
    host: git.example.com
    password:
      file: /run/secrets/git_token
  example_ssh:
    type: ssh
    username: git
    host: git.example.com
    private_key:
      file: /run/secrets/git_key
    known_hosts:
      file: /etc/declarack/git_known_hosts

items.title: Named credential profiles
items.text:
Connections — Centralize entered values or mounted-file references, then select profile IDs on connections.

Use Settings → Credentials to paste/upload values or edit paths. Replace the example secret paths. Profiles are stored in configuration and history; inline values also appear in exports and write-back files.

Requires: Standalone Docker (including their prerequisites), or equivalent existing definitions.

Suggested filename: 05-credentials.yaml.

credentials:
  example_api_token:
    type: token
    label: Example API token
    token: {file: /run/secrets/api_token}
  example_registry:
    type: basic
    label: Example registry login
    username: deploy
    password: {file: /run/secrets/registry_password}

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text:
Start with the active configuration, target/provider, exact error and controller logs. A configured view is not proof that an upstream engine/API granted every action.

Symptom Check Configs or secrets absent on standalone Expected. Native Docker configs/secrets are Swarm resources. New integration is saved but not visible Reload configuration after saving the fragment. Add integration cannot save Use a writable folder mount plus DECLARACK_CONFIG_EDIT=1. Save/review says the configuration changed Read sources/catalog again and review against the current revision. Environment membership disappears A later list replaces an earlier list. Check source ordering and the merged preview. SSH connection fails Container-visible identity/known_hosts paths, user, port, host keys and manager reachability. Remote Swarm inventory works but node jobs fail Matching published job image, node pull access, node eligibility and job support. Existing Compose YAML unavailable Labels contain paths, not file contents; mount the host source or use a saved source. Volume size unavailable Run explicit collection and inspect per-node errors; missing data is not zero. Dropdown shows no choices Inspect its read-operation error, dependencies, mapping and explicit Load options requirement. Check is healthy during a failure Thresholds count consecutive results; inspect the latest result and failure counter. No email/webhook after failure Outbound notifications are not implemented. Check history records local transitions. Operation says interrupted Inspect resources and completed steps; the backend does not replay interrupted mutations.

items.title: Read controller logs
items.text:
For the default checkout deployment:

docker compose logs --tail=100 declarack

For the real lab:

docker compose -f examples/multi-environment/compose.yaml logs --tail=100 declarack

Use Settings → Test all connections to probe configured targets, or the wizard's Test connection for one draft. A transport probe is not a test of every feature. Do not retry destructive operations simply because a response timed out: a remote write may have completed. Re-read inventory first.

items.title: Separate the failure layers
items.text:
1. Bootstrap: can the controller read its config, password and data mount?
  2. Connection: can it reach the socket, SSH host or API origin?
  3. Operation: are inputs, permissions and the provider binding valid?
  4. Mapping: does JSONata match the actual response shape?
  5. Presentation: are dependencies, filters and source states hiding the result?

Keep the response shape and source/target names when reporting mapping failures. The Inspect JSON and export flows are unmasked; choose what to share deliberately.

For exact constraints, use configuration limits and current coverage.

items.title: Build, maintain and host the documentation
items.text: This site is a static documentation build, separate from the Declarack runtime. It uses Zensical, with its MkDocs-compatible configuration format. Documentation dependencies are pinned in docs/requirements.txt; application dependencies and image build stages are unchanged.

items.title: Preview locally
items.text:
From a repository checkout:

python3 -m venv .venv-docs
.venv-docs/bin/pip install -r docs/requirements.txt
.venv-docs/bin/python tools/docs.py serve --port 9100

Open http://127.0.0.1:9100. The server binds to loopback. Changes to guides/reference sources rebuild the preview. Preview sources, output and caches are isolated from clean builds, so a build can run beside the preview. Search is local to the built site, fonts use the system stack, and no external analytics are configured.

items.title: Build and check
items.text:
.venv-docs/bin/python tools/docs.py build

The command stages maintained sources, runs a strict static-site build and checks local HTML links/anchors. Output is .docs-build/site/, which can be served by any static host. To preview that exact artifact:

python3 -m http.server 9100 --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory .docs-build/site

Set DOCS_SITE_URL to the final canonical URL, including its project prefix, when building for a different host/domain:

DOCS_SITE_URL=https://docs.example.com/ .venv-docs/bin/python tools/docs.py build

The production canonical URL is https://daniellmorris.com/declarack/docs/. Local live preview uses its own loopback canonical URL.

items.title: Where to edit
items.text:
Source Purpose docs/site/ Homepage, guides, tutorials, styles and logo Existing docs/*.md Canonical detailed references; reused without a second maintained copy configurations/ Downloadable starting configurations examples/tutorial-api/ Runnable training API and tutorial fragments examples/multi-environment/ Real Docker-in-Docker lab guide and source files landing/ Product landing page HTML, CSS and curated public assets mkdocs.yml Navigation, theme, extensions and validation docs/published-files.txt Explicit allowlist of downloadable example/configuration files tools/docs_stage.py Explicit source staging; excludes runtime/hidden/generated content tools/check_tutorial.py Exercises tutorial mappings and an authenticated controller against the training API

Do not edit .docs-build/; its staged sources, preview files and build output are generated. The stager places website pages at the site root and preserves existing reference and example paths. Internal website links use those staged paths. No runtime config, SSH keys, generated credentials or backend data volumes are included by the staging allowlist. The checked-in tutorial screenshots under docs/site/assets/screenshots/ are intentionally published site assets.

items.title: Build and publication workflow
items.text:
.github/workflows/docs.yml builds the documentation and browser demo together. Pull requests validate both and upload the declarack-site artifact. Main-branch pushes and manual runs additionally publish generated demo/, docs/, landing-page assets and HTML into public/declarack/ in the existing public personal website repository. The Astro Pages workflow there performs the final deployment.

The application repository stays private. The publisher copies the curated docs build and compiled demo, not the checkout. Only the generated Declarack directory is updated, preserving the website’s other pages. A repository-scoped SSH deploy key is stored as the source repository’s DECLARACK_SITE_DEPLOY_KEY Actions secret. The key grants writes to the website repository; the publishing script restricts its own changes to the generated paths. Pull requests never receive a publish job.

The resulting locations are docs and demo. See the browser playground guide for local bundle builds and credential rotation. Neither output needs a running backend or database. Normal GitHub Actions usage limits still apply.

items.title: Maintaining the walkthrough screenshots
items.text:
The tutorials and guides include 25 screenshots captured from the actual application with synthetic training data. Each has descriptive alt text and a caption explaining the next action or expected result. Images load lazily; select any image to open the original PNG at full size. They are static illustrations, not live dashboards, and contain no production resources.

To refresh them after UI changes:

  1. Build the frontend and run the two APIs from the first tutorial and dashboard tutorial.
  2. Run a separate folder-backed controller with the three checked-in tutorial fragments, editable configuration, and its own temporary data directory.
  3. Capture the table and detail page before changing counters. Capture one row confirmation/result and the two-resource bulk review. Cancel that bulk review.
  4. In Restart by team, select Platform/Catalog API, then switch to Product and capture the cleared application field before selecting Customer portal.
  5. Capture the complete dashboard. Stop only Staging for the partial-failure screenshot and restart it afterward.
  6. Open Checks and its readiness detail. Stop Training, run two checks and capture the one-failure and threshold-reached states. Scheduled runs also count, so verify the displayed state before saving each image. Restart Training, run a check, capture recovery, then pause/capture/resume.
  7. In Settings, edit only a comment in 20-checks.yaml, capture the draft, save it, capture the save status, then reload and capture its status. Use New file with 30-notes.yaml and {} as an illustration; Cancel without creating it.
  8. Use Custom HTTP API to add training-copy with /apps, rows items, environment tutorial and the host-reachable API origin. Capture the catalog, fields, reviewed YAML/test result and saved fragment before reloading. Test all connections in Settings afterward.
  9. For the generic selector guide, add selectors.yaml, open Applications by team, select Product and capture the resulting Customer portal row.
  10. Replace the matching PNGs in docs/site/assets/screenshots/, preserve readable text and surrounding navigation, then run python tools/docs.py build. Inspect the rendered guides and open a full-size image to verify its link.

Workspace totals, timestamps and counters change as the tutorials progress. Keep captions focused on the meaningful controls and states. Screenshots are excluded from the runtime Docker build context; they are served only by the documentation website. Capture genuine UI results rather than drawing replacement controls.

items.title: Configuration diagrams
items.text: The configuration overview uses committed SVGs so diagrams render without JavaScript or external services. Edit tools/docs_diagrams.py and regenerate with python3 tools/docs_diagrams.py, then build the docs and inspect the diagrams. The complete example is examples/configuration-overview.yaml; keep the guide’s copy in sync and validate it with the installed backend before publishing.

items.title: Concepts and terminology
items.text:
Declarack turns a system configuration into an administration interface. YAML chooses connections, operations and views; JSONata maps returned data. Adapters supply execution mechanisms and resource-specific rules.

Start with How configuration fits together for diagrams, a complete example and the edit/review/save/reload workflow.

items.title: The configuration model
items.text:
Term Meaning Example Target A configured connection A Docker socket, Swarm manager, SSH host or HTTP API Environment A group of target references with navigation placement Production contains its Swarm, monitoring API and SSH hosts Operation A named request or command with an input schema List applications or restart a selected service Binding How an operation runs for a provider An HTTP request or Docker API call Feature A resource view plus its actions/workflows Containers, applications or dashboard inventory Page A custom layout combining read sources Cards and charts across multiple targets Workflow A config-defined form and action sequence in the UI Collect inputs, preview changes, confirm and execute Check A scheduled connection or read-operation evaluation API readiness every 30 seconds Adapter Trusted code and YAML discovered from a folder Docker, Swarm, SSH or HTTP Integration template A starting configuration expanded from form values Add a second Grafana instance

An environment organizes targets. It is not a transport or an authorization boundary, and targets can belong to multiple groups or none. Features belong to targets. The reserved root environment is Home; it is not an inheritance parent. Pages and fleet tools are placed through environment membership lists, including root. Page sources explicitly name targets and are independent of page placement.

items.title: What the YAML controls
items.text:
targets: {}                 # At least one connection
environments: {}            # Groups; explicit empty leaves only reserved root
operations: {}              # Named requests/commands
features: {}                # Resource views and actions
pages: {}                   # Multi-source layouts
checks: {}                  # Scheduled evaluations
batches: {}                 # Configured multi-target operation pages
integration_templates: {}   # Additional trusted setup presets
# auth: ...                # Installation-wide authentication

The system configuration is broader than a dashboard layout. It does not replace a Compose file, Docker's daemon settings or application deployment source. Enabling a feature does not deploy an application.

items.title: A request through the framework
items.text:
1. An enabled feature invokes a named operation on a target.
  2. The backend validates the operation's declared inputs and selects its provider binding.
  3. An adapter executes the request, command or node job.
  4. JSONata maps the response into rows, fields, cards or chart points.
  5. The shared renderer presents the result and its configured actions.

Docker/Swarm details remain in adapters and their YAML. The UI does not need a new resource-specific component for each external API.

items.title: State and execution
items.text:
The active database revision defines behavior; its documents retain the YAML schema. The shared database stores saved source records, legacy encrypted credentials, check history, operation runs and configuration revisions. SQLite under the data directory is the default; PostgreSQL is optional. Local checkouts, materialized Compose files and other transient working files still use the data directory. YAML files seed or explicitly update database configuration. Only one active controller is supported. Browser preferences such as density/page size are separate. Charts do not retain time-series samples.

Most reads run on demand or when opening a view. Browser auto-refresh is opt-in; scheduled checks run in the controller process even when the browser is closed. A server-owned operation plan continues after its browser closes, but an interrupted backend does not automatically resume that plan.

Configuration reference · Storage · Architecture

items.title: How configuration fits together
items.text: Declarack has one active system configuration revision in the database. It contains YAML documents merged into one configuration. Files seed an empty installation and remain explicit import/export sources. It describes connections, administration views and execution. It is broader than a dashboard layout, and it is separate from the Compose files used to deploy your applications.

items.title: From deployment to the running system
items.text:
Layer What you configure Where it lives Deployment / bootstrap Config source, database connection, mounts, process settings and mounted secrets Compose or Swarm service specification and environment variables System configuration Targets, environments, navigation, pages, features, operations, batches, checks and auth references Active database revision containing logical YAML documents Adapter definitions Connection types, executors and bundled features/operations Trusted adapter folders loaded at startup Application sources Compose YAML, Git repository/ref and deployment inputs External folders/repositories or adapter source records Runtime state Check history, tracked runs, saved source metadata and configuration revisions SQLite by default, or PostgreSQL

The database owns both active configuration and runtime state. YAML source files are no longer required for ordinary restarts after the initial import. Browser preferences and transient sessions are separate again. An external database does not enable multiple active controllers; one controller remains supported. See deployment and storage.

items.title: Definitions reference each other
items.text:
• Target: where you connect, and which features that connection exposes.
  • Environment: a group of existing targets with page, fleet-tool and navigation placement. A target can belong to several environments or none.
  • Root: the reserved environment named root, normally labelled Home. It owns links to installation-wide tools. It is not an inheritance parent for other environments, and it does not automatically contain every target.
  • Page: a reusable dashboard whose sources explicitly name targets and read operations. Placing a page in an environment does not filter its sources to that environment; it may intentionally query several environments.
  • Batch / fleet tool: a reusable operation run across selected targets. If its targets list is omitted, eligible targets are inferred from environments that assign it. The UI limits selection to the current environment's targets and the batch's eligible list. Every inferred target must support the operation.
  • Feature and operation: a feature describes a resource view and its actions; named operations describe requests or commands, with provider bindings that select adapter execution. JSONata maps returned data into the view.
  • Check: a scheduled connection test or safe read operation naming a target. It does not require that target to be visible in an environment.

Settings, the complete target inventory, checks and operation history remain installation-wide. Root navigation can order, group, relabel or hide their links. Navigation visibility is not authorization.

Root always exists. Without an environments section, Declarack also generates one environment per target. With environments: {}, only root remains. Root starts with no targets or batches and all custom pages unless its pages list is explicit. Other environments default to empty target/page/batch lists. Explicit navigation replaces that environment's generated links; it does not merge them. The old page top_level field is not supported.

items.title: A folder is one merged document
items.text:
config/
  00-targets.yaml
  20-dashboards.yaml
  30-fleet-tools.yaml
  40-environments.yaml
  50-checks.yaml

Files are discovered recursively and sorted by relative path, case-sensitively. Folder names are organizational: they do not create environment scope or namespaces. Mappings merge recursively; a later list, scalar or different type replaces the earlier value at that key. Duplicate YAML keys inside a file fail validation. Hidden files/directories and non-YAML files are ignored.

For example, a later environments.engines.targets: [engine_b] replaces an earlier [engine_a, engine_b]; it does not append. Prefer one owning file per environment so its complete definition can be edited through the form. See exact merge rules and limits.

items.title: Complete example: two Docker targets
items.text:
The copyable YAML file uses bundled Docker definitions; it needs no custom adapter, operation or frontend code. Adapt the socket paths and mount both engines' sockets before use. Socket paths are relative to the Declarack process/container, not your browser. The second path is illustrative: this example does not create a remote tunnel or an engine. Configure installation authentication through your deployment, such as DECLARACK_PASSWORD or the supported mounted-secret configuration.

# Adapt both socket mounts before use. Loading this file does not connect to them.
targets:
  engine_a:
    label: Engine A
    connection: docker_socket
    socket: /var/run/docker.sock
    features: [containers]
  engine_b:
    label: Engine B
    connection: docker_socket
    socket: /run/engine-b/docker.sock
    features: [containers]

pages:
  workloads:
    title: Workload overview
    sources:
      a: {target: engine_a, operation: containers.list}
      b: {target: engine_b, operation: containers.list}
    cards:
      - {label: Engine A containers, value: '$count(data.a)'}
      - {label: Engine B containers, value: '$count(data.b)'}

batches:
  inventory:
    title: Collect container inventory
    operation: containers.list
    columns:
      - {label: Containers, value: '$count(result)'}

environments:
  root:
    label: Home
    pages: [workloads]
    navigation:
      - {item: environments, group: Workspace}
      - {page: workloads}
      - {item: targets, group: Administration}
      - {item: checks}
      - {item: operations}
      - {item: settings}
  engines:
    label: Docker engines
    targets: [engine_a, engine_b]
    pages: [workloads]
    batches: [inventory]
    navigation:
      - {page: workloads, group: Overview}
      - {batch: inventory, label: Collect inventory, group: Tools}

checks:
  engine_a_connection:
    title: Engine A connection
    target: engine_a
    every: 1m

What this produces:

Location Result Home Workload overview and the chosen installation-wide links; no target membership Docker engines Engine A and B workspaces, the shared dashboard, and Collect inventory Workload overview Separate container counts queried from both engines, regardless of where the page is opened Collect inventory On-demand reads from selected targets in Docker engines; each target returns its own result Checks An Engine A connection check scheduled every minute after activation

The example connects to existing engines; it does not deploy containers. Engine B has no scheduled check here. The connection check does not assert that every container is healthy. Both target workspaces expose the bundled Containers view. Loading/validating the YAML does not execute its inventory operations or checks.

For SSH fleets, use SSH targets with mounted identity and known-hosts files, enable host_metrics / ssh_commands, and assign a metrics or confirmed command batch to their environment. Use the complete SSH fleet example for those transport prerequisites and execution limits.

items.title: The operator workflow
items.text:
1. Add connections: use Settings → Add integration, or configure target YAML. Add integration creates a source fragment in an editable configuration folder; unsupported setup cases and single-file installations use YAML.
  2. Arrange your workspace: open Settings → Home & environments. Choose Home, select an existing environment, or create one. Assign existing targets, dashboards and fleet tools, then arrange navigation labels and groups.
  3. Review the draft: validation covers the full proposed merge. Inspect the generated YAML, document diff and effective merged diff. Existing environments use their owning logical document; new ones need a document destination.
  4. Save: a revision/digest-checked save stores a pending database revision and history. It does not change the active configuration or filesystem sources.
  5. Activate: apply the saved revision. With WRITE_BACK=1, conflict-checked file publication completes first. On restart the active database revision is loaded; pending saved changes remain pending. FORCE_LOAD=1 instead imports source files on every startup. Both flags default off.
  6. Recover: restore history into a draft, review, save and activate. For an interrupted write-back, reconcile conflicts or permissions and retry activation or restart. See the storage contract.

The form does not create new dashboard layouts, feature schemas or operation bindings. Define those through the appropriate YAML/deployment workflow, then select them in the environment editor. Existing environment IDs cannot be renamed there, and deleting definitions remains a YAML operation. Split-file environment definitions must be consolidated first. Form saves normalize YAML formatting and remove comments in the affected file; the review exposes that change.

The database owns the active revision for all source providers. Git and Swarm sources retain explicit publication workflows; publishing does not implicitly activate their contents locally. Imports are reviewed before activation. Auth changes require a restart/import. Storage settings explain defaults, flags, exports and write-back recovery.

items.text:
