items.title: Browsing an environment
items.text:
Select an environment to keep its targets and shared workflows together. Each member target has a collapsible sidebar group populated from its enabled feature definitions. Opening a resource, detail, terminal or deployment workflow keeps the same environment selected. Breadcrumbs show environment, target and feature. Changing environments is explicit through the selector or Home.

The environment overview collects each target’s configured summary cards and existing summary panels together. Panels show up to five rows, with View all opening the target’s full resource page inside the same environment. Requests are bounded and failures remain isolated by target/feature. Manual operations such as host metrics are not automatically triggered. No cross-target mutation is implied by displaying resources together.

Environment batches expose shared operations such as SSH fleet metrics or fleet commands. Their eligible targets are intersected with the environment membership; the execution page lets the operator choose a subset and reports each target’s result separately. These workflows remain alongside individual target features. navigation continues to control labels, grouping and ordering; target membership determines the collapsible resource groups. Installation settings remain at Home.

Scoped resource URLs use #/environments/<environment>/targets/<target>/<feature> and retain this prefix for details and workflows. Direct #/<target>/<feature> bookmarks still work without implicitly selecting an environment. An explicit scoped URL cannot open a target outside that environment. Environment membership controls presentation, not user permissions: all signed-in accounts are administrators.

items.title: Refreshing the current page
items.text:
Use Refresh in the top bar to refresh the current environment, dashboard or resource page. It updates the configured automatic summaries/sources together; target cards and individual panels do not have separate refresh buttons. A compact collection status sits to the left of Refresh; separate source loading cards and per-target loading badges are omitted. If collection fails, hover, focus or tap the info icon to see the affected targets, sources and errors. These are data collection outcomes, not workload-health checks. File browsing uses the same top-level control to reload the current directory. Automatic refresh intervals, where configured, remain available.

Manual resource collection and on-demand dashboard sources keep an explicit Collect action. A page refresh does not start those jobs. Creation forms and interactive terminals do not show a refresh button.

items.title: Get started with Declarack
items.text: Choose a real Docker installation, a sample-data preview, or the API tutorial. All commands below run from the repository root.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
For Docker management, install Docker with Compose and ensure the engine is running. For the source-based API tutorial, use Python 3.12+ and Node 22.12+ instead. The examples use Linux containers, including on Docker Desktop.

git clone https://github.com/daniellmorris/declarack.git
cd declarack

The repository currently requires access to the private GitHub project. Use your normal authorized Git credentials; do not put a token in a copied clone URL.

items.title: Run against your Docker engine
items.text:
export DECLARACK_PASSWORD='choose-a-strong-local-password'
docker compose up -d --build

Open http://127.0.0.1:8080, sign in as admin, and use the password you exported. The default bootstrap detects a standalone engine or a local Swarm manager. You should see inventory from that engine, not sample data.

The base Compose file mounts the Docker socket and persists application data in declarack-data. Socket access gives administrative control of the engine. Keep this installation on loopback or behind your normal authenticated HTTPS access.

items.title: Enable guided integration setup
items.text:
The Add integration wizard saves new files, so it needs folder-backed settings. Follow the configuration workflow to mount a writable folder. Then open Targets → Add integration, choose a template, review the generated YAML, test the connection, save, and activate configuration.

A target is a connection. An environment is an optional group of targets; adding a connection does not require a new environment. Read the terminology.

items.title: Explore sample data instead
items.text:
docker build -t declarack .
docker run --rm -e DECLARACK_MODE=demo -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 declarack

Stop the other port-8080 installation first, or publish this preview on a different host port. Demo mode uses sample inventory and temporary data; it does not prove that real Docker mutations, SSH connections or container cloning work.

items.title: Learn the framework without Docker
items.text: The first API interface tutorial starts a real local HTTP server and connects Declarack to it. You will inspect data, perform a harmless training action and use dynamic dropdowns before building a dashboard across targets.

items.title: Stop and return later
items.text:
docker compose stop

Start again with docker compose up -d. Keep the data volume and configuration folder. Do not remove volumes as a routine shutdown step. See deployment and persistence before moving an installation.

items.title: Build your first API administration interface
items.text:
Outcome: a working application table, detail pages, confirmed row/bulk actions, and a form whose application choices depend on the selected team. You need a repository checkout, Python 3.12+ and Node 22.12+. No Docker engine is required.

This tutorial uses an actual local HTTP server with synthetic data. Its restart endpoint increments a counter; it does not restart real applications. All state in that API resets when the training server restarts.

items.title: 1. Install and build Declarack
items.text:
From the repository root:

python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt
npm --prefix frontend ci
npm --prefix frontend run build

If you already have that development environment, reuse it. The example files are the training server and the complete system configuration.

items.title: 2. Start the training API
items.text:
In one terminal:

python3 examples/tutorial-api/server.py

Keep it running. In another terminal, verify the response:

curl http://127.0.0.1:9010/apps

You should receive an object with an items array containing Catalog API, Queue worker and Customer portal. Each record has id, name, team, status and restarts. Two records are running and one is stopped.

items.title: 3. Start a separate Declarack instance
items.text:
In the second terminal, from the repository root:

DECLARACK_CONFIG=examples/tutorial-api/declarack.yaml \
DECLARACK_CONFIG_FORCE_LOAD=1 \
DECLARACK_DATA=/tmp/declarack-tutorial-data \
DECLARACK_PASSWORD='choose-a-local-tutorial-password' \
PORT=9081 .venv/bin/python -m backend.server

Open http://127.0.0.1:9081, sign in as admin, and use your chosen password. Select Training API → Applications. This instance uses port 9081 so it can coexist with the real lab on 9080 and a normal installation on 8080.

These loopback URLs assume both Python processes run on your host. Inside a Docker container, 127.0.0.1 identifies that container, so do not copy this origin unchanged into a container deployment. Use a reachable container-network/host address there.

items.title: 4. Understand the table
items.text:
Expected result: three applications, two running and one stopped. Search, Status, column sorting, exports and page size are above/below the rows. The screenshots follow the combined tutorial configuration, so later captures may also show Staging API in the workspace. Select the image to open it at full size.

The checked-in file connects the target to an enabled feature:

targets:
  training:
    label: Training API
    connection: http
    base_url: http://127.0.0.1:9010
    features: [tutorial.apps]

A named operation supplies data. The provider binding says how to retrieve it:

operations:
  tutorial.apps.list:
    bindings:
      http: {executor: http.request, path: /apps}

The feature extracts rows with JSONata and chooses their columns:

operation: tutorial.apps.list
rows: items
columns:
  - {label: Application, value: name}
  - {label: Team, value: team}
  - {label: Status, value: status}
  - {label: Restarts, value: restarts}

Click headers to sort, filter by Status, search by name and export the resulting rows. Exports include filtered rows beyond the current page. JSON exports contain the mapped records; CSV uses the visible columns.

items.title: 5. Open details and run an action
items.text:
Click Catalog API to see its dedicated detail page, then return to the list. Use its Restart example app row action and confirm the message. Refresh if needed: its restart counter should increase by one.

Open Catalog API from its name in the table; Back to applications returns to the list. Select the image to open it at full size.

Review the target, resource and effect before choosing Confirm. This example only increments a counter. Select the image to open it at full size.

After confirmation, the completion message appears and Catalog API shows Restarts = 1. Select the image to open it at full size.

The operation maps a validated id into an encoded path and sends a POST request. The feature's row: {id: id} supplies the selected record's identity. The installed example also enables bulk: true: select two rows and review the eligible resources before confirming. Results appear in the global Operations view.

Select the two row checkboxes, then Restart example app selected. Review both identities before confirming the two operations; Cancel leaves them unchanged. Select the image to open it at full size.

The API server—not JSX—owns the training state change. In your own integration, the operation would call your actual management API with its own authorization and resource checks.

items.title: 6. Try dependent dropdowns
items.text:
Choose Restart by team above the table:

  1. Select Platform. The application field loads Catalog API and Queue worker.
  2. Select Catalog API, then switch the team to Product.
  3. The application value clears and its choices become Customer portal.
  4. Select Customer portal and confirm the training action.

Platform loads two application choices. Selecting Catalog API enables the action. Select the image to open it at full size.

Changing Team to Product clears the prior application. Choose Customer portal before proceeding; the disabled action prevents submitting the old choice. Select the image to open it at full size.

The field definitions use options_from, with the second field depending on team and mapping form.team into a read-operation input. The lookup features establish read roles but are not enabled in navigation. This shows how a form can query supporting resources without adding extra sidebar views.

Dynamic form reference explains manual sources, stale requests and validation.

items.title: 7. Customize it
items.text:
Copy the complete configuration before adapting it for a real API. Change the origin, resource paths, response mappings, columns and operation schemas. Use a mounted bearer credential reference with HTTPS where required. Do not send actual credentials to the unauthenticated training server.

After external YAML edits, use Settings → Review import from files → Import & activate, or restart this tutorial process (FORCE_LOAD imports files at startup). For GUI file creation and integration setup, switch to folder configuration.

Next: keep these processes running and build a dashboard across two targets, then add scheduled checks. Stop either process with Ctrl+C when finished. The tutorial data directory is separate from your regular installation; its persisted run/check history can be kept for a later session.

items.title: Schedule a readiness check
items.text: Outcome: a scheduled read with consecutive failure/recovery thresholds and persisted result history. Start with the folder from the dashboard tutorial. Only the Training API is required for this check.

items.title: 1. Add the check fragment
items.text:
cp examples/tutorial-api/checks.yaml /tmp/declarack-tutorial-config/20-checks.yaml

In Declarack Settings, choose Review import from files, inspect the diff, and select Import & activate. Alternatively restart the tutorial with FORCE_LOAD=1. The fragment is:

checks:
  tutorial-readiness:
    title: Training API readiness
    target: training
    operation: tutorial.health
    healthy: status = "ok"
    every: 10s
    failure_threshold: 2
    recovery_threshold: 1

tutorial.health is already declared in the base tutorial configuration with check_safe: true and a GET binding for /health. You can omit operation for a connector-level connection check instead. A scheduler operation must be an eligible read or explicitly check-safe; mutating HTTP/Docker methods are refused.

items.title: 2. Inspect the first result
items.text:
Open Checks, select Training API readiness, and choose Run now. A successful JSON response with status: ok should make the check healthy. Its history and last-success information appear on the detail page.

Find the check in the workspace Checks view. Its target and operation appear underneath its name. Select the image to open it at full size.

Choose the check name to open history, then Run now. The current state, last-success time and recent results are visible together. Select the image to open it at full size.

Definitions live in YAML. Runtime results, current state and operator pauses live in the shared database (state.sqlite under the data directory by default). The tutorial's /tmp data path is for local training; use a persistent deployment volume for production.

items.title: 3. Trigger and recover from failure
items.text:
Stop the Training API with Ctrl+C. Choose Run now twice, waiting for each result to finish, or allow two scheduled runs. The latest result fails immediately, but a prior healthy state can remain until the second consecutive failure reaches the configured threshold. Then the check becomes failing.

One failure records a Failed result while the prior healthy alarm state remains below the threshold. Scheduled runs can advance this state before you capture it. Select the image to open it at full size.

After the second consecutive failure, the alarm state becomes failing. Read Result and Alarm state separately in history. Select the image to open it at full size.

Restart the API:

python3 examples/tutorial-api/server.py

Choose Run now again. One successful result meets the recovery threshold and returns the check to healthy. The API's example restart counters reset because its data is in memory; Declarack's check history remains in its separate data directory.

One successful result meets recovery_threshold: 1. The newest history row marks the healthy transition; earlier failed results remain. Select the image to open it at full size.

items.title: 4. Pause deliberately
items.text:
Pause and resume the check from its detail page. Pause is persisted separately from YAML enabled: false; it survives a controller restart. Paused or disabled checks cannot be run manually. A run already in flight may finish.

Pause changes the operator state to paused and disables Run now. Resume restores scheduling; it does not erase history. Select the image to open it at full size.

These transitions are local alarms and recovery records. Declarack currently sends no email/webhook notifications and has no maintenance windows or uptime-percentage calculation. Do not interpret this tutorial as outbound alert delivery.

Check behavior, retention and limits · Health sources

items.title: Build a dashboard across targets
items.text: Outcome: one custom page showing counts, a grouped bar chart and two resource tables from independent APIs. Complete the first tutorial first. Keep the training API on port 9010 running.

items.title: 1. Start a second API
items.text:
In another terminal:

python3 examples/tutorial-api/server.py --port 9011 --label Staging

These are separate in-memory datasets. An action on port 9010 does not change the counters returned by port 9011.

items.title: 2. Assemble a configuration folder
items.text:
From the repository root:

mkdir -p /tmp/declarack-tutorial-config
cp examples/tutorial-api/declarack.yaml /tmp/declarack-tutorial-config/00-api.yaml
cp examples/tutorial-api/dashboard.yaml /tmp/declarack-tutorial-config/10-dashboard.yaml

If you used this folder in an earlier session, inspect its other YAML files first: all visible YAML fragments participate in the merge. Stop only the tutorial Declarack process on port 9081, then restart it with the folder:

DECLARACK_CONFIG=/tmp/declarack-tutorial-config \
DECLARACK_CONFIG_FORCE_LOAD=1 \
DECLARACK_CONFIG_EDIT=1 \
DECLARACK_DATA=/tmp/declarack-tutorial-data \
DECLARACK_PASSWORD='choose-a-local-tutorial-password' \
PORT=9081 .venv/bin/python -m backend.server

The new fragment adds staging and reuses the existing tutorial.apps feature. Its environment target list replaces the original one with [training, staging]. The complete fragment is ready to inspect.

items.title: 3. Open Application overview
items.text:
The custom page is available at the workspace level and through the Tutorial environment. It should show six applications in total and, for each target, two running applications out of three.

Expected result: both sources Loaded, six applications overall, and Running = 2 / Total = 3 for each target. Restart counters may differ if you ran earlier actions. Select the image to open it at full size.

Its source definitions name the target and read operation explicitly:

sources:
  training: {target: training, operation: tutorial.apps.list}
  staging: {target: staging, operation: tutorial.apps.list}

Each source result becomes data.<source-name>. Sources also expose loading, availability and collection state under sources.

items.title: 4. Read the chart mapping
items.text:
The chart first creates category rows from both API responses, then maps values from each category into series:

type: bar
sources: [training, staging]
rows: >-
  [{"target":"Training","running":$count(data.training.items[status="running"]),"total":$count(data.training.items)},
   {"target":"Staging","running":$count(data.staging.items[status="running"]),"total":$count(data.staging.items)}]
x: target
series:
  - {label: Running, value: running}
  - {label: Total, value: total}

Use this pattern for Docker, SSH or another HTTP source; the renderer does not know what an application or target count means. Line charts require ordered numeric samples supplied by a source. Declarack does not accumulate chart history itself.

The two table panels link to their corresponding target's detail pages and support search, sorting, page-size selection and CSV/JSON export.

items.title: 5. Observe a partial failure
items.text:
Stop only the Staging API with Ctrl+C, then refresh the custom page. Staging should be unavailable. The combined card/chart cannot claim a complete result; the Training panel can still show its own successfully collected source. Missing data is not a healthy empty list or a zero count.

The failed source is explicitly Unavailable. The combined card/chart cannot report a total, while the independent Training table still works. Select the image to open it at full size.

Restart Staging with the same command and refresh again. Turn on browser auto-refresh if useful, then turn it off when finished. It does not run while the page is closed, and it does not collect manual/on-demand sources automatically.

Next: schedule a readiness check, or see the custom page reference for layout and environment placement.
